sources.title: OpenAI tightens controls on its new model over cybersecurity risks, as AI security debate intensifies - CNBC
passages: OpenAI has halted some "internal activities" involving a new model amid fears over the cyber threat it potentially poses, amid a wave of security incidents involving major AI labs.
U.S. lawmakers, meanwhile, are stepping up efforts to introduce an "AI Kill Switch" bill.

"While we continue to benchmark and assess this model, our preliminary evaluations indicate strong enough performance that we cannot rule out Critical capability level at this time," OpenAI said in a statement.
"We have implemented universal monitoring for risky actions and misalignment across all agentic applications of Astra, including training and evaluation," OpenAI said.
It would require AI companies to maintain the ability to shut down, throttle or suspend their models.
"We need to get this bill across the finish line this year because the advanced closed-weight models are already doing, as you noted, unauthorized hacks of other companies," Rep.
Ted Lieu, D-Calif, said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Thursday.
The company added it was implementing stricter security controls for higher capability models, including isolated testing environments and additional monitoring and detection capabilities.
Lawmakers in the U.S. have called for measures to mitigate risks around AI models after the recent security incidents.

extraction.body: OpenAI has halted some "internal activities" involving a new model amid fears over the cyber threat it potentially poses, amid a wave of security incidents involving major AI labs. Recent disclosures that AI systems from Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta were involved in security incidents prompted a wave of concerns over the development of models. U.S. lawmakers, meanwhile, are stepping up efforts to introduce an "AI Kill Switch" bill. Last week, Meta disclosed that an AI model it was developing had hacked a third-party system by accessing the internet, due to a misconfiguration by an independent testing company it was working with. The U.K. AI Security Institute also said Anthropic's Mythos model created fake online identities in an attempt to pressure humans into approving malicious code updates to an open-source project. On Friday, OpenAI revealed concerns about its unreleased model Astra, saying it could not rule out it had reached "Critical" capability, meaning it could launch cyberattacks against sophisticated cyber defenses autonomously, without prompts specifying how to do it. "While we continue to benchmark and assess this model, our preliminary evaluations indicate strong enough performance that we cannot rule out Critical capability level at this time," OpenAI said in a statement. The company added it was implementing stricter security controls for higher capability models, including isolated testing environments and additional monitoring and detection capabilities. "We have implemented universal monitoring for risky actions and misalignment across all agentic applications of Astra, including training and evaluation," OpenAI said. Lawmakers in the U.S. have called for measures to mitigate risks around AI models after the recent security incidents. Following models developed by OpenAI hacking into startup Hugging Face's digital infrastructure, the "AI Kill Switch Act" bill was introduced into Congress in July. It would require AI companies to maintain the ability to shut down, throttle or suspend their models. "We need to get this bill across the finish line this year because the advanced closed-weight models are already doing, as you noted, unauthorized hacks of other companies," Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif, said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Thursday. Governments are also working to roll out new frameworks and regulations around AI companies. The White House has also been stepping up moves to engage with AI executives as it develops a framework around new models. Earlier this month, the European Union gained new powers to inspect AI models due for release in the bloc, restrict EU market access and fine model providers. Got a confidential news tip? sources.title: In the Wake of Anthropic’s Mythos, OpenAI Has a New Cybersecurity Model—and Strategy
passages: The news comes in the wake of an announcement last week by competitor Anthropic that its new Claude Mythos Preview model is only being privately released for now—because, the company says, it could be exploited by hackers and bad actors.

OpenAI says that the initiative fits into its broader security efforts, including an application security AI agent launched last month known as Codex Security, a cybersecurity grants program that began in 2023, a recent donation to the Linux Foundation to support open source security, and the “Preparedness Framework” that is meant to assess and defend against “severe harm from frontier AI capabilities.” Anthropic's claims last week that more capable AI models necessitate a cybersecurity reckoning have been controversial among security experts.
Anthropic also announced an industry coalition, including competitors like Google, focused on how advances in generative AI across the field will impact cybersecurity.

extraction.body: The news comes in the wake of an announcement last week by competitor Anthropic that its new Claude Mythos Preview model is only being privately released for now—because, the company says, it could be exploited by hackers and bad actors. Anthropic also announced an industry coalition, including competitors like Google, focused on how advances in generative AI across the field will impact cybersecurity. OpenAI seemed to be seeking to differentiate its message on Tuesday by striking a less catastrophic tone and touting its existing guardrails and defenses while hinting at the need for more advanced protections in the long term. “We believe the class of safeguards in use today sufficiently reduce cyber risk enough to support broad deployment of current models,” the company wrote in a blog post. “We expect versions of these safeguards to be sufficient for upcoming more powerful models, while models explicitly trained and made more permissive for cybersecurity work require more restrictive deployments and appropriate controls. Over the long term, to ensure the ongoing sufficiency of AI safety in cybersecurity, we also expect the need for more expansive defenses for future models, whose capabilities will rapidly exceed even the best purpose-built models of today.” The company says that it has homed in on three pillars for its cybersecurity approach. The first involves so-called “know your customer” validation systems to allow controlled access to new models that is as broad and “democratized” as possible. “We design mechanisms which avoid arbitrarily deciding who gets access for legitimate use and who doesn’t,” the company wrote on Tuesday. OpenAI is combining a model where it partners with certain organizations on limited releases with an automated system introduced in February, known as Trusted Access for Cyber or TAC. The second component of the strategy involves “iterative deployment,” or a process of “carefully” releasing and then refining new capabilities so the company can get real-world insight and feedback. The blog post particularly highlights “resilience to jailbreaks and other adversarial attacks, and improving defensive capabilities.” Finally, the third focus is on investments that the company says support software security and other digital defense as generative AI proliferates. OpenAI says that the initiative fits into its broader security efforts, including an application security AI agent launched last month known as Codex Security, a cybersecurity grants program that began in 2023, a recent donation to the Linux Foundation to support open source security, and the “Preparedness Framework” that is meant to assess and defend against “severe harm from frontier AI capabilities.” Anthropic's claims last week that more capable AI models necessitate a cybersecurity reckoning have been controversial among security experts. Others, though, emphasize that vulnerabilities and shortcomings in current security defenses are well known and really could be exploited with new speed and intensity by an even broader range of bad actors in the age of agentic AI.

sources.title: OpenAI released a new cybersecurity model. Is that enough?
passages: Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development.
Yesterday, OpenAI said that the same model had been used to scan and prepare patches for vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, finding 948 potential issues.
OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser.
It’s unclear if frontier labs are devoting enough of their resources to this issue.
Still, OpenAI says just “thousands” of cybersecurity professionals are participating in the Daybreak program, versus a far larger number of potential hackers.
OpenAI has insisted that there is a narrow window of time for the people who safeguard digital infrastructure to take action before AI models become even better at hacking and easier to access.
Justicz said that he personally spent about $5,000 on subscriptions and tokens to find several exploits.

Max Justicz, the chief technology officer and co-founder of the startup Charge Robotics, used an OpenAI model to find a severe vulnerability that — if exploited — could allow hackers to take control of servers running Ubuntu, a widely used open source Linux-based operating system.

extraction.body: Max Justicz, the chief technology officer and co-founder of the startup Charge Robotics, used an OpenAI model to find a severe vulnerability that — if exploited — could allow hackers to take control of servers running Ubuntu, a widely used open source Linux-based operating system. Justicz, who has a hobbyist’s interest in cybersecurity and previously found a vulnerability in the same codebase, told TechCrunch that he found this issue using GPT 5.6 Sol, released in July, through the AI maker’s Daybreak Blue, a program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to powerful frontier models. “I literally just aimed ChatGPT at the same body of code and said ‘I found this bug previously that was fixed several years ago, please find bugs as bad or worse,’ and it came back in two hours with this,” Justicz said. “It’s extremely convoluted and hard for a human to find, but it works!” He reported the issue to the Debian Project, which maintains the software in question and issued a patch to fix the vulnerability. There has been no known evidence of exploitation. Still, the ease with which he found it suggests that we’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg when it comes to potential exploits that even novice hackers can utilize with the help of AI models. “I can only imagine what one could do with more time and access to less neutered models. We should expect some extremely crazy bugs to be found and exploited over the next few months,” Justicz wrote in a social media thread discussing his finding. “This might be obvious to most folks here, but there is currently huge alpha in taking some code or binary someone has not audited yet and just aiming a powerful AI model at it.” OpenAI appears to have noticed. Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development. Yesterday, OpenAI said that the same model had been used to scan and prepare patches for vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, finding 948 potential issues. OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser. “Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers,” the frontier lab said in a statement. OpenAI has insisted that there is a narrow window of time for the people who safeguard digital infrastructure to take action before AI models become even better at hacking and easier to access. For cyber defenders, however, it can feel like the frontier labs have unleashed a mountain of new work that outstrips their resources. Justicz said that he personally spent about $5,000 on subscriptions and tokens to find several exploits. Besides Daybreak’s model access, OpenAI has also announced a $1 billion initiative to support cybersecurity professionals in the program who work on critical infrastructure like the electrical grid or water systems. The Daybreak program has its own critiques. Justicz notes that the frontier lab appears to have recently “nerfed” Daybreak Blue to make it less useful at finding vulnerabilities. On one hand, it may be good to limit access from potential bad actors — Justicz said he just uploaded a photo of his driver’s license to join the program. On the other, cybersecurity professionals say they have one hand tied if they can’t use frontier technology while bad actors can deploy open-weight models with abliterated guardrails . Still, OpenAI says just “thousands” of cybersecurity professionals are participating in the Daybreak program, versus a far larger number of potential hackers. It’s unclear if frontier labs are devoting enough of their resources to this issue. Eric Wallace, a researcher on OpenAI’s technical staff, said that “we are now allocating a significant amount of our frontier compute towards discovering and patching vulnerabilities in open source codebases, fully pro bono.” But the Linux bug hunt cost $1.2 million, which is significantly less than the approximate $6 million token spend the company invested in finding a potential solution to a famous problem of fluid dynamics. If there is a narrow window of time to patch the digital infrastructure the world depends on, more urgency may be required. Recent disclosures that AI systems from Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta were involved in security incidents prompted a wave of concerns over the development of models. U.S. lawmakers, meanwhile, are stepping up efforts to introduce an "AI Kill Switch" bill. Last week, Meta disclosed that an AI model it was developing had hacked a third-party system by accessing the internet, due to a misconfiguration by an independent testing company it was working with. The U.K. AI Security Institute also said Anthropic's Mythos model created fake online identities in an attempt to pressure humans into approving malicious code updates to an open-source project. On Friday, OpenAI revealed concerns about its unreleased model Astra, saying it could not rule out it had reached "Critical" capability, meaning it could launch cyberattacks against sophisticated cyber defenses autonomously, without prompts specifying how to do it. "While we continue to benchmark and assess this model, our preliminary evaluations indicate strong enough performance that we cannot rule out Critical capability level at this time," OpenAI said in a statement. The company added it was implementing stricter security controls for higher capability models, including isolated testing environments and additional monitoring and detection capabilities. "We have implemented universal monitoring for risky actions and misalignment across all agentic applications of Astra, including training and evaluation," OpenAI said. Lawmakers in the U.S. have called for measures to mitigate risks around AI models after the recent security incidents. Following models developed by OpenAI hacking into startup Hugging Face's digital infrastructure, the "AI Kill Switch Act" bill was introduced into Congress in July. It would require AI companies to maintain the ability to shut down, throttle or suspend their models. "We need to get this bill across the finish line this year because the advanced closed-weight models are already doing, as you noted, unauthorized hacks of other companies," Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif, said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Thursday. Governments are also working to roll out new frameworks and regulations around AI companies. The White House has also been stepping up moves to engage with AI executives as it develops a framework around new models. Anthropic also announced an industry coalition, including competitors like Google, focused on how advances in generative AI across the field will impact cybersecurity. OpenAI seemed to be seeking to differentiate its message on Tuesday by striking a less catastrophic tone and touting its existing guardrails and defenses while hinting at the need for more advanced protections in the long term. “We believe the class of safeguards in use today sufficiently reduce cyber risk enough to support broad deployment of current models,” the company wrote in a blog post. “We expect versions of these safeguards to be sufficient for upcoming more powerful models, while models explicitly trained and made more permissive for cybersecurity work require more restrictive deployments and appropriate controls. Over the long term, to ensure the ongoing sufficiency of AI safety in cybersecurity, we also expect the need for more expansive defenses for future models, whose capabilities will rapidly exceed even the best purpose-built models of today.” The company says that it has homed in on three pillars for its cybersecurity approach. The first involves so-called “know your customer” validation systems to allow controlled access to new models that is as broad and “democratized” as possible. “We design mechanisms which avoid arbitrarily deciding who gets access for legitimate use and who doesn’t,” the company wrote on Tuesday. OpenAI is combining a model where it partners with certain organizations on limited releases with an automated system introduced in February, known as Trusted Access for Cyber or TAC. The second component of the strategy involves “iterative deployment,” or a process of “carefully” releasing and then refining new capabilities so the company can get real-world insight and feedback. The blog post particularly highlights “resilience to jailbreaks and other adversarial attacks, and improving defensive capabilities.” Finally, the third focus is on investments that the company says support software security and other digital defense as generative AI proliferates. OpenAI says that the initiative fits into its broader security efforts, including an application security AI agent launched last month known as Codex Security, a cybersecurity grants program that began in 2023, a recent donation to the Linux Foundation to support open source security, and the “Preparedness Framework” that is meant to assess and defend against “severe harm from frontier AI capabilities.” Anthropic's claims last week that more capable AI models necessitate a cybersecurity reckoning have been controversial among security experts. Others, though, emphasize that vulnerabilities and shortcomings in current security defenses are well known and really could be exploited with new speed and intensity by an even broader range of bad actors in the age of agentic AI.

extraction.body: Max Justicz, the chief technology officer and co-founder of the startup Charge Robotics, used an OpenAI model to find a severe vulnerability that — if exploited — could allow hackers to take control of servers running Ubuntu, a widely used open source Linux-based operating system. Justicz, who has a hobbyist’s interest in cybersecurity and previously found a vulnerability in the same codebase, told TechCrunch that he found this issue using GPT 5.6 Sol, released in July, through the AI maker’s Daybreak Blue, a program that gives cybersecurity defenders access to powerful frontier models. “I literally just aimed ChatGPT at the same body of code and said ‘I found this bug previously that was fixed several years ago, please find bugs as bad or worse,’ and it came back in two hours with this,” Justicz said. “It’s extremely convoluted and hard for a human to find, but it works!” He reported the issue to the Debian Project, which maintains the software in question and issued a patch to fix the vulnerability. There has been no known evidence of exploitation. Still, the ease with which he found it suggests that we’ve only seen the tip of the iceberg when it comes to potential exploits that even novice hackers can utilize with the help of AI models. “I can only imagine what one could do with more time and access to less neutered models. We should expect some extremely crazy bugs to be found and exploited over the next few months,” Justicz wrote in a social media thread discussing his finding. “This might be obvious to most folks here, but there is currently huge alpha in taking some code or binary someone has not audited yet and just aiming a powerful AI model at it.” OpenAI appears to have noticed. Today, the AI giant announced a new model focused on cybersecurity, ChatGPT Cyber, would be made available to the highest tier of users in the cybersecurity program, Daybreak Red, which allows offensive cybersecurity researchers tools for vulnerability hunting and development. Yesterday, OpenAI said that the same model had been used to scan and prepare patches for vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, finding 948 potential issues. OpenAI also found 81 “novel” vulnerabilities in Firefox, the web browser. “Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers,” the frontier lab said in a statement. OpenAI has insisted that there is a narrow window of time for the people who safeguard digital infrastructure to take action before AI models become even better at hacking and easier to access. For cyber defenders, however, it can feel like the frontier labs have unleashed a mountain of new work that outstrips their resources. Justicz said that he personally spent about $5,000 on subscriptions and tokens to find several exploits. Besides Daybreak’s model access, OpenAI has also announced a $1 billion initiative to support cybersecurity professionals in the program who work on critical infrastructure like the electrical grid or water systems. The Daybreak program has its own critiques. Justicz notes that the frontier lab appears to have recently “nerfed” Daybreak Blue to make it less useful at finding vulnerabilities. On one hand, it may be good to limit access from potential bad actors — Justicz said he just uploaded a photo of his driver’s license to join the program. On the other, cybersecurity professionals say they have one hand tied if they can’t use frontier technology while bad actors can deploy open-weight models with abliterated guardrails . Still, OpenAI says just “thousands” of cybersecurity professionals are participating in the Daybreak program, versus a far larger number of potential hackers. It’s unclear if frontier labs are devoting enough of their resources to this issue. Eric Wallace, a researcher on OpenAI’s technical staff, said that “we are now allocating a significant amount of our frontier compute towards discovering and patching vulnerabilities in open source codebases, fully pro bono.” But the Linux bug hunt cost $1.2 million, which is significantly less than the approximate $6 million token spend the company invested in finding a potential solution to a famous problem of fluid dynamics. If there is a narrow window of time to patch the digital infrastructure the world depends on, more urgency may be required. sources.title: Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too
passages: Meta will let you tweak the way your Muse avatar sounds — you can already customize the way it looks — and a new Muse Realtime Avatar model will inform how it moves.
Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.
Muse launched earlier this month, and it’s seemingly proving to be a hit, topping the App Store charts and reportedly being downloaded more than ChatGPT on mobile in its first 12 days.
Muse agents are getting their own email addresses that they can use for accomplishing tasks.
You’ll also be able to communicate with your Muse agent over the new email addresses, too.
Meta appears to be capitalizing on the popularity by quickly introducing the new videocalling features, but that’s not all that’s new for the agent.

sources.title: Meta says US users can now video chat with their Muse AI avatar
passages: The added support for video chats and calls comes just before Meta’s plan to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for its Muse AI agent before year-end.
When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them.
Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character.

As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.)
Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device.
The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action.
His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!)

extraction.body: Muse Voice, a feature that lets users call and video chat with Meta’s consumer AI agent, Muse, is now available to everyone in the U.S., the company announced on Thursday. First introduced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September, the video-chatting feature involves new AI models, Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technology, which help power the digital avatar that chats with the user. While other AI competitors offer voice chat features, Meta’s Muse offers a cute, animated avatar (nicknamed Jolly), which users interact with as they ask questions or request tasks to be handled on their behalf. Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character. The company believes that anthropomorphizing Muse in this way could make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent — a connection that could grow even stronger as they begin to engage in live conversations with it. As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.) The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action. The video saw Wang joking around, referencing his love of posting memes on X, which he told his Muse may have gotten him in trouble with his boss. His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!) CTO Andrew Bosworth called the device an exploration and said it isn't the core of Meta's AI hardware strategy.

coreStoryFacts.text: Meta will let you tweak the way your Muse avatar sounds — you can already customize the way it looks — and a new Muse Realtime Avatar model will inform how it moves.
Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.
Muse launched earlier this month, and it’s seemingly proving to be a hit, topping the App Store charts and reportedly being downloaded more than ChatGPT on mobile in its first 12 days.
Muse agents are getting their own email addresses that they can use for accomplishing tasks.
You’ll also be able to communicate with your Muse agent over the new email addresses, too.
Meta appears to be capitalizing on the popularity by quickly introducing the new videocalling features, but that’s not all that’s new for the agent.
The added support for video chats and calls comes just before Meta’s plan to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for its Muse AI agent before year-end.
When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them.
Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character.

As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.)
Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device.
The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action.
His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!)
Meta said it has made the Muse Voice feature available to all users in the United States, allowing them to make calls and communicate in video chats with its Muse AI agent.
During the conversation, the agent is represented by an animated digital avatar that users can customize as they wish.
Meta first unveiled the video communication feature at its Connect developer conference in September.
The company uses Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technologies for it.
Meta's director of artificial intelligence, Alexandr Wang, also showed a demonstration of Muse in X.
In the video, he spoke with an avatar in the form of a fluffy white dog and joked about posting memes on the social network.
By the end of the year, the company also plans to release a wearable device for Muse, which TechCrunch compares to a Tamagotchi.
According to Meta, users can choose the avatar's appearance: it can resemble a human, an animal, or another character.
Meta later plans to add this capability to its AI Glasses and the future Muse Charm device.

First introduced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September, the video-chatting feature involves new AI models, Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technology, which help power the digital avatar that chats with the user. While other AI competitors offer voice chat features, Meta’s Muse offers a cute, animated avatar (nicknamed Jolly), which users interact with as they ask questions or request tasks to be handled on their behalf. Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character. The company believes that anthropomorphizing Muse in this way could make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent — a connection that could grow even stronger as they begin to engage in live conversations with it. His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!) His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!)

extraction.body: The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is moving forward with plans to overhaul custody rules for investment advisers and investment companies, potentially giving institutions greater clarity on how they can hold crypto assets for clients while complying with federal securities rules. The proposed rule was sent on Aug. 25 to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), part of the White House Office of Management and Budget, for review before it can move back to the SEC and potentially be released for public comment. SEC submits “Amendments to the Custody Rules” to OIRA. Source: Reginfo.gov According to the SEC’s regulatory agenda, the agency is considering changing existing rules or introducing new ones under the Investment Advisers Act and Investment Company Act. The changes would cover how investment advisers and funds hold client assets, including crypto. The regulator said the changes are intended to clear up uncertainty around how companies can hold crypto for clients while staying within its rules. The proposal has not yet been made public, and the White House Office of Management and Budget can request changes before sending it back to the SEC. The commission would then vote on whether to release it for public comment. As Bloomberg reported, the proposed rule is part of the agency’s broader push to advance the Trump administration’s digital asset agenda as the CLARITY market structure bill remains stalled in the Senate. The bill is expected to face a cloture vote after lawmakers return from the August recess in September. SEC shifts from crypto enforcement to rulemaking The SEC has taken a more crypto-friendly approach since Paul Atkins became chair in 2025, shifting its focus from enforcement actions toward developing clearer rules for the industry. Atkins vowed to end the agency’s previous “regulation through enforcement” approach and said policymaking should instead be carried out through formal rulemaking. The shift has also been reflected in enforcement. The SEC dismissed several cases against major crypto companies in 2025, including its lawsuit against Coinbase, as it moved to reshape its approach to digital assets. extraction.body: HIGHLIGHTS The White House is reviewing SEC proposals covering financial requirements for broker-dealers handling crypto assets. The SEC plans amendments to capital, customer protection, recordkeeping, and reporting rules for crypto brokers. The SEC's proposed crypto broker rule changes remain under White House review The White House has begun reviewing an SEC proposal covering financial rules for crypto broker-dealers. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) received the filing as OIRA lists the proposal under regulatory identifier 3235-AN48. SEC Proposal Covers Broker Capital And Customer Protection The SEC's regulatory agenda includes Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3. Rule 15c3-1 sets net capital requirements for broker-dealers, while Rule 15c3-3 governs how firms protect customer assets. In the meantime, the SEC is proposing to amend Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, which regulate the business records and retention of the business records. The agency's agenda outlines updates to the requirements as they relate to cryptocurrencies. An SEC spokesperson told Bloomberg the commission expects to consider "fit-for-purpose rules" for crypto markets. A previous report described the SEC's proposals for these broker-dealer rules, along with separate proposals for crypto. The proposals are each assigned an identifier in the agenda for crypto offerings and exchange trading rules. White House Review Remains Pending Without A Deadline According to OIRA, the submission is economically important and is in the proposed-rule stage. The designation includes regulatory activities that have been identified by the federal rules of review to have an anticipated economic impact. However, OIRA's record lists no legal deadline for finishing the White House review. The government has not provided the full text of the proposal, nor has it announced a date for its publication. Accordingly, no documents exist that would show a reduction in any specific capital or recordkeeping requirements. While the draft is being reviewed, the filing does not alter existing requirements for broker-dealers. Registered Broker-Dealers Expand Tokenized Stock Trading Early this month, Securitize expanded its tokenized stock offering to 25 equities. The trading service is done through an SEC-registered broker dealer, Securitize Markets, for US customers. Securitize had announced its set of 12 stocks, and to this list it has now added 13 stocks, including Disney, Salesforce and ExxonMobil. The company says trading can extend beyond regular market hours, while it continues working toward round-the-clock access. Securitize Markets conducts this trading under existing US securities laws, the company said.

extraction.body: The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is moving forward with plans to overhaul custody rules for investment advisers and investment companies, potentially giving institutions greater clarity on how they can hold crypto assets for clients while complying with federal securities rules. The proposed rule was sent on Aug. 25 to the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), part of the White House Office of Management and Budget, for review before it can move back to the SEC and potentially be released for public comment. SEC submits “Amendments to the Custody Rules” to OIRA. Source: Reginfo.gov According to the SEC’s regulatory agenda, the agency is considering changing existing rules or introducing new ones under the Investment Advisers Act and Investment Company Act. The changes would cover how investment advisers and funds hold client assets, including crypto. The regulator said the changes are intended to clear up uncertainty around how companies can hold crypto for clients while staying within its rules. The proposal has not yet been made public, and the White House Office of Management and Budget can request changes before sending it back to the SEC. The commission would then vote on whether to release it for public comment. As Bloomberg reported, the proposed rule is part of the agency’s broader push to advance the Trump administration’s digital asset agenda as the CLARITY market structure bill remains stalled in the Senate. The bill is expected to face a cloture vote after lawmakers return from the August recess in September. SEC shifts from crypto enforcement to rulemaking The SEC has taken a more crypto-friendly approach since Paul Atkins became chair in 2025, shifting its focus from enforcement actions toward developing clearer rules for the industry. Atkins vowed to end the agency’s previous “regulation through enforcement” approach and said policymaking should instead be carried out through formal rulemaking. The shift has also been reflected in enforcement. The SEC dismissed several cases against major crypto companies in 2025, including its lawsuit against Coinbase, as it moved to reshape its approach to digital assets. extraction.body: HIGHLIGHTS The White House is reviewing SEC proposals covering financial requirements for broker-dealers handling crypto assets. The SEC plans amendments to capital, customer protection, recordkeeping, and reporting rules for crypto brokers. The SEC's proposed crypto broker rule changes remain under White House review The White House has begun reviewing an SEC proposal covering financial rules for crypto broker-dealers. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) received the filing as OIRA lists the proposal under regulatory identifier 3235-AN48. SEC Proposal Covers Broker Capital And Customer Protection The SEC's regulatory agenda includes Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3. Rule 15c3-1 sets net capital requirements for broker-dealers, while Rule 15c3-3 governs how firms protect customer assets. In the meantime, the SEC is proposing to amend Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, which regulate the business records and retention of the business records. The agency's agenda outlines updates to the requirements as they relate to cryptocurrencies. An SEC spokesperson told Bloomberg the commission expects to consider "fit-for-purpose rules" for crypto markets. A previous report described the SEC's proposals for these broker-dealer rules, along with separate proposals for crypto. The proposals are each assigned an identifier in the agenda for crypto offerings and exchange trading rules. White House Review Remains Pending Without A Deadline According to OIRA, the submission is economically important and is in the proposed-rule stage. The designation includes regulatory activities that have been identified by the federal rules of review to have an anticipated economic impact. However, OIRA's record lists no legal deadline for finishing the White House review. The government has not provided the full text of the proposal, nor has it announced a date for its publication. Accordingly, no documents exist that would show a reduction in any specific capital or recordkeeping requirements. While the draft is being reviewed, the filing does not alter existing requirements for broker-dealers. Registered Broker-Dealers Expand Tokenized Stock Trading Early this month, Securitize expanded its tokenized stock offering to 25 equities. The trading service is done through an SEC-registered broker dealer, Securitize Markets, for US customers. Securitize had announced its set of 12 stocks, and to this list it has now added 13 stocks, including Disney, Salesforce and ExxonMobil. The company says trading can extend beyond regular market hours, while it continues working toward round-the-clock access. Securitize Markets conducts this trading under existing US securities laws, the company said.

extraction.body: Nothing CEO Carl Pei said in a post on X that the company’s launching its first AI device in December. That’s just a little over a year after Pei announced plans for “AI-native” devices and an AI operating system. He didn’t give away much about what exactly the new device is, only that one feature it won’t have is a screen: > “Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.” Pei shared an image with the post that says “NOTHING(R)” in the top left corner, above an ambiguous black rounded corner. passages: Nothing is set to launch its first AI-native product in December 2026, CEO Carl Pei announced in a post on X on November 4.
For Nothing, the December launch will be its first step towards translating this approach into a dedicated hardware product.
Nothing had previously outlined plans to develop AI-native devices alongside an operating system designed around AI.

Carl Pei says AI’s next big opportunity lies in productivity Pei believes the industry is currently focusing too much on finding a single device that could become the equivalent of the iPhone for artificial intelligence.
The upcoming product will be a screen-free device designed to make artificial intelligence more useful in everyday workflows.
It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.
However, Pei’s accompanying post, titled ‘Toolmakers’, provides some insight into the thinking behind the product and Nothing’s broader AI strategy.
The announcement comes as Nothing looks to expand beyond smartphones and audio products into AI-powered hardware.

extraction.body: Nothing is set to launch its first AI-native product in December 2026, CEO Carl Pei announced in a post on X on November 4. The upcoming product will be a screen-free device designed to make artificial intelligence more useful in everyday workflows. Pei said the product is being built as a dedicated tool rather than an application, although he did not reveal its name, design, pricing or specific features. “Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app,” Pei wrote. The announcement comes as Nothing looks to expand beyond smartphones and audio products into AI-powered hardware. The company has been discussing its plans to build AI-native devices and an operating system designed around artificial intelligence. The teaser offers little information about the device’s form factor. However, Pei’s accompanying post, titled ‘Toolmakers’, provides some insight into the thinking behind the product and Nothing’s broader AI strategy. Carl Pei says AI’s next big opportunity lies in productivity Pei believes the industry is currently focusing too much on finding a single device that could become the equivalent of the iPhone for artificial intelligence. “The whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life. According to Pei, the adoption of AI will follow a trajectory similar to that of personal computers and smartphones, where workplace applications helped drive initial adoption before the technology became part of everyday consumer life. He argued that personal computers first became useful through tools such as spreadsheets and word processors, while smartphones gained traction through practical applications before becoming central to entertainment and communication. “Product-market fit for AI will come in productivity first, in the tools people rely on to get real things done, and that’s where the real opportunity is today,” Pei wrote. While AI models have become increasingly capable, they often lack access to the information and context needed to perform tasks effectively. He said that even when users connect their inboxes, calendars and messaging platforms to AI agents, important information from everyday interactions can still be missed. “Think about the last time someone said something worth keeping: an idea over coffee, a throwaway comment that unblocks your whole week. Close it, and everything AI can already do gets dramatically more useful.” Pei believes the next generation of AI tools will need to move beyond chat interfaces and become more proactive. Tomorrow, it will work for you,” he said, arguing that AI could eventually change how individuals collaborate with each other, how organisations interact with people and how humans work alongside intelligent agents. For Nothing, the December launch will be its first step towards translating this approach into a dedicated hardware product. The company has not yet disclosed whether the device will be a wearable, an audio product or another category of hardware. Nothing had previously outlined plans to develop AI-native devices alongside an operating system designed around AI. The upcoming product will be its first concrete offering under that strategy. The launch also comes amid growing interest in dedicated AI hardware. Products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend AI pendant have attempted to bring AI assistants beyond smartphones, while other technology companies are exploring smart glasses and voice-enabled devices. However, Pei cautioned against expecting one device to immediately transform the AI industry. “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end,” he wrote. Nothing is expected to share more details about its first AI-native product ahead of its December launch.

He argued that personal computers first became useful through tools such as spreadsheets and word processors, while smartphones gained traction through practical applications before becoming central to entertainment and communication. “Product-market fit for AI will come in productivity first, in the tools people rely on to get real things done, and that’s where the real opportunity is today,” Pei wrote. While AI models have become increasingly capable, they often lack access to the information and context needed to perform tasks effectively. He said that even when users connect their inboxes, calendars and messaging platforms to AI agents, important information from everyday interactions can still be missed. “Think about the last time someone said something worth keeping: an idea over coffee, a throwaway comment that unblocks your whole week. Close it, and everything AI can already do gets dramatically more useful.” Pei believes the next generation of AI tools will need to move beyond chat interfaces and become more proactive. Tomorrow, it will work for you,” he said, arguing that AI could eventually change how individuals collaborate with each other, how organisations interact with people and how humans work alongside intelligent agents. Products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend AI pendant have attempted to bring AI assistants beyond smartphones, while other technology companies are exploring smart glasses and voice-enabled devices. However, Pei cautioned against expecting one device to immediately transform the AI industry. “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end,” he wrote. Products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend AI pendant have attempted to bring AI assistants beyond smartphones, while other technology companies are exploring smart glasses and voice-enabled devices.

“Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end,” he wrote.

sources.title: Harbinger raises $240M after expanding into defense
passages: Electric truck startup Harbinger has raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications.
FedEx invested again after leading last year’s round, and other repeat investors included Maniv, Greycroft, and Leitmotif, a VC firm backed by Volkswagen .
Also investing this time was institutional giant Fidelity Management, which tends to invest in pre-IPO startups. (Harbinger is reportedly weighing going public.)
Founded in 2022 by former employees of now-defunct EV startup Canoo and battery company QuantumScape, Harbinger started by focusing on making one electric truck chassis.
The company has steadily expanded its efforts since.
It bought autonomy startup Phantom AI , has begun developing hybrid emergency vehicles , and revealed a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military.
While it didn’t lead this round, FedEx’s relationship with Harbinger continues to deepen.
The shipping giant’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, Paul Melander, has joined Harbinger’s board of directors.
FedEx also recently placed its first large order with Harbinger — a deal for 2,000 trucks valued at more than $300 million.
Harbinger has now raised more than $650 million to date, according to Bloomberg News, which first reported the round.

sources.title: Harbinger raises $240M to expand EV platform beyond trucks - FreightWaves
passages: Harbinger raised $240 million in Series D funding to push its electric vehicle platform into energy storage, power generation, autonomy, and defense while it ramps production for a 2,000-truck order from FedEx .
Tiger Global, Capricorn’s Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline co-led the round, the Garden Grove, California, company said Thursday.
The Series D follows a $160 million Series C last November , when FedEx placed an initial order for 53 trucks.
Harbinger said it has raised more than $650 million since its 2021 founding.

Zero-emission trucks reached a record 4.14% of U.S. truck deployments in the second half of 2025, according to CALSTART’s June 2026 Zeroing in on Zero-Emission Trucks market update , as total truck sales fell 35% year over year.
Cargo vans supplied 12,158 of the 12,996 new units.
Every other segment, including medium-duty step vans and trucks, added 838.
Harbinger’s Class 4 through Class 6 trucks fall in that group.
The release describes Harbinger as “an American industrial technology platform company” and lists commercial vehicles as one of five markets the new funding covers.
Harris told Bloomberg News in September that Harbinger had recently finished its 1,000th vehicle.
The FedEx order alone calls for twice that many trucks by the end of 2027.
Harbinger said the new money will fund the continued ramp of its medium-duty manufacturing capacity alongside the newer businesses.

Its HC Series Cab, unveiled in March , adds a gasoline range extender good for up to 500 miles, depending on configuration, and up to 15 kilowatts of exportable power, so crews don’t need a separate generator.
The company also acquired autonomy software maker Phantom AI.
Harbinger’s first defense deal came this summer: it is building the platform for an uncrewed Army supply vehicle under an American Rheinmetall contract .
It has also started selling its batteries for energy storage, Bloomberg News reported .
The Army program is in a prototype phase that typically runs three to 10 units, and no contract value has been disclosed.

“Electrification is at the core of everything we do, and increasingly, electrification is at the core of industry, defense, mobility, and AI,” said John Harris, Harbinger’s co-founder and CEO, in the release.
Fidelity Management & Research Company, Squarepoint Capital, and Xantium joined as crossover investors, and Maniv and Greycroft returned.

In an interview with Bloomberg News, Harris said the company has focused on bringing in investors that are “generally crossover or public markets focused.” FedEx and THOR Industries came in as strategic investors through TechNexus, the release said.
Paul Melander, FedEx’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, recently joined Harbinger’s board.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley served as placement agents.
“Harbinger excels at electrification, and electrification has become one of the most pressing bottlenecks of the AI era,” said Griffin Schroeder, a partner at Tiger Global.
“Harbinger’s role is not simply to give customers another option,” Harris said.
“It is to reset expectations for what critical systems should deliver.”

extraction.body: Harbinger just closed a $240 million funding round that pushes the Los Angeles-based autonomous vehicle startup past $650 million in total capital raised. The fresh cash comes as the company shifts gears from commercial electric trucks into military and defense applications, betting that Pentagon contracts will provide the revenue stability that has eluded many autonomous vehicle startups. It's a strategic pivot that mirrors OpenAI's recent defense push and signals where smart money sees the autonomous vehicle market headed. Harbinger is making a calculated bet that the path to profitability in autonomous vehicles runs through the Pentagon, not consumer driveways. The Los Angeles-based startup's $240 million raise announced today brings its total funding north of $650 million and validates a strategic shift that began quietly earlier this year when the company started developing driverless platforms specifically for military applications. Defense contractors and tech startups alike are racing to capture what industry insiders estimate could be a $50 billion market for autonomous military vehicles over the next decade. Harbinger's pivot puts it in direct competition with established players like Oshkosh Defense and emerging startups that have already secured initial Pentagon contracts. What sets Harbinger apart is its three-pronged approach. The company continues developing commercial electric trucks for fleet operators, builds specialized emergency vehicles for first responders, and now engineers autonomous platforms designed to operate in combat zones without human drivers. That diversification strategy addresses the revenue problem that has plagued pure-play autonomous vehicle startups, many of which have burned through billions chasing a consumer market that remains years away from meaningful adoption. The defense angle isn't just about new revenue streams. Military contracts typically come with longer development timelines, more patient capital expectations, and customers willing to pay premium prices for cutting-edge technology. Harbinger's approach mirrors moves across the broader tech industry. OpenAI recently hired a former Army Secretary to lead its national security efforts, while Salesforce dropped $375 million on defense AI startup Rune just weeks ago. The message is clear: government contracts, particularly in defense, offer the kind of stable, high-margin revenue that can sustain expensive R&D programs. The $240 million round itself signals strong investor confidence in this strategy. While the company hasn't disclosed the round's lead investor or valuation, the size suggests participation from both traditional venture capital firms and potentially defense-focused investment vehicles. That mix of backers could prove crucial as Harbinger navigates the complex world of military procurement, where relationships and security clearances matter as much as technology. Military contracts require navigating byzantine procurement processes, maintaining strict security protocols, and accepting that sales cycles can stretch for years. The company will need to balance the demands of commercial customers expecting rapid iteration with military clients requiring exhaustive testing and certification. Managing that dual-track development could strain resources, even with $650 million in the bank. The autonomous vehicle market has become a graveyard for overhyped startups. Companies that once commanded multi-billion dollar valuations have scaled back ambitions, merged with competitors, or shut down entirely. Harbinger's bet is that military applications will provide the proving ground and revenue base needed to perfect the technology before commercial markets fully materialize. That strategy is already attracting attention from other startups watching funding dry up in traditional autonomous vehicle categories. The shift toward defense applications could accelerate as more companies realize that Pentagon budgets offer a lifeline while consumer adoption remains sluggish. It's reminiscent of how fusion startups have increasingly traded equity for federal funding as private capital becomes more selective. Harbinger's emergency vehicle platform represents another smart hedge. Autonomous fire trucks or ambulances that can navigate through traffic more efficiently could save lives while generating revenue and real-world data to improve the underlying technology. The company's $650 million war chest positions it to weather the current funding environment, where rising bond yields have made AI infrastructure buildouts more expensive and investors have grown skeptical of long development timelines. But money alone won't guarantee success in the defense sector, where winning contracts requires demonstrating not just technical capability but also reliability, security, and the ability to scale production. What happens next will test whether Harbinger's multi-market strategy can deliver where pure-play approaches have struggled. The company needs to start converting its technology into actual military contracts while keeping commercial customers engaged and emergency vehicle programs on track. Harbinger's $240 million raise and defense expansion represent more than just another funding round in the autonomous vehicle space. It's a signal that the industry's most promising path forward may run through military bases rather than suburban garages. Whether that bet pays off depends on the company's ability to navigate defense procurement while maintaining momentum in commercial markets.

coreStoryFacts.text: Electric truck startup Harbinger has raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications.
FedEx invested again after leading last year’s round, and other repeat investors included Maniv, Greycroft, and Leitmotif, a VC firm backed by Volkswagen .
Also investing this time was institutional giant Fidelity Management, which tends to invest in pre-IPO startups. (Harbinger is reportedly weighing going public.)
Founded in 2022 by former employees of now-defunct EV startup Canoo and battery company QuantumScape, Harbinger started by focusing on making one electric truck chassis.
The company has steadily expanded its efforts since.
It bought autonomy startup Phantom AI , has begun developing hybrid emergency vehicles , and revealed a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military.
While it didn’t lead this round, FedEx’s relationship with Harbinger continues to deepen.
The shipping giant’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, Paul Melander, has joined Harbinger’s board of directors.
FedEx also recently placed its first large order with Harbinger — a deal for 2,000 trucks valued at more than $300 million.
Harbinger has now raised more than $650 million to date, according to Bloomberg News, which first reported the round.

Harbinger raised $240 million in Series D funding to push its electric vehicle platform into energy storage, power generation, autonomy, and defense while it ramps production for a 2,000-truck order from FedEx .
Tiger Global, Capricorn’s Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline co-led the round, the Garden Grove, California, company said Thursday.
The Series D follows a $160 million Series C last November , when FedEx placed an initial order for 53 trucks.
Harbinger said it has raised more than $650 million since its 2021 founding.

Zero-emission trucks reached a record 4.14% of U.S. truck deployments in the second half of 2025, according to CALSTART’s June 2026 Zeroing in on Zero-Emission Trucks market update , as total truck sales fell 35% year over year.
Cargo vans supplied 12,158 of the 12,996 new units.
Every other segment, including medium-duty step vans and trucks, added 838.
Harbinger’s Class 4 through Class 6 trucks fall in that group.
The release describes Harbinger as “an American industrial technology platform company” and lists commercial vehicles as one of five markets the new funding covers.
Harris told Bloomberg News in September that Harbinger had recently finished its 1,000th vehicle.
The FedEx order alone calls for twice that many trucks by the end of 2027.
Harbinger said the new money will fund the continued ramp of its medium-duty manufacturing capacity alongside the newer businesses.

Its HC Series Cab, unveiled in March , adds a gasoline range extender good for up to 500 miles, depending on configuration, and up to 15 kilowatts of exportable power, so crews don’t need a separate generator.
The company also acquired autonomy software maker Phantom AI.

facts.text: Electric truck startup Harbinger has raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications.
FedEx invested again after leading last year’s round, and other repeat investors included Maniv, Greycroft, and Leitmotif, a VC firm backed by Volkswagen .
Also investing this time was institutional giant Fidelity Management, which tends to invest in pre-IPO startups. (Harbinger is reportedly weighing going public.)
Founded in 2022 by former employees of now-defunct EV startup Canoo and battery company QuantumScape, Harbinger started by focusing on making one electric truck chassis.
The company has steadily expanded its efforts since.
It bought autonomy startup Phantom AI , has begun developing hybrid emergency vehicles , and revealed a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military.
While it didn’t lead this round, FedEx’s relationship with Harbinger continues to deepen.
The shipping giant’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, Paul Melander, has joined Harbinger’s board of directors.
FedEx also recently placed its first large order with Harbinger — a deal for 2,000 trucks valued at more than $300 million.
Harbinger has now raised more than $650 million to date, according to Bloomberg News, which first reported the round.

Harbinger raised $240 million in Series D funding to push its electric vehicle platform into energy storage, power generation, autonomy, and defense while it ramps production for a 2,000-truck order from FedEx .
Tiger Global, Capricorn’s Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline co-led the round, the Garden Grove, California, company said Thursday.
The Series D follows a $160 million Series C last November , when FedEx placed an initial order for 53 trucks.
Harbinger said it has raised more than $650 million since its 2021 founding.

Zero-emission trucks reached a record 4.14% of U.S. truck deployments in the second half of 2025, according to CALSTART’s June 2026 Zeroing in on Zero-Emission Trucks market update , as total truck sales fell 35% year over year.
Cargo vans supplied 12,158 of the 12,996 new units.
Every other segment, including medium-duty step vans and trucks, added 838.
Harbinger’s Class 4 through Class 6 trucks fall in that group.
The release describes Harbinger as “an American industrial technology platform company” and lists commercial vehicles as one of five markets the new funding covers.
Harris told Bloomberg News in September that Harbinger had recently finished its 1,000th vehicle.
The FedEx order alone calls for twice that many trucks by the end of 2027.
Harbinger said the new money will fund the continued ramp of its medium-duty manufacturing capacity alongside the newer businesses.

Its HC Series Cab, unveiled in March , adds a gasoline range extender good for up to 500 miles, depending on configuration, and up to 15 kilowatts of exportable power, so crews don’t need a separate generator.
The company also acquired autonomy software maker Phantom AI.
Harbinger’s first defense deal came this summer: it is building the platform for an uncrewed Army supply vehicle under an American Rheinmetall contract .
It has also started selling its batteries for energy storage, Bloomberg News reported .
The Army program is in a prototype phase that typically runs three to 10 units, and no contract value has been disclosed.

“Electrification is at the core of everything we do, and increasingly, electrification is at the core of industry, defense, mobility, and AI,” said John Harris, Harbinger’s co-founder and CEO, in the release.
Fidelity Management & Research Company, Squarepoint Capital, and Xantium joined as crossover investors, and Maniv and Greycroft returned.

In an interview with Bloomberg News, Harris said the company has focused on bringing in investors that are “generally crossover or public markets focused.” FedEx and THOR Industries came in as strategic investors through TechNexus, the release said.
Paul Melander, FedEx’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, recently joined Harbinger’s board.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley served as placement agents.
“Harbinger excels at electrification, and electrification has become one of the most pressing bottlenecks of the AI era,” said Griffin Schroeder, a partner at Tiger Global.
“Harbinger’s role is not simply to give customers another option,” Harris said.
“It is to reset expectations for what critical systems should deliver.”

Its HC Series Cab, unveiled in March , adds a gasoline range extender good for up to 500 miles, depending on configuration, and up to 15 kilowatts of exportable power, so crews don’t need a separate generator. The company also acquired autonomy software maker Phantom AI.

Harbinger’s first defense deal came this summer: it is building the platform for an uncrewed Army supply vehicle under an American Rheinmetall contract . It has also started selling its batteries for energy storage, Bloomberg News reported . The release did not name any energy storage or power generation customers.
The Series D follows a $160 million Series C last November , when FedEx placed an initial order for 53 trucks. Harbinger said it has raised more than $650 million since its 2021 founding.

Fidelity Management & Research Company, Squarepoint Capital, and Xantium joined as crossover investors, and Maniv and Greycroft returned. In an interview with Bloomberg News, Harris said the company has focused on bringing in investors that are “generally crossover or public markets focused.” FedEx and THOR Industries came in as strategic investors through TechNexus, the release said. Paul Melander, FedEx’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, recently joined Harbinger’s board. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley served as placement agents.
BuildGroup, named in the release as a strategic investor in data centers, also took part. Tiger Global tied its investment to the AI buildout.
“Harbinger excels at electrification, and electrification has become one of the most pressing bottlenecks of the AI era,” said Griffin Schroeder, a partner at Tiger Global.

Zero-emission trucks reached a record 4.14% of U.S. truck deployments in the second half of 2025, according to CALSTART’s June 2026 Zeroing in on Zero-Emission Trucks market update , as total truck sales fell 35% year over year. Cargo vans supplied 12,158 of the 12,996 new units. Every other segment, including medium-duty step vans and trucks, added 838. Harbinger’s Class 4 through Class 6 trucks fall in that group.
But challenges remain. Harris told Bloomberg News in September that Harbinger had recently finished its 1,000th vehicle. The FedEx order alone calls for twice that many trucks by the end of 2027.

The release did not disclose Harbinger’s valuation, its current production capacity, or how the new money splits between trucks and the newer businesses. The Army program is in a prototype phase that typically runs three to 10 units, and no contract value has been disclosed.
The company plans to carry the in-house engineering behind its trucks into each new market, the release said.
“Harbinger’s role is not simply to give customers another option,” Harris said. “It is to reset expectations for what critical systems should deliver.”

Why it matters: Fleets pricing medium-duty electric delivery trucks now have a builder backed by Fidelity, Tiger Global, and FedEx itself, with $240 million in fresh capital. Its FedEx deliveries through 2027 will show whether that backing turns into trucks at scale.

extraction.body: Harbinger just closed a $240 million funding round that pushes the Los Angeles-based autonomous vehicle startup past $650 million in total capital raised. The fresh cash comes as the company shifts gears from commercial electric trucks into military and defense applications, betting that Pentagon contracts will provide the revenue stability that has eluded many autonomous vehicle startups. It's a strategic pivot that mirrors OpenAI's recent defense push and signals where smart money sees the autonomous vehicle market headed. Harbinger is making a calculated bet that the path to profitability in autonomous vehicles runs through the Pentagon, not consumer driveways. The Los Angeles-based startup's $240 million raise announced today brings its total funding north of $650 million and validates a strategic shift that began quietly earlier this year when the company started developing driverless platforms specifically for military applications. Defense contractors and tech startups alike are racing to capture what industry insiders estimate could be a $50 billion market for autonomous military vehicles over the next decade. Harbinger's pivot puts it in direct competition with established players like Oshkosh Defense and emerging startups that have already secured initial Pentagon contracts. What sets Harbinger apart is its three-pronged approach. The company continues developing commercial electric trucks for fleet operators, builds specialized emergency vehicles for first responders, and now engineers autonomous platforms designed to operate in combat zones without human drivers. That diversification strategy addresses the revenue problem that has plagued pure-play autonomous vehicle startups, many of which have burned through billions chasing a consumer market that remains years away from meaningful adoption. The defense angle isn't just about new revenue streams. Military contracts typically come with longer development timelines, more patient capital expectations, and customers willing to pay premium prices for cutting-edge technology. Harbinger's approach mirrors moves across the broader tech industry. OpenAI recently hired a former Army Secretary to lead its national security efforts, while Salesforce dropped $375 million on defense AI startup Rune just weeks ago. The message is clear: government contracts, particularly in defense, offer the kind of stable, high-margin revenue that can sustain expensive R&D programs. The $240 million round itself signals strong investor confidence in this strategy. While the company hasn't disclosed the round's lead investor or valuation, the size suggests participation from both traditional venture capital firms and potentially defense-focused investment vehicles. That mix of backers could prove crucial as Harbinger navigates the complex world of military procurement, where relationships and security clearances matter as much as technology. Military contracts require navigating byzantine procurement processes, maintaining strict security protocols, and accepting that sales cycles can stretch for years. The company will need to balance the demands of commercial customers expecting rapid iteration with military clients requiring exhaustive testing and certification. Managing that dual-track development could strain resources, even with $650 million in the bank. The autonomous vehicle market has become a graveyard for overhyped startups. Companies that once commanded multi-billion dollar valuations have scaled back ambitions, merged with competitors, or shut down entirely. Harbinger's bet is that military applications will provide the proving ground and revenue base needed to perfect the technology before commercial markets fully materialize. That strategy is already attracting attention from other startups watching funding dry up in traditional autonomous vehicle categories. The shift toward defense applications could accelerate as more companies realize that Pentagon budgets offer a lifeline while consumer adoption remains sluggish. It's reminiscent of how fusion startups have increasingly traded equity for federal funding as private capital becomes more selective. Harbinger's emergency vehicle platform represents another smart hedge. Autonomous fire trucks or ambulances that can navigate through traffic more efficiently could save lives while generating revenue and real-world data to improve the underlying technology. The company's $650 million war chest positions it to weather the current funding environment, where rising bond yields have made AI infrastructure buildouts more expensive and investors have grown skeptical of long development timelines. But money alone won't guarantee success in the defense sector, where winning contracts requires demonstrating not just technical capability but also reliability, security, and the ability to scale production. What happens next will test whether Harbinger's multi-market strategy can deliver where pure-play approaches have struggled. The company needs to start converting its technology into actual military contracts while keeping commercial customers engaged and emergency vehicle programs on track. Harbinger's $240 million raise and defense expansion represent more than just another funding round in the autonomous vehicle space. It's a signal that the industry's most promising path forward may run through military bases rather than suburban garages. Whether that bet pays off depends on the company's ability to navigate defense procurement while maintaining momentum in commercial markets.

sources.title: Blue Origin launches twin NASA Mars probes in second flight of New Glenn rocket
passages: The next such window opens in 2026.To make Wednesday's New Glenn launch work in 2025, mission planners with Advanced Space LLC came up with an innovative flight plan, one that will take Blue and Gold longer to reach Mars but will enable more flexible trajectories for future missions.The probes were deployed on a trajectory that will carry them a million miles out, well past the moon's orbit, where they will loiter for the next 11 months before heading back toward Earth.Passing within 600 miles of Earth in November 2027, the ESCAPADE probes will make velocity-boosting gravity assist flybys, augmented by onboard propulsion, to finally head for Mars.In all, the twin spacecraft will spend a full year in that initial kidney bean-shaped orbit out past the moon and back, and another 10 months in transit to Mars.

But for a variety of reasons, the Mars satellites mission ultimately ended up on New Glenn's second flight.Mars launch windows typically open every two years when Earth and the red planet reach favorable positions in their orbits to permit direct flights using current rockets.

Much like returning SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, the larger New Glenn booster will be hauled back to Port Canaveral and, depending on its condition, be refurbished and readied for use on an upcoming New Glenn flight.The second stage, meanwhile, pressed ahead, carrying out two firings of its twin engines to reach the planned Earth-escape trajectory.

ET, majestically pushing the booster skyward atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust.The launch came three days late due to stormy weather on Earth and in space, where a powerful solar storm buffeted Earth's atmosphere with a torrent of high-energy radiation that could have caused electrical problems with the rocket or its payloads.The storm had abated by launch time Wednesday, and Blue Origin employees, looking on from viewing sites several miles from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station launch pad, cheered and applauded as the booster climbed skyward, followed moments later by the booming roar of its engines sweeping across the Space Coast.
This time around, the big rocket flew itself to an on-target touchdown, prompting more cheers and applause from Blue Origin workers.
