extraction.body: ET, majestically pushing the booster skyward atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust.The launch came three days late due to stormy weather on Earth and in space, where a powerful solar storm buffeted Earth's atmosphere with a torrent of high-energy radiation that could have caused electrical problems with the rocket or its payloads.The storm had abated by launch time Wednesday, and Blue Origin employees, looking on from viewing sites several miles from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station launch pad, cheered and applauded as the booster climbed skyward, followed moments later by the booming roar of its engines sweeping across the Space Coast. The New Glenn's maiden flight last January successfully boosted a Blue Origin payload into orbit, but the reusable first stage failed in its attempt to reach an offshore landing ship, named after Bezos' mother, Jacklyn. The 188-foot-tall first stage launched Wednesday, nicknamed "Never Tell Me The Odds," featured a variety of upgrades to improve performance. This time around, the big rocket flew itself to an on-target touchdown, prompting more cheers and applause from Blue Origin workers. Much like returning SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, the larger New Glenn booster will be hauled back to Port Canaveral and, depending on its condition, be refurbished and readied for use on an upcoming New Glenn flight.The second stage, meanwhile, pressed ahead, carrying out two firings of its twin engines to reach the planned Earth-escape trajectory. Thirty-three minutes after liftoff, the ESCAPADE satellites were released to fly on their own.The NASA-sponsored payload, managed by the University of California, Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory, is made up of two small, low-budget satellites known as Blue and Gold that make up the heart of the ESCAPADE mission. The acronym stands for Escape, Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers.The probes were built for UC Berkeley by Rocketlab under a NASA program intended to develop lower-cost, fast-track planetary missions.ESCAPADE cost $107.4 million, a bargain compared to the cost of more traditional, more sophisticated planetary spacecraft that can cost hundreds of millions to well over a billion dollars each.The ESCAPADE probes were originally expected to hitch a ride to Mars a few years ago with NASA's Psyche asteroid probe. But for a variety of reasons, the Mars satellites mission ultimately ended up on New Glenn's second flight.Mars launch windows typically open every two years when Earth and the red planet reach favorable positions in their orbits to permit direct flights using current rockets. "We know that atmospheric escape from Mars is a major driver for the evolution of the Martian climate. We know that Mars at least was episodically warm and wet for a couple billion years, but hasn't been so for about 2 billion years or so. And we think atmospheric escape is a major reason for that."Blue and Gold will provide what amounts to a stereo view of those processes."If you only have one spacecraft, you can either measure what the sun is throwing at Mars, the so-called space weather environment upstream of Mars, or you can measure the conditions close to Mars in its upper atmosphere, where the atmosphere is escaping," Lillis said."You can't be in two places at once. We've never had that before, and that's really exciting," Lillis said.

extraction.body: Last week’s explosion of a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket on the pad at Cape Canaveral prompted dire predictions that the company might not be able to launch again until late 2027 at the earliest. CEO Dave Limp, though, said that’s not the case. “Now that we’ve had access to the pad and integration facility, we can share a bit of good news,” he said in an update on X. “We will fly again before the end of this year.” He said the propellant farm, oxygen, liquid hydrogen and liquefied natural gas tanks were all in decent shape. “This is good luck because these are very long lead items. The water tower is also good. The big support tower is damaged, but it can be repaired in place rather than torn down and replaced,” he said. Here's our video of the explosion at Launch Complex 36. It happened about 9 pm ET (0100 UTC) as Blue Origin was beginning a static fire test of its New Glenn rocket. The pad was engulfed in a fireball from a static fire test last Thursday. A New Glenn rocket had been preparing for what would have been the fourth launch of its kind for Jeff Bezos’ rocket company when it burst into a mushroom cloud. The nighttime explosion could be seen as far away as Orlando and measured 2.5 on the Richter scale, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. The rocket and the transporter erector tower that was holding it in place for the test were destroyed while one of the two lightning towers on the pad crumbled to the ground. Limp said the company had already been working on eliminating the need for the transporter-erector in favor of an alternative concept. “We’ll now go directly to that; so we don’t need a new transporter-erector,” he said. He also said rocket parts that had been within a neighboring building fared well. That includes what for now is the lone remaining New Glenn first stage, “Never Tell Me The Odds,” which was flown and recovered on the rocket’s second and third missions. CEO Dave Limp, though, said that’s not the case.
“Now that we’ve had access to the pad and integration facility, we can share a bit of good news,” he said in an update on X. “We will fly again before the end of this year.”
He said the propellant farm, oxygen, liquid hydrogen and liquefied natural gas tanks were all in decent shape.

“This is good luck because these are very long lead items. The water tower is also good. The big support tower is damaged, but it can be repaired in place rather than torn down and replaced,” he said.
Here's our video of the explosion at Launch Complex 36. It happened about 9 pm ET (0100 UTC) as Blue Origin was beginning a static fire test of its New Glenn rocket.

The pad was engulfed in a fireball from a static fire test last Thursday. A New Glenn rocket had been preparing for what would have been the fourth launch of its kind for Jeff Bezos’ rocket company when it burst into a mushroom cloud. The nighttime explosion could be seen as far away as Orlando and measured 2.5 on the Richter scale, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
The rocket and the transporter erector tower that was holding it in place for the test were destroyed while one of the two lightning towers on the pad crumbled to the ground.
Limp said the company had already been working on eliminating the need for the transporter-erector in favor of an alternative concept.
“We’ll now go directly to that; so we don’t need a new transporter-erector,” he said.

He also said rocket parts that had been within a neighboring building fared well. That includes what for now is the lone remaining New Glenn first stage, “Never Tell Me The Odds,” which was flown and recovered on the rocket’s second and third missions.

SpaceX suffered a similar launch pad explosion a decade ago at Canaveral’s Space Launch Complex 40, and was not able to fly again from that pad for another 15 months.
Limp, though, said he expects a much more optimistic timeline.

Before the explosion, Blue Origin had been looking to fly the first of 24 contracted missions for the Amazon Leo satellite constellation. The 48 satellites were not installed on the rocket when it exploded, but those will have to wait.

Earlier this year, Limp stated he hoped New Glenn would launch at least eight times.
New Kennedy Space Center Director Brian Hughes said Tuesday during a Space Florida board meeting that NASA was keen to get Blue Origin back online.
“We certainly will do everything in our power at NASA and working with our friends at Space Force to be there as partners to make that happen,” he said.

Blue Origin was also in line to fly the larger Blue Moon MK2, a crew-capable version of its lander, as part of the Artemis III mission, which seeks to test out the ability of NASA’s Orion spacecraft to dock with moon landers during a low-Earth orbit mission that was aiming to fly by mid 2027.

coreStoryFacts.text: Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff.
Blue Origin , which is run by Amazon.com founder Jeff Bezos , announced today (Feb.
25) that it's pushing the target date for the debut launch of its heavy-lift New Glenn rocket from late 2021 to the fourth quarter of 2022.
Blue Origin continues to make good progress on New Glenn and its launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, company representatives wrote in today's update.
The company has already scored New Glenn launch contracts with Eutelsat, Mu Space, OneWeb, Sky Perfect JSAT and Telesat, as Space News noted .
And NASA recently made New Glenn eligible to compete for contracts under the agency's Launch Services II program, which applies to launches through December 2027.
"We hope to launch NSSL payloads in the future, and remain committed to serving the U.S. national defense mission."
The rocket will be capable of launching 50 tons (45 metric tons) to low Earth orbit when it's up and running, according to its specifications page .
Bezos has said he hopes New Glenn will fly people as well as payloads.
Such reuse is key to Blue Origin's overall vision, which involves helping humanity extend its footprint out into the final frontier .
For example, the company's New Shepard rocket-capsule combo , which is designed to take people and payloads to suborbital space, is fully reusable.
One New Shepard vehicle has flown seven uncrewed test flights, acing its landing each time. (New Shepard is not yet operational, but its first crewed spaceflights could happen soon .)

New Glenn is a two-stage rocket that stands 322 feet tall (98 meters) and is named after NASA astronaut John Glenn, who in February 1962 became the first American to circle Earth. (Cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin was the first person overall, pulling off the feat in April 1961.)

extraction.body: Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space. In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process. “This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT.
“Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

sources.title: Blue Origin launches twin NASA Mars probes in second flight of New Glenn rocket
passages: The next such window opens in 2026.To make Wednesday's New Glenn launch work in 2025, mission planners with Advanced Space LLC came up with an innovative flight plan, one that will take Blue and Gold longer to reach Mars but will enable more flexible trajectories for future missions.The probes were deployed on a trajectory that will carry them a million miles out, well past the moon's orbit, where they will loiter for the next 11 months before heading back toward Earth.Passing within 600 miles of Earth in November 2027, the ESCAPADE probes will make velocity-boosting gravity assist flybys, augmented by onboard propulsion, to finally head for Mars.In all, the twin spacecraft will spend a full year in that initial kidney bean-shaped orbit out past the moon and back, and another 10 months in transit to Mars.

But for a variety of reasons, the Mars satellites mission ultimately ended up on New Glenn's second flight.Mars launch windows typically open every two years when Earth and the red planet reach favorable positions in their orbits to permit direct flights using current rockets.

Much like returning SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, the larger New Glenn booster will be hauled back to Port Canaveral and, depending on its condition, be refurbished and readied for use on an upcoming New Glenn flight.The second stage, meanwhile, pressed ahead, carrying out two firings of its twin engines to reach the planned Earth-escape trajectory.

ET, majestically pushing the booster skyward atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust.The launch came three days late due to stormy weather on Earth and in space, where a powerful solar storm buffeted Earth's atmosphere with a torrent of high-energy radiation that could have caused electrical problems with the rocket or its payloads.The storm had abated by launch time Wednesday, and Blue Origin employees, looking on from viewing sites several miles from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station launch pad, cheered and applauded as the booster climbed skyward, followed moments later by the booming roar of its engines sweeping across the Space Coast.
This time around, the big rocket flew itself to an on-target touchdown, prompting more cheers and applause from Blue Origin workers.

extraction.body: ET, majestically pushing the booster skyward atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust.The launch came three days late due to stormy weather on Earth and in space, where a powerful solar storm buffeted Earth's atmosphere with a torrent of high-energy radiation that could have caused electrical problems with the rocket or its payloads.The storm had abated by launch time Wednesday, and Blue Origin employees, looking on from viewing sites several miles from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station launch pad, cheered and applauded as the booster climbed skyward, followed moments later by the booming roar of its engines sweeping across the Space Coast. The New Glenn's maiden flight last January successfully boosted a Blue Origin payload into orbit, but the reusable first stage failed in its attempt to reach an offshore landing ship, named after Bezos' mother, Jacklyn. The 188-foot-tall first stage launched Wednesday, nicknamed "Never Tell Me The Odds," featured a variety of upgrades to improve performance. This time around, the big rocket flew itself to an on-target touchdown, prompting more cheers and applause from Blue Origin workers. Much like returning SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, the larger New Glenn booster will be hauled back to Port Canaveral and, depending on its condition, be refurbished and readied for use on an upcoming New Glenn flight.The second stage, meanwhile, pressed ahead, carrying out two firings of its twin engines to reach the planned Earth-escape trajectory. Thirty-three minutes after liftoff, the ESCAPADE satellites were released to fly on their own.The NASA-sponsored payload, managed by the University of California, Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory, is made up of two small, low-budget satellites known as Blue and Gold that make up the heart of the ESCAPADE mission. The acronym stands for Escape, Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers.The probes were built for UC Berkeley by Rocketlab under a NASA program intended to develop lower-cost, fast-track planetary missions.ESCAPADE cost $107.4 million, a bargain compared to the cost of more traditional, more sophisticated planetary spacecraft that can cost hundreds of millions to well over a billion dollars each.The ESCAPADE probes were originally expected to hitch a ride to Mars a few years ago with NASA's Psyche asteroid probe. But for a variety of reasons, the Mars satellites mission ultimately ended up on New Glenn's second flight.Mars launch windows typically open every two years when Earth and the red planet reach favorable positions in their orbits to permit direct flights using current rockets. The next such window opens in 2026.To make Wednesday's New Glenn launch work in 2025, mission planners with Advanced Space LLC came up with an innovative flight plan, one that will take Blue and Gold longer to reach Mars but will enable more flexible trajectories for future missions.The probes were deployed on a trajectory that will carry them a million miles out, well past the moon's orbit, where they will loiter for the next 11 months before heading back toward Earth.Passing within 600 miles of Earth in November 2027, the ESCAPADE probes will make velocity-boosting gravity assist flybys, augmented by onboard propulsion, to finally head for Mars.In all, the twin spacecraft will spend a full year in that initial kidney bean-shaped orbit out past the moon and back, and another 10 months in transit to Mars. "We know that atmospheric escape from Mars is a major driver for the evolution of the Martian climate. We know that Mars at least was episodically warm and wet for a couple billion years, but hasn't been so for about 2 billion years or so. And we think atmospheric escape is a major reason for that."Blue and Gold will provide what amounts to a stereo view of those processes."If you only have one spacecraft, you can either measure what the sun is throwing at Mars, the so-called space weather environment upstream of Mars, or you can measure the conditions close to Mars in its upper atmosphere, where the atmosphere is escaping," Lillis said."You can't be in two places at once. We've never had that before, and that's really exciting," Lillis said.

We know that Mars at least was episodically warm and wet for a couple billion years, but hasn't been so for about 2 billion years or so.

And we think atmospheric escape is a major reason for that."Blue and Gold will provide what amounts to a stereo view of those processes."If you only have one spacecraft, you can either measure what the sun is throwing at Mars, the so-called space weather environment upstream of Mars, or you can measure the conditions close to Mars in its upper atmosphere, where the atmosphere is escaping," Lillis said."You can't be in two places at once.
We've never had that before, and that's really exciting," Lillis said.

extraction.description: Blue Origin, owned by Jeff Bezos, plans to challenge SpaceX with the powerful, partially reusable New Glenn rocket.

But for a variety of reasons, the Mars satellites mission ultimately ended up on New Glenn's second flight.Mars launch windows typically open every two years when Earth and the red planet reach favorable positions in their orbits to permit direct flights using current rockets.

Much like returning SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, the larger New Glenn booster will be hauled back to Port Canaveral and, depending on its condition, be refurbished and readied for use on an upcoming New Glenn flight.The second stage, meanwhile, pressed ahead, carrying out two firings of its twin engines to reach the planned Earth-escape trajectory.

ET, majestically pushing the booster skyward atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust.The launch came three days late due to stormy weather on Earth and in space, where a powerful solar storm buffeted Earth's atmosphere with a torrent of high-energy radiation that could have caused electrical problems with the rocket or its payloads.The storm had abated by launch time Wednesday, and Blue Origin employees, looking on from viewing sites several miles from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station launch pad, cheered and applauded as the booster climbed skyward, followed moments later by the booming roar of its engines sweeping across the Space Coast.
This time around, the big rocket flew itself to an on-target touchdown, prompting more cheers and applause from Blue Origin workers.

extraction.body: Last week’s explosion of a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket on the pad at Cape Canaveral prompted dire predictions that the company might not be able to launch again until late 2027 at the earliest. CEO Dave Limp, though, said that’s not the case. “Now that we’ve had access to the pad and integration facility, we can share a bit of good news,” he said in an update on X. “We will fly again before the end of this year.” He said the propellant farm, oxygen, liquid hydrogen and liquefied natural gas tanks were all in decent shape. “This is good luck because these are very long lead items. The water tower is also good. The big support tower is damaged, but it can be repaired in place rather than torn down and replaced,” he said. Here's our video of the explosion at Launch Complex 36. It happened about 9 pm ET (0100 UTC) as Blue Origin was beginning a static fire test of its New Glenn rocket. The pad was engulfed in a fireball from a static fire test last Thursday. A New Glenn rocket had been preparing for what would have been the fourth launch of its kind for Jeff Bezos’ rocket company when it burst into a mushroom cloud. The nighttime explosion could be seen as far away as Orlando and measured 2.5 on the Richter scale, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. The rocket and the transporter erector tower that was holding it in place for the test were destroyed while one of the two lightning towers on the pad crumbled to the ground. Limp said the company had already been working on eliminating the need for the transporter-erector in favor of an alternative concept. “We’ll now go directly to that; so we don’t need a new transporter-erector,” he said. He also said rocket parts that had been within a neighboring building fared well. That includes what for now is the lone remaining New Glenn first stage, “Never Tell Me The Odds,” which was flown and recovered on the rocket’s second and third missions. Limp also noted that while the company had been working at an adjacent launch pad at Canaveral’s Launch Complex 36 to support a planned larger version of the New Glenn rocket in the future, the company would not simply shift efforts to that, and would keep its efforts going for the current rocket design. The first and second stages for New Glenn continue to be manufactured at the company’s massive site on neighboring Merritt Island. Limp said that work has been going well. “We’re going to continue that at pace as planned and store the stages for use,” he said. SpaceX suffered a similar launch pad explosion a decade ago at Canaveral’s Space Launch Complex 40, and was not able to fly again from that pad for another 15 months. Limp, though, said he expects a much more optimistic timeline. Before the explosion, Blue Origin had been looking to fly the first of 24 contracted missions for the Amazon Leo satellite constellation. The 48 satellites were not installed on the rocket when it exploded, but those will have to wait. Blue Origin had also planned on launching its first moon mission with its uncrewed Blue Moon MK1 lander as part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services mission as early as this fall. Earlier this year, Limp stated he hoped New Glenn would launch at least eight times. New Kennedy Space Center Director Brian Hughes said Tuesday during a Space Florida board meeting that NASA was keen to get Blue Origin back online. “We certainly will do everything in our power at NASA and working with our friends at Space Force to be there as partners to make that happen,” he said. Blue Origin was also in line to fly the larger Blue Moon MK2, a crew-capable version of its lander, as part of the Artemis III mission, which seeks to test out the ability of NASA’s Orion spacecraft to dock with moon landers during a low-Earth orbit mission that was aiming to fly by mid 2027. “So the impact to NASA’s planning exists,” Hughes said. “We obviously … had launch needs that were scheduled to be met by Blue, so part of the reason we’ll be rooting for them to get back on their feet as quick as possible is some of that planning.” He noted with surprise just how resilient some of the launch pad infrastructure had been despite the explosion, crediting the design and planning that has gone into the newer launch pads on the Space Coast. He said getting back to business at LC-36 before the end of the year isn’t out of the question. “It is ambitious, but I would never count out the folks in those companies, because they have a pretty good record of turning ambition into action,” he said. sources.title: AMD posts record first-quarter results, driven by skyrocketing data center CPU demand — company expects consumer and gaming revenue to decline in Q2 over rising memory and component costs - Tom's Hardware
passages: On Tuesday, AMD reported its financial results for the first quarter of 2026.

Driven by record demand for AMD's EPYC server processors, Ryzen CPUs, and Instinct accelerators, the company's revenue totaled $10.253 billion, slightly down quarter-over-quarter (QoQ), but up significantly year-over-year (YoY).
Furthermore, AMD raised its long-term outlook for the server CPU market, expecting it to reach $120 billion by 2030 due to increased demand from AI and agentic AI workloads.
At the same time, the company admitted that sales of its AI accelerators were down sequentially.
Looking ahead, we expect server growth to accelerate meaningfully as we scale supply to meet demand."
AMD said server CPU sales increased more than 50% from the same quarter last year, with both cloud and enterprise demand growing over 50%.
AMD warned that both client and gaming revenue in the second half of the year would decline by more than 20% compared to the first half because of higher memory and component costs.
"In response to this demand, we are working closely with our supply chain partners to meaningfully increase our wafer and back-end capacity to support this growth," Su said.
Client revenue alone reached $2.9 billion, up 26%, driven by strong Ryzen processor demand and commercial PC share gains.
Gaming revenue rose 11% to $720 million due to stronger Radeon GPU demand.

"[Q2 results will be ]driven by a very strong growth in our data center segment, [modest] growth in our client and the gaming segment, and a double-digit growth in our embedded segment," said Jean Hu, AMD executive vice president, CFO and treasurer.
The business unit generated $338 million operating income, up from $328 million a year ago.
AMD projects Q2 2026 revenue to reach about $11.2 billion ± $300 million.
The company also expects non-GAAP gross margin to be around 56%.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.

"In graphics, revenue increased year-over-year, led by demand for our latest generation Radeon nine thousand series GPUs. sources.title: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters
passages: AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company’s gaming segment cratered.
AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs .
AMD CFO Jean Hu said, “We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%.
As reported by Tom’s Hardware , Intel’s Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion.
That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel’s revenue for the first time in history.
The gaming segment of AMD’s business is composed of two main sources.
There are semi-custom processors that AMD supplies to other manufacturers’ consoles, as well as its own Radeon graphics business.
Embedded segment revenue, or all the SoCs , FPGAs , and boards under AMD’s umbrella that go into other hardware, was $1.1 billion, up 29 percent.
AMD attributed this growth to gains made in the “aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial end markets.”

AMD also announced that Windows-based systems running on its Ryzen AI Halo platform will be “coming soon.” Known as Project Zenith , the effort will support a developer-focused Windows experience on the current PRO 400 Series platform .

On the call, Su stated that AMD “started shipping MI455X in volume in the quarter, and lead customers, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle, brought their first Helios racks online quickly.”
The new AMD Threadripper Halo Station , which AMD first showed at IFA in September , pairs a Threadripper 9995WX CPU with up to four Instinct MI350P GPUs and can run trillion-parameter LLMs locally.
The system is slated for a release sometime in 2027, with pricing still to be announced.

AMD CFO Jean Hu said, “We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel’s revenue for the first time in history. The data center segment of AMD’s business was up 97 percent year over year, with a record $8.5 billion. AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs . Sales of AMD Ryzen mobile chips led growth in the Client business, which includes desktop Ryzen processors and posted $2.95 billion in revenue, up 7 percent year over year. Gaming revenue fell sharply for the company, posting a 40 percent drop in revenue at $773 million, which AMD attributes to “lower semi-custom and graphics revenue.” Operating margins in AMD’s data center business expanded from 25 percent to 34 percent, with operating income surging 168 percent to $2.88 billion. Embedded segment revenue, or all the SoCs , FPGAs , and boards under AMD’s umbrella that go into other hardware, was $1.1 billion, up 29 percent. There are semi-custom processors that AMD supplies to other manufacturers’ consoles, as well as its own Radeon graphics business. Where things can get confusing is that Ryzen processors, like those commonly installed in gaming PCs, are counted under the company’s client business, not gaming. According to AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su , “In Gaming, revenue declined 40% year over year to $773 million, primarily due to lower semi-custom sales as expected at this stage of the console cycle.” The financial results do not break down the split between console chip sales and PC graphics cards. sources.title: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters
passages: AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company’s gaming segment cratered.
AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs .
AMD CFO Jean Hu said, “We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%.
As reported by Tom’s Hardware , Intel’s Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion.
That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel’s revenue for the first time in history.
The gaming segment of AMD’s business is composed of two main sources.
There are semi-custom processors that AMD supplies to other manufacturers’ consoles, as well as its own Radeon graphics business.
Embedded segment revenue, or all the SoCs , FPGAs , and boards under AMD’s umbrella that go into other hardware, was $1.1 billion, up 29 percent.
AMD attributed this growth to gains made in the “aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial end markets.”

AMD also announced that Windows-based systems running on its Ryzen AI Halo platform will be “coming soon.” Known as Project Zenith , the effort will support a developer-focused Windows experience on the current PRO 400 Series platform .

On the call, Su stated that AMD “started shipping MI455X in volume in the quarter, and lead customers, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle, brought their first Helios racks online quickly.”
The new AMD Threadripper Halo Station , which AMD first showed at IFA in September , pairs a Threadripper 9995WX CPU with up to four Instinct MI350P GPUs and can run trillion-parameter LLMs locally.
The system is slated for a release sometime in 2027, with pricing still to be announced.

extraction.body: AMD’s gaming revenue fell 40 percent in an otherwise record $13.4 billion quarter. AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company’s gaming segment cratered. AMD CFO Jean Hu said, “We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. The middle point of our guidance represents approximately 66% year-over-year revenue growth, primarily driven by the acceleration of our Data Center segment.” AMD says its Q4 revenue projections are up another 27 percent from this quarter’s results. As reported by Tom’s Hardware , Intel’s Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion. That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel’s revenue for the first time in history. The data center segment of AMD’s business was up 97 percent year over year, with a record $8.5 billion. AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs . Sales of AMD Ryzen mobile chips led growth in the Client business, which includes desktop Ryzen processors and posted $2.95 billion in revenue, up 7 percent year over year. Gaming revenue fell sharply for the company, posting a 40 percent drop in revenue at $773 million, which AMD attributes to “lower semi-custom and graphics revenue.” Operating margins in AMD’s data center business expanded from 25 percent to 34 percent, with operating income surging 168 percent to $2.88 billion. Embedded segment revenue, or all the SoCs , FPGAs , and boards under AMD’s umbrella that go into other hardware, was $1.1 billion, up 29 percent. AMD attributed this growth to gains made in the “aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial end markets.” The gaming segment of AMD’s business is composed of two main sources. There are semi-custom processors that AMD supplies to other manufacturers’ consoles, as well as its own Radeon graphics business. Where things can get confusing is that Ryzen processors, like those commonly installed in gaming PCs, are counted under the company’s client business, not gaming. According to AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su , “In Gaming, revenue declined 40% year over year to $773 million, primarily due to lower semi-custom sales as expected at this stage of the console cycle.” The financial results do not break down the split between console chip sales and PC graphics cards. Along with the Q3 financial results, AMD used the occasion to highlight hardware still in the hopper. The new AMD Threadripper Halo Station , which AMD first showed at IFA in September , pairs a Threadripper 9995WX CPU with up to four Instinct MI350P GPUs and can run trillion-parameter LLMs locally. The system is slated for a release sometime in 2027, with pricing still to be announced. AMD also announced that Windows-based systems running on its Ryzen AI Halo platform will be “coming soon.” Known as Project Zenith , the effort will support a developer-focused Windows experience on the current PRO 400 Series platform . Built on the Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 processor , the chip supports up to 192GB of unified system memory, with up to 160GB of that available to be allocated for graphics, and is capable of running 300 billion-parameter models at 4-bit quantization. extraction.body: After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers. In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear. "National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future." In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!" According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress. Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%. Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers. South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline." In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C." Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers." Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said. Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign. "When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight." extraction.body: After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers. In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear. "National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future." In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!" According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress. Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%. Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers. South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline." In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C." Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers." Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said. Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign. "When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight." The gunman then got out of his vehicle with a rifle and fatally shot a woman. An armed security guard employed by Citibank shot the suspect inside a nearby building's cafeteria during a gunfire exchange, authorities said. The gunman was taken to Tampa General Hospital where he later died. "The security guard that's employed by Citibank stopped the threat," Losat said. So kudos to that security guard and the people they employ." Four people were also treated at a local hospital for injuries that were not life-threatening. It is unclear where the victims were wounded during the incident. SHOOTING AFTER MAGIC CITY CLASSIC IN ALABAMA LEAVES 1 DEAD, 8 INJURED Officials said deputies with the sheriff's office responded to the scene within minutes of the reported shooting. At the time the chaotic scene broke out, there were 3,200 Citibank employees on the property, Losat said. "With that being said, with that many witnesses… we will be doing interviews well into the night," Losat said. Our crime scene will be processing the scene, which will take several hours, if not until tomorrow." Losat did not release the name of the suspected gunman or the victim, pending notification to the next of kin. Authorities have cleared the Citibank property. extraction.body: TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — A gunman plowed a car into a courtyard on Citibank’s sprawling Tampa business campus on Wednesday and opened fire with a rifle, killing a woman before a security guard fatally shot him, authorities said. The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office did not give a motive for the shooting or say whether the gunman and his lone victim knew each other. The attack sent workers scrambling as the suspect crashed his car among outdoor tables where people were eating lunch, then started shooting, said Chief Deputy Frank Losat of the sheriff’s office. He said 3,200 people were on the campus at work during the attack. The gunman fatally shot the woman before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria, Losat said. The guard and the gunman exchanged fire, and the guard killed him, Losat said. “Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely,” Losat told a news conference. ”So kudos to that security guard.” The names of the gunman and the woman killed were not immediately released. Losat said four other people were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. He didn’t know whether any of them had been shot or struck by the gunman’s vehicle. The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant’s employees. David Dzien, a Citibank vice president, told The Associated Press he was returning to work after lunch when he saw the shooter’s sedan crash through a fence about 150 yards (137 meters) away from him, followed by an “incredible clatter” that he later realized was gunfire. People near the crashed car suddenly dispersed and others began to scream, Dzien said, as he sprinted back into the building and evacuated through a fire escape. “I can still hear the particular type of scream,” he said, “and I’m still trying to process it, frankly.” The attack occurred on a day when “VIPs” who don’t normally work at the complex were present for a “quarterly review,” Dzien said. Sheriff’s deputies began arriving at the campus within a minute of the first 911 call, Losat said. The response was huge, with more than 360 deputies — many in tactical gear — rushing to the scene. Those deputies spent 2 1/2 hours searching and clearing the building where the shootings occurred plus adjacent office buildings, Losat said. Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from responding officers described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search as people were found sheltering in locked rooms and closets, then carefully escorted from the buildings and parking garage. Citigroup said in a statement that it was “aware of an incident” at the complex and was cooperating with authorities. Employees at the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel, a few hundred feet from the Citibank complex, were having a monthly employee luncheon in the hotel’s ballroom when they saw a massive flood of police vehicles headed toward the campus. General Manager Matt Chauvin said Citibank employees ran over and told the front desk there was an active shooter. “We at first locked the doors and, you know, went into lockdown, but the employees kept coming over,” Chauvin said. Chauvin estimated the hotel sheltered about 300 Citibank workers. Hotel staff gave them water and lunch, and let some go into hotel rooms “to sort of decompress or make phone calls.” “Luckily we were far enough away that they were all safe,” he said. Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. AP journalists Cybele Mayes-Osterman in Chicago, R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this story. extraction.body: HILLSBOROUGH COUNTY, Fla. — Sheriff Chad Chronister said the Citibank security guard who shot an armed suspect Wednesday was a hero . During a news conference Thursday afternoon, the sheriff provided more details about the incident in which the suspect and a woman were killed. It happened just after noon at the Citibank complex near Interstate 75 and Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Boulevard in Brandon. “Our suspect took one life, and that’s one life too many,” Chronister said, stating that the suspect was carrying 90 rounds of ammunition. The suspect was identified as Jacob Pearson, 35, of Orlando. He was married with a 7-year-old child. Pearson, who didn’t have a previous criminal record, according to Chronister, died at a local hospital. The woman who was killed was identified as Leanne Selman, 41, of Palm Harbor. She worked at Citibank for nine years. Chronister said the security guard’s name is John Fraley. Four people suffered non-life-threatening injuries. Chronister said that some of those injuries likely happened while they were running away from the scene. The sheriff said that at about 9 a.m. Wednesday, Pearson contacted an attorneys' office that is contracted by Citibank for collection. The suspect was angry about a summons over a $2,500 payment. Chronister said the man said, "unless you want me to go over there with my AR-15," to cancel the case. The attorneys' office then contacted security at Citibank. The Orlando Police Department went to Pearson's home to do a welfare check, Chronister said, but he was not there. Chronister said the suspect's wife has been cooperating with investigators. A Citibank employee speaking at Thursday's news conference said resources are being offered to employees struggling in the aftermath of the shooting. He said the company is grateful for its security team and local law enforcement. The sheriff's office showed video from the scene during Thursday's news conference. From the sky, a gray sedan that broke through a fence can be seen making its way into one of the campus' courtyards. The car was just the first tool law enforcement said the shooter used before he fatally shot Leanne Selman. It's a tactic that Rob Chadwick, former FBI active shooter response trainer, said is a trend. The suspect crashed into an outdoor seating area where multiple people were eating lunch just after 12 p.m. upon driving through a fence at the Sabal Park Office Development, Frank Losat, a chief deputy with the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office, told reporters at the scene. The gunman then got out of his vehicle with a rifle and fatally shot a woman. An armed security guard employed by Citibank shot the suspect inside a nearby building's cafeteria during a gunfire exchange, authorities said. The gunman was taken to Tampa General Hospital where he later died. "The security guard that's employed by Citibank stopped the threat," Losat said. So kudos to that security guard and the people they employ." Four people were also treated at a local hospital for injuries that were not life-threatening. It is unclear where the victims were wounded during the incident. SHOOTING AFTER MAGIC CITY CLASSIC IN ALABAMA LEAVES 1 DEAD, 8 INJURED Officials said deputies with the sheriff's office responded to the scene within minutes of the reported shooting. At the time the chaotic scene broke out, there were 3,200 Citibank employees on the property, Losat said. "With that being said, with that many witnesses… we will be doing interviews well into the night," Losat said. Our crime scene will be processing the scene, which will take several hours, if not until tomorrow." Losat did not release the name of the suspected gunman or the victim, pending notification to the next of kin. Authorities have cleared the Citibank property. The scene showed adults with children moving away from the business campus, which has a daycare center, affiliate FOX 13 Tampa Bay reported. "We are aware of an incident impacting our site in Tampa, Florida and are coordinating with law enforcement," Citibank said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Citibank employees were asked to meet at the triage area in the parking lot of the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel. Families of employees were instructed to meet at the reunification site at Staybridge Suites Tampa East. "The low-rise campus is surrounded by lushly landscaped berms with outdoor plazas, fountains, and waterfalls to provide a secluded, tranquil environment," the website states. "Each building is interconnected by enclosed walkways to ensure personnel comfort and building security as well as provide a homogenous atmosphere among the individual buildings and associated staff." extraction.body: TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — A gunman plowed a car into a courtyard on Citibank’s sprawling Tampa business campus on Wednesday and opened fire with a rifle, killing a woman before a security guard fatally shot him, authorities said. The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office did not give a motive for the shooting or say whether the gunman and his lone victim knew each other. The attack sent workers scrambling as the suspect crashed his car among outdoor tables where people were eating lunch, then started shooting, said Chief Deputy Frank Losat of the sheriff’s office. He said 3,200 people were on the campus at work during the attack. The gunman fatally shot the woman before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria, Losat said. The guard and the gunman exchanged fire, and the guard killed him, Losat said. “Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely,” Losat told a news conference. ”So kudos to that security guard.” The names of the gunman and the woman killed were not immediately released. Losat said four other people were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. He didn’t know whether any of them had been shot or struck by the gunman’s vehicle. The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant’s employees. David Dzien, a Citibank vice president, told The Associated Press he was returning to work after lunch when he saw the shooter’s sedan crash through a fence about 150 yards (137 meters) away from him, followed by an “incredible clatter” that he later realized was gunfire. People near the crashed car suddenly dispersed and others began to scream, Dzien said, as he sprinted back into the building and evacuated through a fire escape. “I can still hear the particular type of scream,” he said, “and I’m still trying to process it, frankly.” The attack occurred on a day when “VIPs” who don’t normally work at the complex were present for a “quarterly review,” Dzien said. Sheriff’s deputies began arriving at the campus within a minute of the first 911 call, Losat said. The response was huge, with more than 360 deputies — many in tactical gear — rushing to the scene. Those deputies spent 2 1/2 hours searching and clearing the building where the shootings occurred plus adjacent office buildings, Losat said. Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from responding officers described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search as people were found sheltering in locked rooms and closets, then carefully escorted from the buildings and parking garage. Citigroup said in a statement that it was “aware of an incident” at the complex and was cooperating with authorities. Employees at the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel, a few hundred feet from the Citibank complex, were having a monthly employee luncheon in the hotel’s ballroom when they saw a massive flood of police vehicles headed toward the campus. General Manager Matt Chauvin said Citibank employees ran over and told the front desk there was an active shooter. “We at first locked the doors and, you know, went into lockdown, but the employees kept coming over,” Chauvin said. Chauvin estimated the hotel sheltered about 300 Citibank workers. Hotel staff gave them water and lunch, and let some go into hotel rooms “to sort of decompress or make phone calls.” “Luckily we were far enough away that they were all safe,” he said. Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. AP journalists Cybele Mayes-Osterman in Chicago, R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this story. extraction.body: HILLSBOROUGH COUNTY, Fla. — Sheriff Chad Chronister said the Citibank security guard who shot an armed suspect Wednesday was a hero . During a news conference Thursday afternoon, the sheriff provided more details about the incident in which the suspect and a woman were killed. It happened just after noon at the Citibank complex near Interstate 75 and Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Boulevard in Brandon. “Our suspect took one life, and that’s one life too many,” Chronister said, stating that the suspect was carrying 90 rounds of ammunition. The suspect was identified as Jacob Pearson, 35, of Orlando. He was married with a 7-year-old child. Pearson, who didn’t have a previous criminal record, according to Chronister, died at a local hospital. The woman who was killed was identified as Leanne Selman, 41, of Palm Harbor. She worked at Citibank for nine years. Chronister said the security guard’s name is John Fraley. Four people suffered non-life-threatening injuries. Chronister said that some of those injuries likely happened while they were running away from the scene. The sheriff said that at about 9 a.m. Wednesday, Pearson contacted an attorneys' office that is contracted by Citibank for collection. The suspect was angry about a summons over a $2,500 payment. Chronister said the man said, "unless you want me to go over there with my AR-15," to cancel the case. The attorneys' office then contacted security at Citibank. The Orlando Police Department went to Pearson's home to do a welfare check, Chronister said, but he was not there. Chronister said the suspect's wife has been cooperating with investigators. A Citibank employee speaking at Thursday's news conference said resources are being offered to employees struggling in the aftermath of the shooting. He said the company is grateful for its security team and local law enforcement. The sheriff's office showed video from the scene during Thursday's news conference. From the sky, a gray sedan that broke through a fence can be seen making its way into one of the campus' courtyards. The car was just the first tool law enforcement said the shooter used before he fatally shot Leanne Selman. It's a tactic that Rob Chadwick, former FBI active shooter response trainer, said is a trend. "We've seen a significant uptick in what I'll call vehicle-borne attacks or initiated by a vehicle that are designed to defeat that outer layer," he said. When the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office got on campus, deputies found the shooter had been shot by the security guard. Bodycam footage shows deputies arriving, searching and directing workers. "I believe textbook response, at least the body cameras that I reviewed," Chadwick said. "Obviously, you know, (it) just happened. And their response was absolutely in keeping with the training that, you know, we have been putting out for years now." Chadwick said that the deputies are there to save, protect and stay vigilant. "One of the things that the officers are trained to look for is potentially an accomplice or the shooter, him or herself, trying to escape," he said. "You know, in the crowd, so to speak. We saw that at Marjory Stoneman Douglas." More than 360 officers were at the scene, working with more than 3,000 employees at the campus. Chadwick said he thought the workers made the response easier. "People understand that run, hide, fight type of mentality. They also understand, you know, that just because the police have now arrived, it's not over," he said.

sources.title: Meta warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder
passages: Speaking at the WSJ Tech conference on Wednesday, the Meta exec pointed out that the backlash against data centers — which was very much on the ballot during this election season — was also tied to people’s feelings about AI technology overall.

Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that the Democratic wins in the midterm elections are going to make it a lot harder for companies to build data centers, adding that the industry has “not done as good a job as we needed to explain the benefits of these investments.”
Today, the company has data centers in 23 states, she said, and five of them, including one in Texas, are planned as projects of 1 gigawatt or more.
Meta has pinned its hopes on its AI investments, particularly its consumer AI agent Muse scaling far beyond the 10 million users it has today, to become a business that one day serves billions.
Specifically, communities only want data centers when it benefits them in some way, she explained, laying out the approach that Meta today uses to close its data center deals in local communities.

Successful projects see Meta paying for its own electricity, directing any tax surpluses as a result of the data centers toward teachers and first responders, keeping the labor force local, and getting bipartisan support for the project, among other things.
But Meta is now worried that it could lose some of its investments after politicians ran on anti-data-center platforms during the midterms.
Going forward, she expects data center projects to come under more review and be weighed against whether the constituents actually want them.

sources.title: Meta Warns Election Backlash Could Derail AI Buildout
passages: Meta's warning about election backlash threatening data center expansion marks a pivotal moment for the AI industry.
Meta is sounding the alarm that mounting political opposition to data center construction could seriously hamper its AI ambitions.
The data center backlash also highlights a broader tension in AI development.

For Meta and its rivals, the path forward likely requires not just more capital, but better community engagement and potentially a fundamental rethinking of data center design to address power and water concerns.

extraction.body: Meta is sounding the alarm that mounting political opposition to data center construction could seriously hamper its AI ambitions. The warning comes as communities across the country push back against massive infrastructure projects that demand enormous amounts of power and water. With AI rivals racing to expand computing capacity, Meta's caution signals a potential infrastructure bottleneck that could reshape the entire industry's growth trajectory. Meta just threw cold water on the AI infrastructure boom. The social media giant is warning investors and policymakers that rising political opposition to data center construction could make it harder to execute the massive buildout needed to compete in artificial intelligence. It's a striking admission from a company that's been racing to catch OpenAI and Google in the AI arms race. Meta's warning lands just as the dust settles from the 2026 midterm elections, where voters across multiple states rejected data center projects in what amounted to a stunning rebuke of AI infrastructure expansion. For Meta, the political headwinds couldn't come at a worse time. The company just announced plans for a $25 billion bond sale specifically to fund AI infrastructure spending, one of the largest debt raises in tech history. That capital is earmarked for data centers packed with Nvidia GPUs and custom chips designed to train and run increasingly sophisticated AI models. The backlash reflects a growing disconnect between Silicon Valley's AI ambitions and the communities expected to host the infrastructure. Modern AI data centers can consume as much electricity as a small city, with some facilities requiring 100 megawatts or more of continuous power. In drought-prone regions, that's become a political lightning rod. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have all encountered local resistance to data center projects over the past year. But Meta's public warning suggests the company sees this as more than a temporary speed bump. It's a structural challenge that could fundamentally limit how fast any company can scale AI infrastructure in the United States. The political opposition also threatens to widen the gap between AI leaders and challengers. OpenAI, which got an earlier start on infrastructure deals, may find itself with a built-in advantage if new projects face years of regulatory delays and community battles. Meanwhile, Meta has been pouring resources into AI development, recently rolling out conversational voice features and animated avatars to its Muse app as it tries to compete with ChatGPT. The infrastructure crunch is already reshaping investment patterns. NextDC, an Australian data center operator, saw its stock soar 43% after Goodman and Digital Realty bought stakes, partly because international locations face less political resistance than U.S. sites. Some analysts now expect tech giants to shift more infrastructure spending overseas, potentially giving foreign competitors better access to cutting-edge AI capabilities. For Meta, the stakes extend beyond infrastructure. The company has been betting heavily that AI will drive its next wave of growth, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg positioning the company as a leader in open-source AI models and consumer AI products. Meta's AI-powered ad engine has already widened its revenue growth gap over Google Search to a five-year high, demonstrating real business impact from AI investments. But sustaining that advantage requires continuous infrastructure expansion. Training each new generation of AI models demands exponentially more computing power, and Meta can't afford to fall behind competitors in the race to build bigger, more capable systems. The company's warning suggests it sees real risk that political opposition could force it to slow down just as the AI competition heats up. The data center backlash also highlights a broader tension in AI development. While tech executives tout AI's potential to transform industries and boost productivity, local communities are left dealing with the immediate costs - higher electricity rates, strained water supplies, and increased truck traffic. Until the industry figures out how to share AI's benefits more broadly, expect political opposition to keep growing. Meta's warning about election backlash threatening data center expansion marks a pivotal moment for the AI industry. What started as a few local skirmishes over individual projects has evolved into a systemic political challenge that could reshape where and how fast AI infrastructure gets built. For Meta and its rivals, the path forward likely requires not just more capital, but better community engagement and potentially a fundamental rethinking of data center design to address power and water concerns. The companies that crack that puzzle will have a serious advantage in the AI race ahead.

extraction.body: Meta is sounding the alarm that mounting political opposition to data center construction could seriously hamper its AI ambitions. The warning comes as communities across the country push back against massive infrastructure projects that demand enormous amounts of power and water. With AI rivals racing to expand computing capacity, Meta's caution signals a potential infrastructure bottleneck that could reshape the entire industry's growth trajectory. Meta just threw cold water on the AI infrastructure boom. The social media giant is warning investors and policymakers that rising political opposition to data center construction could make it harder to execute the massive buildout needed to compete in artificial intelligence. It's a striking admission from a company that's been racing to catch OpenAI and Google in the AI arms race. Meta's warning lands just as the dust settles from the 2026 midterm elections, where voters across multiple states rejected data center projects in what amounted to a stunning rebuke of AI infrastructure expansion. For Meta, the political headwinds couldn't come at a worse time. The company just announced plans for a $25 billion bond sale specifically to fund AI infrastructure spending, one of the largest debt raises in tech history. That capital is earmarked for data centers packed with Nvidia GPUs and custom chips designed to train and run increasingly sophisticated AI models. The backlash reflects a growing disconnect between Silicon Valley's AI ambitions and the communities expected to host the infrastructure. Modern AI data centers can consume as much electricity as a small city, with some facilities requiring 100 megawatts or more of continuous power. In drought-prone regions, that's become a political lightning rod. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have all encountered local resistance to data center projects over the past year. But Meta's public warning suggests the company sees this as more than a temporary speed bump. It's a structural challenge that could fundamentally limit how fast any company can scale AI infrastructure in the United States. The political opposition also threatens to widen the gap between AI leaders and challengers. OpenAI, which got an earlier start on infrastructure deals, may find itself with a built-in advantage if new projects face years of regulatory delays and community battles. Meanwhile, Meta has been pouring resources into AI development, recently rolling out conversational voice features and animated avatars to its Muse app as it tries to compete with ChatGPT. The infrastructure crunch is already reshaping investment patterns. NextDC, an Australian data center operator, saw its stock soar 43% after Goodman and Digital Realty bought stakes, partly because international locations face less political resistance than U.S. sites. Some analysts now expect tech giants to shift more infrastructure spending overseas, potentially giving foreign competitors better access to cutting-edge AI capabilities. For Meta, the stakes extend beyond infrastructure. The company has been betting heavily that AI will drive its next wave of growth, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg positioning the company as a leader in open-source AI models and consumer AI products. Meta's AI-powered ad engine has already widened its revenue growth gap over Google Search to a five-year high, demonstrating real business impact from AI investments. But sustaining that advantage requires continuous infrastructure expansion. Training each new generation of AI models demands exponentially more computing power, and Meta can't afford to fall behind competitors in the race to build bigger, more capable systems. The company's warning suggests it sees real risk that political opposition could force it to slow down just as the AI competition heats up. The data center backlash also highlights a broader tension in AI development. While tech executives tout AI's potential to transform industries and boost productivity, local communities are left dealing with the immediate costs - higher electricity rates, strained water supplies, and increased truck traffic. Until the industry figures out how to share AI's benefits more broadly, expect political opposition to keep growing. Meta's warning about election backlash threatening data center expansion marks a pivotal moment for the AI industry. What started as a few local skirmishes over individual projects has evolved into a systemic political challenge that could reshape where and how fast AI infrastructure gets built. For Meta and its rivals, the path forward likely requires not just more capital, but better community engagement and potentially a fundamental rethinking of data center design to address power and water concerns. The companies that crack that puzzle will have a serious advantage in the AI race ahead.

sources.title: Nothing says it is making an 'AI-first' device to help artificial intelligence have its iPhone moment - The Independent
passages: Consumer tech brand Nothing, best known for its transparent phones, says that it is about to release an “ AI -first” device.

But Nothing’s chief executive, Carl Pei, suggested that many of those companies and commentators are confused about how exactly such devices will break into the mainstream, and have their “ iPhone moment”.

AI is “the most important technology of our lifetime, and the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life,” Mr Pei wrote in a long post on X .
He noted that the original iPhone moment only arrived after 30 years of work on mobile devices, which began with “pagers on doctors' belts and finished with a supercomputer in every pocket”.
He suggested that Nothing is in a “rare position” to make such a device, because of the fact that it builds its devices from end to end and is already trusted by tens of millions of users.
He did not say exactly what form Nothing’s device would take.
But it has “no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app”, and will ship from next month, he said.
It will be the latest company to try and harness the excitement about artificial intelligence by building a new device around it.
The long post appeared to be a shot at some other companies that have tried to pitch their devices as iPhone killers, and a way of running their entire lives.

That has already ended in failure for many of the products that have actually launched, such as Humane’s AI Pin, which was heralded as the first post-iPhone device at its launch but led to the collapse of the company who made it last year .

It will be the latest company to try and harness the excitement about artificial intelligence by building a new device around it. It follows launches and rumours about similar devices coming from everyone from Apple to OpenAI . But Nothing’s chief executive, Carl Pei, suggested that many of those companies and commentators are confused about how exactly such devices will break into the mainstream, and have their “ iPhone moment”. That will not come immediately with a blockbuster device but instead arrive after years of work on more specific devices, he suggested. AI is “the most important technology of our lifetime, and the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life,” Mr Pei wrote in a long post on X . “I admire the boldness, but I read this moment differently.” He noted that the original iPhone moment only arrived after 30 years of work on mobile devices, which began with “pagers on doctors' belts and finished with a supercomputer in every pocket”. “It was the payoff for decades of quiet work on tools people used for their jobs,” he wrote. He suggested that, in a similar way, AI devices will initially arrive with specific productivity uses. It will first come “in the tools people rely on to get real things done, and that’s where the real opportunity is today”, he wrote. “When the iPhone of AI does arrive in a few years, it will be built on that work,” he wrote. “It might be a form factor nobody has imagined yet, or three of today's devices collapsing into one.” The long post appeared to be a shot at some other companies that have tried to pitch their devices as iPhone killers, and a way of running their entire lives. extraction.body: Researchers, alumni, faculty, and students in the fields of healthcare innovation, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence gathered on Oct. 29 for the 2026 Sikand Symposium at Cal State LA. With the theme of “ AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine ,” the symposium brought together speakers from Cal State LA, UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and the Sikand Foundation to share their expertise on how computational modeling and artificial intelligence can advance healthcare innovation. The keynote speaker for the symposium, Minjeong Jeon, a professor of advanced quantitative methods at the UCLA School of Education and Information Studies, kicked off the event with her presentation. Jeon discussed her research on measurement science and how network approaches can connect patients and symptoms more accurately. In layman’s terms, people with the same condition—depression, in the case of Jeon’s study—do not necessarily exhibit the same symptoms. Jeon’s proposed model and graphs aim to help researchers better understand the differing health cases of people who are dealing with medical conditions. Jeon also discussed the use of artificial intelligence models in these applications and precision medicine, but emphasized that “AI is only as clinically meaningful as the measurement system behind it.” She hopes student researchers “think about measurement” more precisely when they conduct studies in these fields and work with their data. Student researchers also showcased their collaborative projects during a poster session. One was a study that Cal State LA student researcher Brian Ta worked on, entitled “Can We Trust the Evidence Behind a Biomedical AI Decision?” In his presentation, Ta discussed the importance of understanding how AI can be used in biomedicine. He proposed methods to ensure AI systems have a multifactor authorization system in place to check who made the decisions, where the research came from, and whether that research is complete. Ta’s study recognizes the benefits of AI in this field, but also understands that responsible practices must be in place, especially when dealing with results that can affect medicine and people’s lives. Another project was a collaborative study by student researcher Hector Gardea. It was titled “Physical State Classifier for Closed-loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson’s Disease.” Conducted in collaboration with Duke University, the project focused on using wearable technology to track different levels of tremors in participants with Parkinson’s disease.
