With the theme of “ AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine ,” the symposium brought together speakers from Cal State LA, UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and the Sikand Foundation to share their expertise on how computational modeling and artificial intelligence can advance healthcare innovation.
The keynote speaker for the symposium, Minjeong Jeon, a professor of advanced quantitative methods at the UCLA School of Education and Information Studies, kicked off the event with her presentation.

Jeon discussed her research on measurement science and how network approaches can connect patients and symptoms more accurately. In layman’s terms, people with the same condition—depression, in the case of Jeon’s study—do not necessarily exhibit the same symptoms.
Jeon’s proposed model and graphs aim to help researchers better understand the differing health cases of people who are dealing with medical conditions.

Jeon also discussed the use of artificial intelligence models in these applications and precision medicine, but emphasized that “AI is only as clinically meaningful as the measurement system behind it.” She hopes student researchers “think about measurement” more precisely when they conduct studies in these fields and work with their data.
Student researchers also showcased their collaborative projects during a poster session.
One was a study that Cal State LA student researcher Brian Ta worked on, entitled “Can We Trust the Evidence Behind a Biomedical AI Decision?”

In his presentation, Ta discussed the importance of understanding how AI can be used in biomedicine. He proposed methods to ensure AI systems have a multifactor authorization system in place to check who made the decisions, where the research came from, and whether that research is complete.

Ta’s study recognizes the benefits of AI in this field, but also understands that responsible practices must be in place, especially when dealing with results that can affect medicine and people’s lives.
Another project was a collaborative study by student researcher Hector Gardea. It was titled “Physical State Classifier for Closed-loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson’s Disease.”

Conducted in collaboration with Duke University, the project focused on using wearable technology to track different levels of tremors in participants with Parkinson’s disease. extraction.body: Cal State LA’s Sikand Center for Sustainable and Intelligent Infrastructure hosted a six-hour symposium on Thursday, October 29, 2026, titled “AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine.” According to Cal State LA’s official event listing, the program ran from 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM (PST) in the Golden Eagle Ballrooms and brought UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and LA BioStart into the room with the university’s engineering faculty. The pitch is simple. AI models are only as useful as the data pipelines, compute, and hospital systems underneath them. The Sikand SITI Center, an infrastructure-focused unit, put that argument at the center of a healthcare agenda. That framing separates this symposium from the usual model-launch news cycle, and it explains why the event matters to readers who follow AI and machine learning coverage. A caution on scope before the analysis begins. The story circulating under the headline that top Southern California researchers collaborated with Cal State LA student researchers goes further than the official record. The event listing confirms that researchers, faculty, and students were part of the audience and program. It does not document a specific collaboration, named student projects, or results. This article sticks to what the listing confirms and labels everything else as analysis. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The confirmed facts are compact. The event carried the title “AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine.” It took place on Thursday, October 29, 2026, between 9:00 AM and 3:00 PM (PST). The venue was Cal State LA’s Golden Eagle Ballrooms at 5151 State University, Los Angeles, CA 90032, and one official listing narrows that to the Golden Eagle BR on the third floor. The organizer is the Sikand Center for Sustainable and Intelligent Infrastructure, usually shortened to the Sikand SITI Center. Cal State LA’s listing names UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and LA BioStart as participating organizations. The official description says the symposium would address AI and data-intensive technologies in biomedical research, precision medicine, healthcare delivery, and sustainable healthcare infrastructure. That is the full set of verified detail. The listing does not name products, vendors beyond those three organizations, prices, technical specifications, or student project titles. It also contains no direct quotations from speakers. Readers who want a blow-by-blow account of what was said on stage will have to wait for the university’s own recap or for coverage from attendees. The listing spells out two afternoon blocks. An afternoon-remarks session ran from 1:00 PM to 1:15 PM, and a research-highlights session followed from 1:15 PM to 2:15 PM. The research-highlights hour is the slot where students and faculty most plausibly presented work, though the listing does not say who presented or on what topics. That distinction is worth keeping straight. A research-highlights session at a university symposium usually gives early-career researchers a stage. Whether Cal State LA students used it is plausible, and the headline claim about student collaboration rests on that inference. Without a program book, an abstract list, or a university recap, the claim stays unconfirmed. The morning program and the final hour before 3:00 PM are not itemized in the material available to us. We will not guess at panel formats or keynote topics. If Cal State LA publishes a program or recap, the research-highlights block is the first place to look for concrete project names and datasets. The title leads with intelligent infrastructure, and that word choice carries an argument. Healthcare AI fails or succeeds on plumbing: how records are stored, how data moves between hospitals and labs, how models run inside regulated environments, and how much energy and cost that burden adds. A center built around sustainable and intelligent infrastructure sees those questions as engineering problems with civil, electrical, and computing dimensions. Consider what a precision-medicine workflow needs. Genomic and clinical data must be collected, cleaned, and linked. Models need compute to train and to run. Results need to reach clinicians in a form they trust. Each step depends on facilities, networks, and software that someone has to build and maintain. That is the territory Sikand Engineering’s participation signals. Data availability is the other half of the story. Large open atlases show what shared biomedical data can do, and our coverage of the HuBMAP healthy tissue atlas is a good example of how pooled datasets change what a research group can attempt. A university symposium that pairs data-heavy medicine with infrastructure engineers is working the same problem from the supply side. The sustainability half of the title deserves its own look. Training and running large models draws real power, and hospitals already operate some of the most energy-hungry buildings in any city. A symposium that pairs AI with sustainable systems is acknowledging that every new clinical model adds load to servers, cooling, and networks. Engineers who design that supporting plant, including the kind Sikand Engineering practices, decide whether an AI pilot stays affordable once it scales beyond a single department. Precision medicine means matching treatment to the biology of an individual or a subgroup instead of the average patient. The field leans on machine learning because the signals are subtle and high-dimensional. The two Cedars-Sinai speakers hold computational biomedicine and research-scientist roles, which places their expertise at the model-building layer. We cannot report what Dr. Urbanowicz or Dr. Freda presented, because the listing does not say. What we can say is how their field works in general. Computational biomedicine groups build statistical and machine-learning methods that find patterns in clinical and molecular data, then test whether those patterns hold up across patient populations. The hard part is rarely the algorithm. It is data quality, bias, and validation. A related thread in biomedical research is the move toward richer measurement of body chemistry and digital-twin modeling. We covered one framework in our piece on third-generation metabolomics and digital twins . Symposia like this one give regional researchers a place to compare those methods with what hospitals can actually deploy. UCLA brings a large research university with deep biomedical and computing programs. Cedars-Sinai Medical Center brings a major academic medical center with clinical data and a computational research group. LA BioStart brings a startup-facing perspective, which is the commercialization end of the pipeline. The listing names the organizations and nothing more, so any detail about what each contributed on the day is outside the confirmed record. Cost discipline is part of that conversation. Public institutions run on tight budgets, and a model that needs expensive specialized hardware may never leave the research lab. extraction.body: Researchers, alumni, faculty, and students in the fields of healthcare innovation, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence gathered on Oct. 29 for the 2026 Sikand Symposium at Cal State LA. With the theme of “ AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine ,” the symposium brought together speakers from Cal State LA, UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and the Sikand Foundation to share their expertise on how computational modeling and artificial intelligence can advance healthcare innovation. The keynote speaker for the symposium, Minjeong Jeon, a professor of advanced quantitative methods at the UCLA School of Education and Information Studies, kicked off the event with her presentation. Jeon discussed her research on measurement science and how network approaches can connect patients and symptoms more accurately. In layman’s terms, people with the same condition—depression, in the case of Jeon’s study—do not necessarily exhibit the same symptoms. Jeon’s proposed model and graphs aim to help researchers better understand the differing health cases of people who are dealing with medical conditions. Jeon also discussed the use of artificial intelligence models in these applications and precision medicine, but emphasized that “AI is only as clinically meaningful as the measurement system behind it.” She hopes student researchers “think about measurement” more precisely when they conduct studies in these fields and work with their data. Student researchers also showcased their collaborative projects during a poster session. One was a study that Cal State LA student researcher Brian Ta worked on, entitled “Can We Trust the Evidence Behind a Biomedical AI Decision?” In his presentation, Ta discussed the importance of understanding how AI can be used in biomedicine. He proposed methods to ensure AI systems have a multifactor authorization system in place to check who made the decisions, where the research came from, and whether that research is complete. Ta’s study recognizes the benefits of AI in this field, but also understands that responsible practices must be in place, especially when dealing with results that can affect medicine and people’s lives. Another project was a collaborative study by student researcher Hector Gardea. It was titled “Physical State Classifier for Closed-loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson’s Disease.” Conducted in collaboration with Duke University, the project focused on using wearable technology to track different levels of tremors in participants with Parkinson’s disease. Gardea discussed how an Apple Watch equipped with an accelerometer detects shaking motions and classifies them more accurately. In addition, the symposium featured startup presentations from the LA BioStart training program at Cal State LA, along with research highlights and panels presented by faculty in the university’s College of Engineering, Computer Science, and Technology (ECST). Researchers presented studies on how machine learning can be used to track pollution or even in applications like detecting breast cancer. Participants also had the opportunity to take part in hands-on workshops and coding activities. extraction.body: Researchers, alumni, faculty, and students in the fields of healthcare innovation, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence gathered on Oct. 29 for the 2026 Sikand Symposium at Cal State LA. With the theme of “ AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine ,” the symposium brought together speakers from Cal State LA, UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and the Sikand Foundation to share their expertise on how computational modeling and artificial intelligence can advance healthcare innovation. The keynote speaker for the symposium, Minjeong Jeon, a professor of advanced quantitative methods at the UCLA School of Education and Information Studies, kicked off the event with her presentation. Jeon discussed her research on measurement science and how network approaches can connect patients and symptoms more accurately. In layman’s terms, people with the same condition—depression, in the case of Jeon’s study—do not necessarily exhibit the same symptoms. Jeon’s proposed model and graphs aim to help researchers better understand the differing health cases of people who are dealing with medical conditions. Jeon also discussed the use of artificial intelligence models in these applications and precision medicine, but emphasized that “AI is only as clinically meaningful as the measurement system behind it.” She hopes student researchers “think about measurement” more precisely when they conduct studies in these fields and work with their data. Student researchers also showcased their collaborative projects during a poster session. One was a study that Cal State LA student researcher Brian Ta worked on, entitled “Can We Trust the Evidence Behind a Biomedical AI Decision?” In his presentation, Ta discussed the importance of understanding how AI can be used in biomedicine. He proposed methods to ensure AI systems have a multifactor authorization system in place to check who made the decisions, where the research came from, and whether that research is complete. Ta’s study recognizes the benefits of AI in this field, but also understands that responsible practices must be in place, especially when dealing with results that can affect medicine and people’s lives. Another project was a collaborative study by student researcher Hector Gardea. It was titled “Physical State Classifier for Closed-loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson’s Disease.” Conducted in collaboration with Duke University, the project focused on using wearable technology to track different levels of tremors in participants with Parkinson’s disease. Gardea discussed how an Apple Watch equipped with an accelerometer detects shaking motions and classifies them more accurately. In addition, the symposium featured startup presentations from the LA BioStart training program at Cal State LA, along with research highlights and panels presented by faculty in the university’s College of Engineering, Computer Science, and Technology (ECST). Researchers presented studies on how machine learning can be used to track pollution or even in applications like detecting breast cancer. Participants also had the opportunity to take part in hands-on workshops and coding activities. The event was hosted by the Sikand Center for Sustainable and Intelligent Infrastructure (Sikand SITI Center), housed within Cal State LA’s College of ECST. extraction.body: Cal State LA’s Sikand Center for Sustainable and Intelligent Infrastructure hosted a six-hour symposium on Thursday, October 29, 2026, titled “AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine.” According to Cal State LA’s official event listing, the program ran from 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM (PST) in the Golden Eagle Ballrooms and brought UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and LA BioStart into the room with the university’s engineering faculty. The pitch is simple. AI models are only as useful as the data pipelines, compute, and hospital systems underneath them. The Sikand SITI Center, an infrastructure-focused unit, put that argument at the center of a healthcare agenda. That framing separates this symposium from the usual model-launch news cycle, and it explains why the event matters to readers who follow AI and machine learning coverage. A caution on scope before the analysis begins. The story circulating under the headline that top Southern California researchers collaborated with Cal State LA student researchers goes further than the official record. The event listing confirms that researchers, faculty, and students were part of the audience and program. It does not document a specific collaboration, named student projects, or results. This article sticks to what the listing confirms and labels everything else as analysis. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The confirmed facts are compact. The event carried the title “AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine.” It took place on Thursday, October 29, 2026, between 9:00 AM and 3:00 PM (PST). The venue was Cal State LA’s Golden Eagle Ballrooms at 5151 State University, Los Angeles, CA 90032, and one official listing narrows that to the Golden Eagle BR on the third floor. The organizer is the Sikand Center for Sustainable and Intelligent Infrastructure, usually shortened to the Sikand SITI Center. Cal State LA’s listing names UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and LA BioStart as participating organizations. The official description says the symposium would address AI and data-intensive technologies in biomedical research, precision medicine, healthcare delivery, and sustainable healthcare infrastructure. That is the full set of verified detail. The listing does not name products, vendors beyond those three organizations, prices, technical specifications, or student project titles. It also contains no direct quotations from speakers. Readers who want a blow-by-blow account of what was said on stage will have to wait for the university’s own recap or for coverage from attendees. The listing spells out two afternoon blocks. An afternoon-remarks session ran from 1:00 PM to 1:15 PM, and a research-highlights session followed from 1:15 PM to 2:15 PM. The research-highlights hour is the slot where students and faculty most plausibly presented work, though the listing does not say who presented or on what topics. That distinction is worth keeping straight. A research-highlights session at a university symposium usually gives early-career researchers a stage. Whether Cal State LA students used it is plausible, and the headline claim about student collaboration rests on that inference. Without a program book, an abstract list, or a university recap, the claim stays unconfirmed. The morning program and the final hour before 3:00 PM are not itemized in the material available to us. We will not guess at panel formats or keynote topics. If Cal State LA publishes a program or recap, the research-highlights block is the first place to look for concrete project names and datasets. The title leads with intelligent infrastructure, and that word choice carries an argument. Healthcare AI fails or succeeds on plumbing: how records are stored, how data moves between hospitals and labs, how models run inside regulated environments, and how much energy and cost that burden adds. A center built around sustainable and intelligent infrastructure sees those questions as engineering problems with civil, electrical, and computing dimensions. Consider what a precision-medicine workflow needs. Genomic and clinical data must be collected, cleaned, and linked. Models need compute to train and to run. Results need to reach clinicians in a form they trust. Each step depends on facilities, networks, and software that someone has to build and maintain. That is the territory Sikand Engineering’s participation signals. Data availability is the other half of the story. Large open atlases show what shared biomedical data can do, and our coverage of the HuBMAP healthy tissue atlas is a good example of how pooled datasets change what a research group can attempt. A university symposium that pairs data-heavy medicine with infrastructure engineers is working the same problem from the supply side. The sustainability half of the title deserves its own look. Training and running large models draws real power, and hospitals already operate some of the most energy-hungry buildings in any city. A symposium that pairs AI with sustainable systems is acknowledging that every new clinical model adds load to servers, cooling, and networks. Engineers who design that supporting plant, including the kind Sikand Engineering practices, decide whether an AI pilot stays affordable once it scales beyond a single department. Precision medicine means matching treatment to the biology of an individual or a subgroup instead of the average patient. The field leans on machine learning because the signals are subtle and high-dimensional. The two Cedars-Sinai speakers hold computational biomedicine and research-scientist roles, which places their expertise at the model-building layer. We cannot report what Dr. Urbanowicz or Dr. Freda presented, because the listing does not say. What we can say is how their field works in general. Computational biomedicine groups build statistical and machine-learning methods that find patterns in clinical and molecular data, then test whether those patterns hold up across patient populations. The hard part is rarely the algorithm. It is data quality, bias, and validation. A related thread in biomedical research is the move toward richer measurement of body chemistry and digital-twin modeling. We covered one framework in our piece on third-generation metabolomics and digital twins . Symposia like this one give regional researchers a place to compare those methods with what hospitals can actually deploy. UCLA brings a large research university with deep biomedical and computing programs. Cedars-Sinai Medical Center brings a major academic medical center with clinical data and a computational research group. LA BioStart brings a startup-facing perspective, which is the commercialization end of the pipeline. The listing names the organizations and nothing more, so any detail about what each contributed on the day is outside the confirmed record. Cost discipline is part of that conversation. Public institutions run on tight budgets, and a model that needs expensive specialized hardware may never leave the research lab. Teams that plan for modest compute, shared facilities, and reuse of existing data centers tend to get further than teams that assume unlimited resources. Expect infrastructure engineers to carry more weight in health AI projects over the next few years, since their estimates decide which ideas get funded. The supplied headline says students collaborated with top regional researchers. The official listing supports a narrower reading. It describes an event engaging researchers, students, and faculty. It does not name a student, a student project, a mentorship pairing, or a joint paper. This gap is common in event coverage. Organizers write descriptions weeks ahead in forward-looking language, and secondary outlets repackage them as outcomes. The listing’s own wording says the symposium will address certain topics, which is a statement of intent, not a report. Readers should treat claims of collaboration as likely in spirit but unproven in detail. Medical AI has moved in waves. Early expert systems in the twentieth century tried to encode physician reasoning as rules and stalled on maintenance and data. Machine-learning methods applied to imaging and records in the 2010s produced stronger results on narrow tasks. The generative and foundation-model wave of 2023 through 2026 pushed attention toward language, multimodal data, and general-purpose assistants inside clinical workflows. Each wave exposed the same bottleneck. Models improved faster than the systems that had to host them. Hospitals found that data was scattered across formats, that privacy rules limited sharing, and that clinicians needed explanations they could trust. That pattern explains why a 2026 symposium puts infrastructure in its title instead of treating it as an afterthought. Open model releases have also changed who can participate. Smaller teams can now run capable models locally, which matters for sensitive health data that cannot leave an institution. For a snapshot of the field, see our open-weight model spec sheet . Local deployment is a recurring theme when universities and hospitals talk about privacy-preserving AI. Workforce is the quiet driver here. Healthcare AI needs people who can read a clinical dataset and also stand up a reliable software system. Those hybrids are scarce. Host institutions that expose students early to both worlds help fill the gap, and that is plausibly a core motivation behind the Sikand SITI Center’s programming. Educators face a parallel challenge in using AI themselves. Our coverage of the AISES-T teacher AI self-efficacy scale shows how researchers measure confidence with these tools. The same question applies to students entering biomedical computing: how comfortable are they with the tools, and how do instructors measure it? These are our own analytical expectations, not reported plans. None come from the event listing. The common thread is that the next measurable signal will be documentation. A program book, a recap post, or a published dataset would convert an inferred collaboration into a verified one. The Sikand Symposium is a modest, well-structured regional event with a sharp thesis: healthcare AI is an infrastructure problem as much as a modeling problem. The confirmed record shows a full-day program, five named speakers, three named partner organizations, and a research-highlights hour. It does not show product launches, funding, or documented student projects. That restraint is itself useful. Many AI stories inflate on the way from a listing to a headline. extraction.body: Researchers, alumni, faculty, and students in the fields of healthcare innovation, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence gathered on Oct. 29 for the 2026 Sikand Symposium at Cal State LA. With the theme of “ AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine ,” the symposium brought together speakers from Cal State LA, UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and the Sikand Foundation to share their expertise on how computational modeling and artificial intelligence can advance healthcare innovation. The keynote speaker for the symposium, Minjeong Jeon, a professor of advanced quantitative methods at the UCLA School of Education and Information Studies, kicked off the event with her presentation. Jeon discussed her research on measurement science and how network approaches can connect patients and symptoms more accurately. In layman’s terms, people with the same condition—depression, in the case of Jeon’s study—do not necessarily exhibit the same symptoms. Jeon’s proposed model and graphs aim to help researchers better understand the differing health cases of people who are dealing with medical conditions. Jeon also discussed the use of artificial intelligence models in these applications and precision medicine, but emphasized that “AI is only as clinically meaningful as the measurement system behind it.” She hopes student researchers “think about measurement” more precisely when they conduct studies in these fields and work with their data. Student researchers also showcased their collaborative projects during a poster session. One was a study that Cal State LA student researcher Brian Ta worked on, entitled “Can We Trust the Evidence Behind a Biomedical AI Decision?” In his presentation, Ta discussed the importance of understanding how AI can be used in biomedicine. He proposed methods to ensure AI systems have a multifactor authorization system in place to check who made the decisions, where the research came from, and whether that research is complete. Ta’s study recognizes the benefits of AI in this field, but also understands that responsible practices must be in place, especially when dealing with results that can affect medicine and people’s lives. Another project was a collaborative study by student researcher Hector Gardea. It was titled “Physical State Classifier for Closed-loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson’s Disease.” Conducted in collaboration with Duke University, the project focused on using wearable technology to track different levels of tremors in participants with Parkinson’s disease. Gardea discussed how an Apple Watch equipped with an accelerometer detects shaking motions and classifies them more accurately. In addition, the symposium featured startup presentations from the LA BioStart training program at Cal State LA, along with research highlights and panels presented by faculty in the university’s College of Engineering, Computer Science, and Technology (ECST). Researchers presented studies on how machine learning can be used to track pollution or even in applications like detecting breast cancer. Participants also had the opportunity to take part in hands-on workshops and coding activities. The event was hosted by the Sikand Center for Sustainable and Intelligent Infrastructure (Sikand SITI Center), housed within Cal State LA’s College of ECST. Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: There is new hope for people who have lost their smell. Scientists have successfully tested a breakthrough device that lets people detect the presence of certain odors. This innovative system helps them "smell" again by translating odors into feelings (like touch) inside the nose. The loss of smell (anosmia or hyposmia) is a major problem that affects around 20% of the global population. It can be caused by a variety of factors, such as infections, medications, or injuries and may be permanent or temporary. Unlike hearing loss or vision impairment, where cochlear implants or prosthetics are available, there are no implants or devices that can restore the sense of smell. This new research may be a vital step toward developing a practical solution for more than a billion people. The team behind the device describes their work in a paper published in the journal Science Advances . They developed a system that captures odors using an artificial nose (e-nose) and translates that chemical information into a specific digital code. This code is then passed through an intranasal electrical stimulator (a small magnetic clip) placed on the septum, the wall separating the nostrils, to trigger the trigeminal nerve. Once triggered by an electrical pulse, individuals perceive the code as a distinct sensation. They're not actually smelling, rather, their brain is learning to associate this unique feeling with a specific odor so that they can tell different odors apart. The concept behind the technology is called sensory substitution, where one functional sense transmits information from a sense that is defective. The nasal cavity has two sensory systems, which are the olfactory system for smell and the trigeminal system for temperature, touch and irritation. In this research, the device leverages the trigeminal nerve to deliver information that the olfactory nerve can no longer transmit. "This substitution approach does not allow patients to smell real odors, it is a genuine first substitution solution that we could imagine offering to patients in the future," wrote the researchers in their paper. The study authors tested their innovation on 65 people (13 with normal smell and 52 with smell loss) across four experiments. All were able to detect odorant molecules, and most could distinguish between two distinct odors. The device also worked just as well for patients who couldn't smell as it did for healthy people, meaning the trigeminal system is a reliable pathway for transmitting coded signals for everyone. The work is still in the early stages. Among the next steps for the researchers will be to increase the number of odorants and stimulation patterns tested and to turn the lab prototype into a wearable, miniaturized device for everyday use. This code is then passed through an intranasal electrical stimulator (a small magnetic clip) placed on the septum, the wall separating the nostrils, to trigger the trigeminal nerve.

Once triggered by an electrical pulse, individuals perceive the code as a distinct sensation. They're not actually smelling, rather, their brain is learning to associate this unique feeling with a specific odor so that they can tell different odors apart.

The concept behind the technology is called sensory substitution, where one functional sense transmits information from a sense that is defective. The nasal cavity has two sensory systems, which are the olfactory system for smell and the trigeminal system for temperature, touch and irritation. In this research, the device leverages the trigeminal nerve to deliver information that the olfactory nerve can no longer transmit.

"This substitution approach does not allow patients to smell real odors, it is a genuine first substitution solution that we could imagine offering to patients in the future," wrote the researchers in their paper.

The study authors tested their innovation on 65 people (13 with normal smell and 52 with smell loss) across four experiments. All were able to detect odorant molecules, and most could distinguish between two distinct odors. The device also worked just as well for patients who couldn't smell as it did for healthy people, meaning the trigeminal system is a reliable pathway for transmitting coded signals for everyone.

The work is still in the early stages. Among the next steps for the researchers will be to increase the number of odorants and stimulation patterns tested and to turn the lab prototype into a wearable, miniaturized device for everyday use.

There is new hope for people who have lost their smell. Scientists have successfully tested a breakthrough device that lets people detect the presence of certain odors. This innovative system helps them "smell" again by translating odors into feelings (like touch) inside the nose.

The loss of smell (anosmia or hyposmia) is a major problem that affects around 20% of the global population. It can be caused by a variety of factors, such as infections, medications, or injuries and may be permanent or temporary. Unlike hearing loss or vision impairment, where cochlear implants or prosthetics are available, there are no implants or devices that can restore the sense of smell. This new research may be a vital step toward developing a practical solution for more than a billion people.

The team behind the device describes their work in a paper published in the journal Science Advances . They developed a system that captures odors using an artificial nose (e-nose) and translates that chemical information into a specific digital code. This code is then passed through an intranasal electrical stimulator (a small magnetic clip) placed on the septum, the wall separating the nostrils, to trigger the trigeminal nerve.

Once triggered by an electrical pulse, individuals perceive the code as a distinct sensation. They're not actually smelling, rather, their brain is learning to associate this unique feeling with a specific odor so that they can tell different odors apart.

The concept behind the technology is called sensory substitution, where one functional sense transmits information from a sense that is defective. The nasal cavity has two sensory systems, which are the olfactory system for smell and the trigeminal system for temperature, touch and irritation. In this research, the device leverages the trigeminal nerve to deliver information that the olfactory nerve can no longer transmit.

"This substitution approach does not allow patients to smell real odors, it is a genuine first substitution solution that we could imagine offering to patients in the future," wrote the researchers in their paper.

The study authors tested their innovation on 65 people (13 with normal smell and 52 with smell loss) across four experiments. All were able to detect odorant molecules, and most could distinguish between two distinct odors. The device also worked just as well for patients who couldn't smell as it did for healthy people, meaning the trigeminal system is a reliable pathway for transmitting coded signals for everyone.

The work is still in the early stages. Among the next steps for the researchers will be to increase the number of odorants and stimulation patterns tested and to turn the lab prototype into a wearable, miniaturized device for everyday use.

extraction.body: Our sense of smell shapes how we navigate our environment, but it's a sensation that's notoriously difficult to recreate in the digital world. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed a device that uses an artificial intelligence e-nose to detect and analyze odors. Combined with a wearable release system called Scentronic, which uses machine learning algorithms to classify data in real time, the system passed the smell test in the lab by encouraging better interactions between humans and machines. This work combines innovations in hardware and software to bring new solutions to societal challenges. Our long-term goal here is to incorporate these systems into compact and personalized devices." Jinghua Li, senior author of the study and assistant professor of materials science and engineering, The Ohio State University Used in everything from medical research to online game entertainment, human-to-machine interfaces serve as digital conduits that connect people across incredible distances. Yet the majority of these systems focus on biophysical signals, such as haptic (touch-related), audio and visual cues, rather than smell, a sense critical for perception, flavor and emotional experiences. However, this study establishes a framework for an accurate, hands-free controlled olfactory stimulation device. After being trained on five distinct food scents - coffee, beer, red wine, orange and chocolate cake - field testing revealed that participants could identify individual odors about 73% of the time, and paired scents about 71% of the time. The team also found that even when Scentronic was used in tandem with interfaces that could generate taste, their results demonstrated the feasibility of programmable, cost-effective odor delivery systems to create engaging multisensory experiences, said Li. "We did see that some people are more sensitive to certain odorants than others," she said. "Despite being easy to distinguish, there was still lots of variation in intensity among individuals." The study was recently published in Science Advances. Despite being a prototype, Scentronic's design is so flexible that researchers created multiple versions to serve potential consumers. These include a wristband-type device that would allow users to carry it and lift it to the nose when they want to catch a whiff of a scent, and a necklace version where five odor channels align like pearls on a string, opening only after a signal is received. Although initially fitted with the user's comfort and functionality in mind, the ease with which these sensors were adapted to further demonstrations highlights the system's seamless ability to enhance extended reality experiences beyond mere sight and sound, said Li. Such versatility suggests Scentronic has many potential real-world applications, from supporting future assistive technologies and enhancing virtual training environments to becoming sensory aids in medical contexts, including as a way to reduce the need for frequent clinic visits, improve patient comfort and enable timely, personalized care, said Li. " The loss of olfaction is related to many neurological diseases and infections," she said. "As a result, it's important that we create technologies to first decouple the secrets within our olfactory systems and then try to reconstruct them based on that information. " Still, while it'll be a long time before the internet is fully scratch-and-sniff capable, next steps involve advancing the work by testing other ways to incorporate the team's devices into people's daily accessories, including wearable electronics like watches or other smart jewelry. "There are many potential opportunities for these technologies to shine," she said. "The initial demonstrations are promising, so digitized smells may arrive sooner than you think." Other Ohio State co-authors include Chunyu Yang, Qi Wang, Antonia Akoto-Yeboah, Shaoru Cheng, Billings Amoah, Yizhen Jia, Shulin Chen, Akhil Canumalla, Kai Zhao and Christopher Simons, as well as Chen Wang from Zhejiang Laboratory in China. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation, the Center for Brain Injury Recovery & Discovery Pilot Award at Ohio State, and the Ohio State Alumni Grant for Graduate Research and Scholarship. Dr. Laura Ajram leads the British Neuroscience Association, focusing on enhancing neuroscience research through strategic partnerships and patient engagement. sources.title: Nothing confirms first AI-native product launches next month, teases design - news.lavx.hu
passages: Nothing's first AI-native product is arriving next month, CEO Carl Pei confirmed this week.
The company teased the device with an image showing rounded corners and curved edges, but kept the actual product under wraps.
The company has been building toward this release since then, and the confirmation keeps that timeline intact.
For now, the key takeaways are simple: it launches next month, it has no screen, and it's not an app.
Everything else remains a mystery until Nothing decides to show its hand.
Pei explained that Nothing is well-positioned to build this product because the company designs both hardware and software in-house.
That vertical integration lets the team control the full user experience, something Pei argues is essential for AI-native devices.
Nothing has a track record of drip-feeding information through teasers, so the coming weeks will likely bring more hints about what the device actually does.
Nothing is also rumored to be working on AI-powered wearables, including smart glasses with and without cameras.
The company recently raised $200 million in Series C funding, which Pei said would go toward expanding its AI ambitions.
Nothing has also been pushing software updates across its phone lineup, including the stable Android 17 rollout for the Phone (4a), (4a) Pro, (3a), and (3a) Pro.
The teaser image offers only a glimpse of the device's silhouette.
Pei said the product will carry the "personality and care" associated with Nothing's existing lineup, which includes phones and earbuds.
ACME Inc. is hiring a senior software line specialist to close the gap between AI-native development and production code — a role that exists because some bugs are immune to prompting.
The article also touches on how AI is expected to evolve from a productivity tool into something that works more proactively for users.
Pei suggested that new technologies typically gain traction in the workplace before moving into homes, hinting at where Nothing sees this product fitting.

While Nothing has yet to reveal what the product actually is, Pei has offered a few hints in an article shared on X, staying true to the company's teaser-driven approach.

According to the Nothing CEO, its first AI-native product will not feature a screen. Pei also confirmed that the product “couldn’t have been an app”. The article includes a teaser image, but it only offers a glimpse of a device with rounded corners and curved edges.

No further details about the device have been shared so far. However, Pei notes that it will have the “personality and care” associated with a Nothing product. He also explained that the company was in a great position to develop it because it designs both its hardware and software under one roof.

The article also discusses how artificial intelligence is expected to evolve into something that works for us, while continuing to serve as a productivity tool. It further suggests that new technologies typically win people over in the workplace before making their way into homes.
Nothing is also rumoured to be developing AI-powered wearables , including smart glasses with and without cameras.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nothing's first AI-native product is arriving next month, CEO Carl Pei confirmed this week.
The company teased the device with an image showing rounded corners and curved edges, but kept the actual product under wraps.
The company has been building toward this release since then, and the confirmation keeps that timeline intact.
For now, the key takeaways are simple: it launches next month, it has no screen, and it's not an app.
Everything else remains a mystery until Nothing decides to show its hand.
Pei explained that Nothing is well-positioned to build this product because the company designs both hardware and software in-house.
That vertical integration lets the team control the full user experience, something Pei argues is essential for AI-native devices.
Nothing has a track record of drip-feeding information through teasers, so the coming weeks will likely bring more hints about what the device actually does.
Nothing is also rumored to be working on AI-powered wearables, including smart glasses with and without cameras.
The company recently raised $200 million in Series C funding, which Pei said would go toward expanding its AI ambitions.
Nothing has also been pushing software updates across its phone lineup, including the stable Android 17 rollout for the Phone (4a), (4a) Pro, (3a), and (3a) Pro.
The teaser image offers only a glimpse of the device's silhouette.
Pei said the product will carry the "personality and care" associated with Nothing's existing lineup, which includes phones and earbuds.
ACME Inc. is hiring a senior software line specialist to close the gap between AI-native development and production code — a role that exists because some bugs are immune to prompting.
The article also touches on how AI is expected to evolve from a productivity tool into something that works more proactively for users.
Pei suggested that new technologies typically gain traction in the workplace before moving into homes, hinting at where Nothing sees this product fitting.

Nothing's first AI-native product is arriving next month, CEO Carl Pei confirmed this week. The company teased the device with an image showing rounded corners and curved edges, but kept the actual product under wraps.

Pei shared details in an article on X, confirming the product will not feature a screen. He also said the device "couldn't have been an app," suggesting it's a dedicated piece of hardware rather than software.

The teaser image offers only a glimpse of the device's silhouette. Pei said the product will carry the "personality and care" associated with Nothing's existing lineup, which includes phones and earbuds.

Pei explained that Nothing is well-positioned to build this product because the company designs both hardware and software in-house. That vertical integration lets the team control the full user experience, something Pei argues is essential for AI-native devices.

The announcement follows Pei's September 2025 statement that Nothing planned to launch its first AI-native products in 2026. The company has been building toward this release since then, and the confirmation keeps that timeline intact.

The article also touches on how AI is expected to evolve from a productivity tool into something that works more proactively for users. Pei suggested that new technologies typically gain traction in the workplace before moving into homes, hinting at where Nothing sees this product fitting.

Nothing is also rumored to be working on AI-powered wearables, including smart glasses with and without cameras. Those reports surfaced earlier this year, and it's unclear whether next month's launch is one of those devices or something separate.

The company recently raised $200 million in Series C funding, which Pei said would go toward expanding its AI ambitions. Nothing has also been pushing software updates across its phone lineup, including the stable Android 17 rollout for the Phone (4a), (4a) Pro, (3a), and (3a) Pro.

More details about the AI-native product are expected closer to the launch date. Nothing has a track record of drip-feeding information through teasers, so the coming weeks will likely bring more hints about what the device actually does.
For now, the key takeaways are simple: it launches next month, it has no screen, and it's not an app. Everything else remains a mystery until Nothing decides to show its hand.
ACME Inc. is hiring a senior software line specialist to close the gap between AI-native development and production code — a role that exists because some bugs are immune to prompting.

sources.title: Trump Media Just Moved 4,259 Bitcoin. Is It About to Sell? - Yahoo Finance
passages: Trump Media moved 4,259 Bitcoin pledged as collateral to Crypto.com, but nothing confirms a sale, and the company hasn't explained the transfer.
While no sale has been confirmed, blockchain data shows the coins' movement without clarifying whether they were sold.
These Bitcoins are tied to a debt, and creditors can demand repayment of about $1 billion by November 30.
While a 4,259 BTC transaction is significant for one wallet, it represents only a small fraction of the overall market.
On November 4, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in a net $74.6 million, ending a three-day streak that pulled $1.3 billion from Bitcoin and Ethereum funds.
Trump Media's Bitcoin represents 4.4 times the amount brought into the ETFs that day.
Trump Media shares are trading at $4.54, up 1% but down 24% over the past week.
Although a sale could momentarily affect the price, it remains a minor part of the total market.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Trump Media has not publicly addressed the Bitcoin transfers, nor has it filed any new Form 8-K with the SEC to report significant developments.

Despite reporting a surge in revenue, with Trump Media generating $1.7 million in the second quarter—an 89% year-over-year increase—this amount pales in comparison to its $1.9 billion in financial assets.
However, even if the Bitcoin were sold, the amount wouldn't fully cover the $1 billion debt if all lenders requested cash.
Bitcoin's broader issue lies in the ongoing trend of its value, as it currently trades 39.3% below its all-time high of $126,080.
It remains below its 20-day and 50-day moving averages but stays above its 200-day average.
Arkham tracked the transfer of the coins in two batches, 2,140.03 BTC and 2,119.31 BTC, logged within an hour on that day.

sources.title: Incoming Democratic majorities put AI giants on notice

extraction.body: The period of Republican-controlled Washington's hands-off approach to the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence is about to end. Midterm voters across the country elected Democratic candidates who campaigned on legislative guardrails for AI and passed dozens of state and local ballot measures limiting construction of new data centers. SSRS exit polling found 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their votes for Congress. During a post-election press conference Wednesday with Democratic House leadership, Rep. And that was a bad decision politically and a bad decision on policy. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails on AI," Lieu, the vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus, said. Lieu co-chairs a House Democratic commission on AI formed by Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries last year. He said he and his colleagues will release a document outlining policy priorities for the new Congress. Many of the Democratic candidates who defeated incumbent Republicans ran in part on ideas for broad AI regulation. Less than 48 hours after Election Day, OpenAI announced new commitments for its data centers, including covering energy costs and investing in jobs. Democrats will likely advance policies requiring OpenAI and other AI giants to go much further than what their voluntary safety and accountability standards entail. New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies," the company said in a statement. Though Democrats won sizeable House and Senate majorities, they're not quite large enough to override a presidential veto. President Donald Trump has been a vocal opponent of regulating AI – which he calls SI, short for "super intelligence" – and a champion of data centers, but voters' resounding rejection of Republican policies may push him to find room for compromise.

passages: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027.

Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would.
Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added.
He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip.
Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month.
“Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment.
But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational.
Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.
In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips.
They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that.

extraction.body: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot. In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month. Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything. “Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said. Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would. “What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy—which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.” The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs. In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself. “Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip—from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote. Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year. While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027. The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens. “Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added. “What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy—which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.”

extraction.body: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot. In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month. Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything. “Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said. Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would. “What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy—which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.” The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs. In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself. “Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip—from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote. Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year. While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027. The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens. “Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added. With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet. While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star’s light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope’s configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets. Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function. There are two ways to figure out what the point spread function is. One is to use the telescope to image a known target and use those observations to derive a mathematical description of the point spread function. This is effective at reducing noise but has its limits, as the behavior of the telescope hardware can change over time, and the point spread function may vary with the wavelengths being imaged. The alternative is to try to model the hardware’s behavior and use that model to derive a point spread function. But modern telescopes are incredibly complicated instruments, with many, many factors feeding into their performance in ways that can be difficult to ascertain, even with the full engineering schematics. As a result, these models simply contain too many parameters that need to be tuned to make this route computationally tractable. But anyone paying attention to the world of AI developments will recognize that we’ve become quite successful at tuning billions of parameters in neural networks, in part through a mathematical technique called gradient descent. And, because this is central to training large neural networks, people have put a lot of work into optimizing the performance of gradient descent on GPUs. So a team of researchers has developed a process they’re calling FLIP (a non-acronym for Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets) that uses a physical model of the hardware (in this case, the NIRCam on the James Webb Space Telescope) with 10 6 possible parameters, and then uses software to optimize all its parameters. The optimization starts with a simulated point spread function, then uses gradient descent to optimize its performance on data from an actual star. Run on a current GPU, this process only takes a bit more than half an hour. The researchers then fine-tune the results on the actual scientific image they are analyzing. This last part of the process is critical, since some variables will differ between observations. To test how this works, the researchers used observations of two stars with known exoplanets (HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani), along with a third (TYC 5899) that doesn’t have any known exoplanets but is known to vary a lot between observations. These are young stars, and two of them have massive planets that are still warm from their gravitational collapse, allowing them to have been imaged previously. Using Webb data, the team used FLIP to boost the signal-to-noise ratio by a factor of 1.5 to 2, depending on the observations. At a wavelength that can be used to detect carbon dioxide, they were able to spot one of the planets in the Webb data for the first time. For TYC 5899, the approach boosted the sensitivity of the observations by a factor of 15. The researchers point out that the applications go beyond getting a better view of known planets. extraction.body: Software optimizes a physical model of the telescope to reduce noise. With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet. While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star’s light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope’s configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets. Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function. There are two ways to figure out what the point spread function is. One is to use the telescope to image a known target and use those observations to derive a mathematical description of the point spread function. This is effective at reducing noise but has its limits, as the behavior of the telescope hardware can change over time, and the point spread function may vary with the wavelengths being imaged. The alternative is to try to model the hardware’s behavior and use that model to derive a point spread function. But modern telescopes are incredibly complicated instruments, with many, many factors feeding into their performance in ways that can be difficult to ascertain, even with the full engineering schematics. As a result, these models simply contain too many parameters that need to be tuned to make this route computationally tractable. But anyone paying attention to the world of AI developments will recognize that we’ve become quite successful at tuning billions of parameters in neural networks, in part through a mathematical technique called gradient descent. And, because this is central to training large neural networks, people have put a lot of work into optimizing the performance of gradient descent on GPUs. So a team of researchers has developed a process they’re calling FLIP (a non-acronym for Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets) that uses a physical model of the hardware (in this case, the NIRCam on the James Webb Space Telescope) with 10 6 possible parameters, and then uses software to optimize all its parameters. The optimization starts with a simulated point spread function, then uses gradient descent to optimize its performance on data from an actual star. Run on a current GPU, this process only takes a bit more than half an hour. The researchers then fine-tune the results on the actual scientific image they are analyzing. This last part of the process is critical, since some variables will differ between observations. To test how this works, the researchers used observations of two stars with known exoplanets (HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani), along with a third (TYC 5899) that doesn’t have any known exoplanets but is known to vary a lot between observations. These are young stars, and two of them have massive planets that are still warm from their gravitational collapse, allowing them to have been imaged previously. Using Webb data, the team used FLIP to boost the signal-to-noise ratio by a factor of 1.5 to 2, depending on the observations. At a wavelength that can be used to detect carbon dioxide, they were able to spot one of the planets in the Webb data for the first time. For TYC 5899, the approach boosted the sensitivity of the observations by a factor of 15. The researchers point out that the applications go beyond getting a better view of known planets. By lowering the noise, it should also be possible to spot dimmer (and hence older or lower-mass) ones that had previously eluded detection. They also think they can modify FLIP to highlight where it’s making the most dramatic changes to the model, which can potentially tell us useful things about what’s going on with the telescope’s hardware. sources.title: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
passages: Schools are gaining the ability to block Google’s AI tools, even those in search, while keeping other Google apps.
So schools get more control, even if they don’t get the AI-free search everyone seems to want.
When schools choose which AI features to use under this new system, search will be one of the options.

Schools can leave search off if they want, but opting in will require them to choose the standard AI features or the new Guided Learning version, which won’t give away answers as readily (or so Google claims).
Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts.
The company clarified in a tweet that it will allow schools to disable Gemini apps while leaving search active for students.
Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools .
Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn’t want to use AI.
When Google revealed its new policy, the company’s VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times , which interpreted the situation as Google will “turn off search” if schools reject AI.
This has a nefarious vibe, but it’s probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google’s educational AI system will operate.
Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies.
Many will argue that Google should let schools access web search without chatbots.
However, that’s just not something Google wants to support at any level because it sees AI as the future of search.
While other search engines have settings to turn off AI tools, Google steadfastly refuses to create such a toggle (and those no-AI tricks you rely on may not work forever).
Ultimately, this is the core problem not just for education customers, but for everyone who wants to limit their exposure to AI while using Google.
However, the vagueness of Google’s blog post and public statements didn’t fully explain what it plans to do.
There are still reasons to dislike Google’s approach, but here’s how the company explains the process for schools:
This clarification does not change the calculus for educators who want to allow students to search the Internet without AI tools.
Google won’t offer that, and switching to another provider is easier said than done.
Google still has by far the most expansive index of the Internet, leaving alternatives with numerous gaps.
This could give other provides a chance to improve and offer a more viable alternative to Google.
Google is technically offering schools more choice but not the choices anyone wants.

Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools . Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn’t want to use AI. Google didn’t see the backlash coming, but now that it’s here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what’s changing.

The gist of the new policy, according to Google’s blog post, is that schools using Google apps will have to opt into its AI products going forward. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts.

When Google revealed its new policy, the company’s VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times , which interpreted the situation as Google will “turn off search” if schools reject AI. This has a nefarious vibe, but it’s probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google’s educational AI system will operate. Google’s approach may not be entirely altruistic, but it technically offers schools more choice and control than they have now. Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies.

The company clarified in a tweet that it will allow schools to disable Gemini apps while leaving search active for students. If they don’t want any AI, they can leave it all off. Essentially, Google is giving schools that want to completely block AI the ability to go all the way, even removing search from student accounts.

A Google spokesperson tells Ars that the company has not made any changes to the new policy it announced this week. However, the vagueness of Google’s blog post and public statements didn’t fully explain what it plans to do. There are still reasons to dislike Google’s approach, but here’s how the company explains the process for schools:

As things currently stand, schools can block the Gemini app, but the AI tools in search (AI Overviews and AI Mode) are still present and offer many of the same intellectual shortcuts. When schools choose which AI features to use under this new system, search will be one of the options. Schools can leave search off if they want, but opting in will require them to choose the standard AI features or the new Guided Learning version, which won’t give away answers as readily (or so Google claims).

Schools are gaining the ability to block Google’s AI tools, even those in search, while keeping other Google apps. Notably, the company’s new approach to “responsible AI for learning” does not include the ability to use search without AI. So schools get more control, even if they don’t get the AI-free search everyone seems to want.

Many will argue that Google should let schools access web search without chatbots. However, that’s just not something Google wants to support at any level because it sees AI as the future of search. While other search engines have settings to turn off AI tools, Google steadfastly refuses to create such a toggle (and those no-AI tricks you rely on may not work forever). Ultimately, this is the core problem not just for education customers, but for everyone who wants to limit their exposure to AI while using Google.

This clarification does not change the calculus for educators who want to allow students to search the Internet without AI tools. Google won’t offer that, and switching to another provider is easier said than done. Google still has by far the most expansive index of the Internet, leaving alternatives with numerous gaps. That may change in the near future, though. As a result of Google’s loss in the DOJ’s search antitrust case , it will have to provide competitors limited access to its index of the web. This could give other provides a chance to improve and offer a more viable alternative to Google.
