passages: Nothing is set to launch its first AI-native product in December 2026, CEO Carl Pei announced in a post on X on November 4.
For Nothing, the December launch will be its first step towards translating this approach into a dedicated hardware product.
Nothing had previously outlined plans to develop AI-native devices alongside an operating system designed around AI.

Carl Pei says AI’s next big opportunity lies in productivity Pei believes the industry is currently focusing too much on finding a single device that could become the equivalent of the iPhone for artificial intelligence.
The upcoming product will be a screen-free device designed to make artificial intelligence more useful in everyday workflows.
It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.
However, Pei’s accompanying post, titled ‘Toolmakers’, provides some insight into the thinking behind the product and Nothing’s broader AI strategy.
The announcement comes as Nothing looks to expand beyond smartphones and audio products into AI-powered hardware.

extraction.body: Nothing is set to launch its first AI-native product in December 2026, CEO Carl Pei announced in a post on X on November 4. The upcoming product will be a screen-free device designed to make artificial intelligence more useful in everyday workflows. Pei said the product is being built as a dedicated tool rather than an application, although he did not reveal its name, design, pricing or specific features. “Our first AI-native product ships next month. It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app,” Pei wrote. The announcement comes as Nothing looks to expand beyond smartphones and audio products into AI-powered hardware. The company has been discussing its plans to build AI-native devices and an operating system designed around artificial intelligence. The teaser offers little information about the device’s form factor. However, Pei’s accompanying post, titled ‘Toolmakers’, provides some insight into the thinking behind the product and Nothing’s broader AI strategy. Carl Pei says AI’s next big opportunity lies in productivity Pei believes the industry is currently focusing too much on finding a single device that could become the equivalent of the iPhone for artificial intelligence. “The whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life. According to Pei, the adoption of AI will follow a trajectory similar to that of personal computers and smartphones, where workplace applications helped drive initial adoption before the technology became part of everyday consumer life. He argued that personal computers first became useful through tools such as spreadsheets and word processors, while smartphones gained traction through practical applications before becoming central to entertainment and communication. “Product-market fit for AI will come in productivity first, in the tools people rely on to get real things done, and that’s where the real opportunity is today,” Pei wrote. While AI models have become increasingly capable, they often lack access to the information and context needed to perform tasks effectively. He said that even when users connect their inboxes, calendars and messaging platforms to AI agents, important information from everyday interactions can still be missed. “Think about the last time someone said something worth keeping: an idea over coffee, a throwaway comment that unblocks your whole week. Close it, and everything AI can already do gets dramatically more useful.” Pei believes the next generation of AI tools will need to move beyond chat interfaces and become more proactive. Tomorrow, it will work for you,” he said, arguing that AI could eventually change how individuals collaborate with each other, how organisations interact with people and how humans work alongside intelligent agents. For Nothing, the December launch will be its first step towards translating this approach into a dedicated hardware product. The company has not yet disclosed whether the device will be a wearable, an audio product or another category of hardware. Nothing had previously outlined plans to develop AI-native devices alongside an operating system designed around AI. The upcoming product will be its first concrete offering under that strategy. The launch also comes amid growing interest in dedicated AI hardware. Products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend AI pendant have attempted to bring AI assistants beyond smartphones, while other technology companies are exploring smart glasses and voice-enabled devices. However, Pei cautioned against expecting one device to immediately transform the AI industry. “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end,” he wrote. Nothing is expected to share more details about its first AI-native product ahead of its December launch.

passages: Nothing is preparing to launch its first AI-native device in December, and CEO Carl Pei says it will have no screen.
Pei has offered few details about the upcoming product, but describes it as a standalone tool rather than another AI-powered app.

Pei announced the launch in a post on X, describing the device as “a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product.” He added that it “has no screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”
Nothing has not disclosed the product’s form, features, price, or exact launch date.
The only concrete detail is the absence of a display, alongside a teaser image showing the Nothing logo and an ambiguous black rounded corner.
The announcement comes a little over a year after Pei first outlined Nothing’s plans for AI-native devices and an AI operating system.
There have been rumors that Nothing is developing two pairs of AI smart glasses , one of which reportedly will not have cameras.
Screen-free AI devices are not entirely new, with products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend already attempting to bring AI assistants into standalone gadgets.

He argued that personal computers first became useful through tools such as spreadsheets and word processors, while smartphones gained traction through practical applications before becoming central to entertainment and communication. “Product-market fit for AI will come in productivity first, in the tools people rely on to get real things done, and that’s where the real opportunity is today,” Pei wrote. While AI models have become increasingly capable, they often lack access to the information and context needed to perform tasks effectively. He said that even when users connect their inboxes, calendars and messaging platforms to AI agents, important information from everyday interactions can still be missed. “Think about the last time someone said something worth keeping: an idea over coffee, a throwaway comment that unblocks your whole week. Close it, and everything AI can already do gets dramatically more useful.” Pei believes the next generation of AI tools will need to move beyond chat interfaces and become more proactive. Tomorrow, it will work for you,” he said, arguing that AI could eventually change how individuals collaborate with each other, how organisations interact with people and how humans work alongside intelligent agents. For Nothing, the December launch will be its first step towards translating this approach into a dedicated hardware product. The company has not yet disclosed whether the device will be a wearable, an audio product or another category of hardware. Nothing had previously outlined plans to develop AI-native devices alongside an operating system designed around AI. The upcoming product will be its first concrete offering under that strategy. The launch also comes amid growing interest in dedicated AI hardware. Products such as the Humane AI Pin and Friend AI pendant have attempted to bring AI assistants beyond smartphones, while other technology companies are exploring smart glasses and voice-enabled devices. However, Pei cautioned against expecting one device to immediately transform the AI industry. “Looking for the iPhone of AI today is a dead end,” he wrote. Nothing is expected to share more details about its first AI-native product ahead of its December launch.

sources.title: Harbinger raises $240M after expanding into defense
passages: Electric truck startup Harbinger has raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications.
FedEx invested again after leading last year’s round, and other repeat investors included Maniv, Greycroft, and Leitmotif, a VC firm backed by Volkswagen .
Also investing this time was institutional giant Fidelity Management, which tends to invest in pre-IPO startups. (Harbinger is reportedly weighing going public.)
Founded in 2022 by former employees of now-defunct EV startup Canoo and battery company QuantumScape, Harbinger started by focusing on making one electric truck chassis.
The company has steadily expanded its efforts since.
It bought autonomy startup Phantom AI , has begun developing hybrid emergency vehicles , and revealed a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military.
While it didn’t lead this round, FedEx’s relationship with Harbinger continues to deepen.
The shipping giant’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, Paul Melander, has joined Harbinger’s board of directors.
FedEx also recently placed its first large order with Harbinger — a deal for 2,000 trucks valued at more than $300 million.
Harbinger has now raised more than $650 million to date, according to Bloomberg News, which first reported the round.

sources.title: Harbinger raises $240M to expand EV platform beyond trucks - FreightWaves
passages: Harbinger raised $240 million in Series D funding to push its electric vehicle platform into energy storage, power generation, autonomy, and defense while it ramps production for a 2,000-truck order from FedEx .
Tiger Global, Capricorn’s Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline co-led the round, the Garden Grove, California, company said Thursday.
The Series D follows a $160 million Series C last November , when FedEx placed an initial order for 53 trucks.
Harbinger said it has raised more than $650 million since its 2021 founding.

Zero-emission trucks reached a record 4.14% of U.S. truck deployments in the second half of 2025, according to CALSTART’s June 2026 Zeroing in on Zero-Emission Trucks market update , as total truck sales fell 35% year over year.
Cargo vans supplied 12,158 of the 12,996 new units.
Every other segment, including medium-duty step vans and trucks, added 838.
Harbinger’s Class 4 through Class 6 trucks fall in that group.
The release describes Harbinger as “an American industrial technology platform company” and lists commercial vehicles as one of five markets the new funding covers.
Harris told Bloomberg News in September that Harbinger had recently finished its 1,000th vehicle.
The FedEx order alone calls for twice that many trucks by the end of 2027.
Harbinger said the new money will fund the continued ramp of its medium-duty manufacturing capacity alongside the newer businesses.

Its HC Series Cab, unveiled in March , adds a gasoline range extender good for up to 500 miles, depending on configuration, and up to 15 kilowatts of exportable power, so crews don’t need a separate generator.
The company also acquired autonomy software maker Phantom AI.
Harbinger’s first defense deal came this summer: it is building the platform for an uncrewed Army supply vehicle under an American Rheinmetall contract .
It has also started selling its batteries for energy storage, Bloomberg News reported .
The Army program is in a prototype phase that typically runs three to 10 units, and no contract value has been disclosed.

“Electrification is at the core of everything we do, and increasingly, electrification is at the core of industry, defense, mobility, and AI,” said John Harris, Harbinger’s co-founder and CEO, in the release.
Fidelity Management & Research Company, Squarepoint Capital, and Xantium joined as crossover investors, and Maniv and Greycroft returned.

In an interview with Bloomberg News, Harris said the company has focused on bringing in investors that are “generally crossover or public markets focused.” FedEx and THOR Industries came in as strategic investors through TechNexus, the release said.
Paul Melander, FedEx’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, recently joined Harbinger’s board.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley served as placement agents.
“Harbinger excels at electrification, and electrification has become one of the most pressing bottlenecks of the AI era,” said Griffin Schroeder, a partner at Tiger Global.
“Harbinger’s role is not simply to give customers another option,” Harris said.
“It is to reset expectations for what critical systems should deliver.”

extraction.body: Harbinger just closed a $240 million funding round that pushes the Los Angeles-based autonomous vehicle startup past $650 million in total capital raised. The fresh cash comes as the company shifts gears from commercial electric trucks into military and defense applications, betting that Pentagon contracts will provide the revenue stability that has eluded many autonomous vehicle startups. It's a strategic pivot that mirrors OpenAI's recent defense push and signals where smart money sees the autonomous vehicle market headed. Harbinger is making a calculated bet that the path to profitability in autonomous vehicles runs through the Pentagon, not consumer driveways. The Los Angeles-based startup's $240 million raise announced today brings its total funding north of $650 million and validates a strategic shift that began quietly earlier this year when the company started developing driverless platforms specifically for military applications. Defense contractors and tech startups alike are racing to capture what industry insiders estimate could be a $50 billion market for autonomous military vehicles over the next decade. Harbinger's pivot puts it in direct competition with established players like Oshkosh Defense and emerging startups that have already secured initial Pentagon contracts. What sets Harbinger apart is its three-pronged approach. The company continues developing commercial electric trucks for fleet operators, builds specialized emergency vehicles for first responders, and now engineers autonomous platforms designed to operate in combat zones without human drivers. That diversification strategy addresses the revenue problem that has plagued pure-play autonomous vehicle startups, many of which have burned through billions chasing a consumer market that remains years away from meaningful adoption. The defense angle isn't just about new revenue streams. Military contracts typically come with longer development timelines, more patient capital expectations, and customers willing to pay premium prices for cutting-edge technology. Harbinger's approach mirrors moves across the broader tech industry. OpenAI recently hired a former Army Secretary to lead its national security efforts, while Salesforce dropped $375 million on defense AI startup Rune just weeks ago. The message is clear: government contracts, particularly in defense, offer the kind of stable, high-margin revenue that can sustain expensive R&D programs. The $240 million round itself signals strong investor confidence in this strategy. While the company hasn't disclosed the round's lead investor or valuation, the size suggests participation from both traditional venture capital firms and potentially defense-focused investment vehicles. That mix of backers could prove crucial as Harbinger navigates the complex world of military procurement, where relationships and security clearances matter as much as technology. Military contracts require navigating byzantine procurement processes, maintaining strict security protocols, and accepting that sales cycles can stretch for years. The company will need to balance the demands of commercial customers expecting rapid iteration with military clients requiring exhaustive testing and certification. Managing that dual-track development could strain resources, even with $650 million in the bank. The autonomous vehicle market has become a graveyard for overhyped startups. Companies that once commanded multi-billion dollar valuations have scaled back ambitions, merged with competitors, or shut down entirely. Harbinger's bet is that military applications will provide the proving ground and revenue base needed to perfect the technology before commercial markets fully materialize. That strategy is already attracting attention from other startups watching funding dry up in traditional autonomous vehicle categories. The shift toward defense applications could accelerate as more companies realize that Pentagon budgets offer a lifeline while consumer adoption remains sluggish. It's reminiscent of how fusion startups have increasingly traded equity for federal funding as private capital becomes more selective. Harbinger's emergency vehicle platform represents another smart hedge. Autonomous fire trucks or ambulances that can navigate through traffic more efficiently could save lives while generating revenue and real-world data to improve the underlying technology. The company's $650 million war chest positions it to weather the current funding environment, where rising bond yields have made AI infrastructure buildouts more expensive and investors have grown skeptical of long development timelines. But money alone won't guarantee success in the defense sector, where winning contracts requires demonstrating not just technical capability but also reliability, security, and the ability to scale production. What happens next will test whether Harbinger's multi-market strategy can deliver where pure-play approaches have struggled. The company needs to start converting its technology into actual military contracts while keeping commercial customers engaged and emergency vehicle programs on track. Harbinger's $240 million raise and defense expansion represent more than just another funding round in the autonomous vehicle space. It's a signal that the industry's most promising path forward may run through military bases rather than suburban garages. Whether that bet pays off depends on the company's ability to navigate defense procurement while maintaining momentum in commercial markets.

Also investing this time was institutional giant Fidelity Management, which tends to invest in pre-IPO startups. (Harbinger is reportedly weighing going public.)

It bought autonomy startup Phantom AI , has begun developing hybrid emergency vehicles , and revealed a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military.

The shipping giant’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, Paul Melander, has joined Harbinger’s board of directors.

extraction.body: Harbinger just closed a $240 million funding round that pushes the Los Angeles-based autonomous vehicle startup past $650 million in total capital raised. The fresh cash comes as the company shifts gears from commercial electric trucks into military and defense applications, betting that Pentagon contracts will provide the revenue stability that has eluded many autonomous vehicle startups. It's a strategic pivot that mirrors OpenAI's recent defense push and signals where smart money sees the autonomous vehicle market headed. Harbinger is making a calculated bet that the path to profitability in autonomous vehicles runs through the Pentagon, not consumer driveways. The Los Angeles-based startup's $240 million raise announced today brings its total funding north of $650 million and validates a strategic shift that began quietly earlier this year when the company started developing driverless platforms specifically for military applications. Defense contractors and tech startups alike are racing to capture what industry insiders estimate could be a $50 billion market for autonomous military vehicles over the next decade. Harbinger's pivot puts it in direct competition with established players like Oshkosh Defense and emerging startups that have already secured initial Pentagon contracts. What sets Harbinger apart is its three-pronged approach. The company continues developing commercial electric trucks for fleet operators, builds specialized emergency vehicles for first responders, and now engineers autonomous platforms designed to operate in combat zones without human drivers. That diversification strategy addresses the revenue problem that has plagued pure-play autonomous vehicle startups, many of which have burned through billions chasing a consumer market that remains years away from meaningful adoption. The defense angle isn't just about new revenue streams. Military contracts typically come with longer development timelines, more patient capital expectations, and customers willing to pay premium prices for cutting-edge technology. Harbinger's approach mirrors moves across the broader tech industry. OpenAI recently hired a former Army Secretary to lead its national security efforts, while Salesforce dropped $375 million on defense AI startup Rune just weeks ago. The message is clear: government contracts, particularly in defense, offer the kind of stable, high-margin revenue that can sustain expensive R&D programs. The $240 million round itself signals strong investor confidence in this strategy. While the company hasn't disclosed the round's lead investor or valuation, the size suggests participation from both traditional venture capital firms and potentially defense-focused investment vehicles. That mix of backers could prove crucial as Harbinger navigates the complex world of military procurement, where relationships and security clearances matter as much as technology. Military contracts require navigating byzantine procurement processes, maintaining strict security protocols, and accepting that sales cycles can stretch for years. The company will need to balance the demands of commercial customers expecting rapid iteration with military clients requiring exhaustive testing and certification. Managing that dual-track development could strain resources, even with $650 million in the bank. The autonomous vehicle market has become a graveyard for overhyped startups. Companies that once commanded multi-billion dollar valuations have scaled back ambitions, merged with competitors, or shut down entirely. Harbinger's bet is that military applications will provide the proving ground and revenue base needed to perfect the technology before commercial markets fully materialize. That strategy is already attracting attention from other startups watching funding dry up in traditional autonomous vehicle categories. The shift toward defense applications could accelerate as more companies realize that Pentagon budgets offer a lifeline while consumer adoption remains sluggish. It's reminiscent of how fusion startups have increasingly traded equity for federal funding as private capital becomes more selective. Harbinger's emergency vehicle platform represents another smart hedge. Autonomous fire trucks or ambulances that can navigate through traffic more efficiently could save lives while generating revenue and real-world data to improve the underlying technology. The company's $650 million war chest positions it to weather the current funding environment, where rising bond yields have made AI infrastructure buildouts more expensive and investors have grown skeptical of long development timelines. But money alone won't guarantee success in the defense sector, where winning contracts requires demonstrating not just technical capability but also reliability, security, and the ability to scale production. What happens next will test whether Harbinger's multi-market strategy can deliver where pure-play approaches have struggled. The company needs to start converting its technology into actual military contracts while keeping commercial customers engaged and emergency vehicle programs on track. Harbinger's $240 million raise and defense expansion represent more than just another funding round in the autonomous vehicle space. It's a signal that the industry's most promising path forward may run through military bases rather than suburban garages. Whether that bet pays off depends on the company's ability to navigate defense procurement while maintaining momentum in commercial markets.

facts.text: Electric truck startup Harbinger has raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications.
FedEx invested again after leading last year’s round, and other repeat investors included Maniv, Greycroft, and Leitmotif, a VC firm backed by Volkswagen .
Also investing this time was institutional giant Fidelity Management, which tends to invest in pre-IPO startups. (Harbinger is reportedly weighing going public.)
Founded in 2022 by former employees of now-defunct EV startup Canoo and battery company QuantumScape, Harbinger started by focusing on making one electric truck chassis.
The company has steadily expanded its efforts since.
It bought autonomy startup Phantom AI , has begun developing hybrid emergency vehicles , and revealed a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military.
While it didn’t lead this round, FedEx’s relationship with Harbinger continues to deepen.
The shipping giant’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, Paul Melander, has joined Harbinger’s board of directors.
FedEx also recently placed its first large order with Harbinger — a deal for 2,000 trucks valued at more than $300 million.
Harbinger has now raised more than $650 million to date, according to Bloomberg News, which first reported the round.

Harbinger raised $240 million in Series D funding to push its electric vehicle platform into energy storage, power generation, autonomy, and defense while it ramps production for a 2,000-truck order from FedEx .
Tiger Global, Capricorn’s Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline co-led the round, the Garden Grove, California, company said Thursday.
The Series D follows a $160 million Series C last November , when FedEx placed an initial order for 53 trucks.
Harbinger said it has raised more than $650 million since its 2021 founding.

Zero-emission trucks reached a record 4.14% of U.S. truck deployments in the second half of 2025, according to CALSTART’s June 2026 Zeroing in on Zero-Emission Trucks market update , as total truck sales fell 35% year over year.
Cargo vans supplied 12,158 of the 12,996 new units.
Every other segment, including medium-duty step vans and trucks, added 838.
Harbinger’s Class 4 through Class 6 trucks fall in that group.
The release describes Harbinger as “an American industrial technology platform company” and lists commercial vehicles as one of five markets the new funding covers.
Harris told Bloomberg News in September that Harbinger had recently finished its 1,000th vehicle.
The FedEx order alone calls for twice that many trucks by the end of 2027.
Harbinger said the new money will fund the continued ramp of its medium-duty manufacturing capacity alongside the newer businesses.

Its HC Series Cab, unveiled in March , adds a gasoline range extender good for up to 500 miles, depending on configuration, and up to 15 kilowatts of exportable power, so crews don’t need a separate generator.
The company also acquired autonomy software maker Phantom AI.
Harbinger’s first defense deal came this summer: it is building the platform for an uncrewed Army supply vehicle under an American Rheinmetall contract .
It has also started selling its batteries for energy storage, Bloomberg News reported .
The Army program is in a prototype phase that typically runs three to 10 units, and no contract value has been disclosed.

“Electrification is at the core of everything we do, and increasingly, electrification is at the core of industry, defense, mobility, and AI,” said John Harris, Harbinger’s co-founder and CEO, in the release.
Fidelity Management & Research Company, Squarepoint Capital, and Xantium joined as crossover investors, and Maniv and Greycroft returned.

In an interview with Bloomberg News, Harris said the company has focused on bringing in investors that are “generally crossover or public markets focused.” FedEx and THOR Industries came in as strategic investors through TechNexus, the release said.
Paul Melander, FedEx’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, recently joined Harbinger’s board.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley served as placement agents.
“Harbinger excels at electrification, and electrification has become one of the most pressing bottlenecks of the AI era,” said Griffin Schroeder, a partner at Tiger Global.
“Harbinger’s role is not simply to give customers another option,” Harris said.
“It is to reset expectations for what critical systems should deliver.”

In total, the maker of medium-duty electric trucks has now raised over $650 million since 2021, the company said in a statement.

“We’ve been focused for a long time on pretty carefully curating what the investor mix looks like to reflect the stage that the company is at,” said John Harris, co-founder and CEO of Harbinger in an interview with Bloomberg News.

extraction.body: Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space. In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process. “This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

relevantPassages.text: Blue Origin , which is run by Amazon.com founder Jeff Bezos , announced today (Feb.
25) that it's pushing the target date for the debut launch of its heavy-lift New Glenn rocket from late 2021 to the fourth quarter of 2022.
Blue Origin continues to make good progress on New Glenn and its launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, company representatives wrote in today's update.
The company has already scored New Glenn launch contracts with Eutelsat, Mu Space, OneWeb, Sky Perfect JSAT and Telesat, as Space News noted .
And NASA recently made New Glenn eligible to compete for contracts under the agency's Launch Services II program, which applies to launches through December 2027.
"We hope to launch NSSL payloads in the future, and remain committed to serving the U.S. national defense mission."
The rocket will be capable of launching 50 tons (45 metric tons) to low Earth orbit when it's up and running, according to its specifications page .
Bezos has said he hopes New Glenn will fly people as well as payloads.
Such reuse is key to Blue Origin's overall vision, which involves helping humanity extend its footprint out into the final frontier .
For example, the company's New Shepard rocket-capsule combo , which is designed to take people and payloads to suborbital space, is fully reusable.
One New Shepard vehicle has flown seven uncrewed test flights, acing its landing each time. (New Shepard is not yet operational, but its first crewed spaceflights could happen soon .)

New Glenn is a two-stage rocket that stands 322 feet tall (98 meters) and is named after NASA astronaut John Glenn, who in February 1962 became the first American to circle Earth. (Cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin was the first person overall, pulling off the feat in April 1961.)

sources.title: Blue Origin launches twin NASA Mars probes in second flight of New Glenn rocket
passages: The next such window opens in 2026.To make Wednesday's New Glenn launch work in 2025, mission planners with Advanced Space LLC came up with an innovative flight plan, one that will take Blue and Gold longer to reach Mars but will enable more flexible trajectories for future missions.The probes were deployed on a trajectory that will carry them a million miles out, well past the moon's orbit, where they will loiter for the next 11 months before heading back toward Earth.Passing within 600 miles of Earth in November 2027, the ESCAPADE probes will make velocity-boosting gravity assist flybys, augmented by onboard propulsion, to finally head for Mars.In all, the twin spacecraft will spend a full year in that initial kidney bean-shaped orbit out past the moon and back, and another 10 months in transit to Mars.

But for a variety of reasons, the Mars satellites mission ultimately ended up on New Glenn's second flight.Mars launch windows typically open every two years when Earth and the red planet reach favorable positions in their orbits to permit direct flights using current rockets.

Much like returning SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, the larger New Glenn booster will be hauled back to Port Canaveral and, depending on its condition, be refurbished and readied for use on an upcoming New Glenn flight.The second stage, meanwhile, pressed ahead, carrying out two firings of its twin engines to reach the planned Earth-escape trajectory.

ET, majestically pushing the booster skyward atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust.The launch came three days late due to stormy weather on Earth and in space, where a powerful solar storm buffeted Earth's atmosphere with a torrent of high-energy radiation that could have caused electrical problems with the rocket or its payloads.The storm had abated by launch time Wednesday, and Blue Origin employees, looking on from viewing sites several miles from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station launch pad, cheered and applauded as the booster climbed skyward, followed moments later by the booming roar of its engines sweeping across the Space Coast.
This time around, the big rocket flew itself to an on-target touchdown, prompting more cheers and applause from Blue Origin workers.

The New Glenn's maiden flight last January successfully boosted a Blue Origin payload into orbit, but the reusable first stage failed in its attempt to reach an offshore landing ship, named after Bezos' mother, Jacklyn. We've never had that before, and that's really exciting," Lillis said.

extraction.body: Last week’s explosion of a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket on the pad at Cape Canaveral prompted dire predictions that the company might not be able to launch again until late 2027 at the earliest. CEO Dave Limp, though, said that’s not the case. “Now that we’ve had access to the pad and integration facility, we can share a bit of good news,” he said in an update on X. “We will fly again before the end of this year.” He said the propellant farm, oxygen, liquid hydrogen and liquefied natural gas tanks were all in decent shape. “This is good luck because these are very long lead items. The water tower is also good. The big support tower is damaged, but it can be repaired in place rather than torn down and replaced,” he said. Here's our video of the explosion at Launch Complex 36. It happened about 9 pm ET (0100 UTC) as Blue Origin was beginning a static fire test of its New Glenn rocket. The pad was engulfed in a fireball from a static fire test last Thursday. A New Glenn rocket had been preparing for what would have been the fourth launch of its kind for Jeff Bezos’ rocket company when it burst into a mushroom cloud. The nighttime explosion could be seen as far away as Orlando and measured 2.5 on the Richter scale, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. The rocket and the transporter erector tower that was holding it in place for the test were destroyed while one of the two lightning towers on the pad crumbled to the ground. Limp said the company had already been working on eliminating the need for the transporter-erector in favor of an alternative concept. “We’ll now go directly to that; so we don’t need a new transporter-erector,” he said. He also said rocket parts that had been within a neighboring building fared well. That includes what for now is the lone remaining New Glenn first stage, “Never Tell Me The Odds,” which was flown and recovered on the rocket’s second and third missions. Limp also noted that while the company had been working at an adjacent launch pad at Canaveral’s Launch Complex 36 to support a planned larger version of the New Glenn rocket in the future, the company would not simply shift efforts to that, and would keep its efforts going for the current rocket design. The first and second stages for New Glenn continue to be manufactured at the company’s massive site on neighboring Merritt Island. Limp said that work has been going well. “We’re going to continue that at pace as planned and store the stages for use,” he said. SpaceX suffered a similar launch pad explosion a decade ago at Canaveral’s Space Launch Complex 40, and was not able to fly again from that pad for another 15 months. Limp, though, said he expects a much more optimistic timeline. Before the explosion, Blue Origin had been looking to fly the first of 24 contracted missions for the Amazon Leo satellite constellation. The 48 satellites were not installed on the rocket when it exploded, but those will have to wait. Blue Origin had also planned on launching its first moon mission with its uncrewed Blue Moon MK1 lander as part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services mission as early as this fall. Earlier this year, Limp stated he hoped New Glenn would launch at least eight times. New Kennedy Space Center Director Brian Hughes said Tuesday during a Space Florida board meeting that NASA was keen to get Blue Origin back online. “We certainly will do everything in our power at NASA and working with our friends at Space Force to be there as partners to make that happen,” he said. Blue Origin was also in line to fly the larger Blue Moon MK2, a crew-capable version of its lander, as part of the Artemis III mission, which seeks to test out the ability of NASA’s Orion spacecraft to dock with moon landers during a low-Earth orbit mission that was aiming to fly by mid 2027. “So the impact to NASA’s planning exists,” Hughes said. “We obviously … had launch needs that were scheduled to be met by Blue, so part of the reason we’ll be rooting for them to get back on their feet as quick as possible is some of that planning.” He noted with surprise just how resilient some of the launch pad infrastructure had been despite the explosion, crediting the design and planning that has gone into the newer launch pads on the Space Coast. He said getting back to business at LC-36 before the end of the year isn’t out of the question. “It is ambitious, but I would never count out the folks in those companies, because they have a pretty good record of turning ambition into action,” he said. extraction.body: Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space. In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process. “This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . We'll have to wait another year to see Blue Origin's giant orbital rocket get off the ground. Blue Origin , which is run by Amazon.com founder Jeff Bezos , announced today (Feb. 25) that it's pushing the target date for the debut launch of its heavy-lift New Glenn rocket from late 2021 to the fourth quarter of 2022. "This updated maiden flight target follows the recent Space Force decision to not select New Glenn for the National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 2 Launch Services Procurement (LSP)," Blue Origin representatives wrote in an update today . Related: NASA taps Blue Origin's New Glenn to launch future missions Blue Origin and Northrop Grumman lost out to SpaceX and United Launch Alliance in that national-security launch decision, which the Space Force announced in August 2020 . New Glenn is a two-stage rocket that stands 322 feet tall (98 meters) and is named after NASA astronaut John Glenn, who in February 1962 became the first American to circle Earth. (Cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin was the first person overall, pulling off the feat in April 1961.) The rocket will be capable of launching 50 tons (45 metric tons) to low Earth orbit when it's up and running, according to its specifications page . Bezos has said he hopes New Glenn will fly people as well as payloads. Each New Glenn first stage will be capable of launching 25 missions, Blue Origins representatives say. Shortly after liftoff, the booster will come back to Earth and land on a ship at sea, as we've already seen the first stages of SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets do. Such reuse is key to Blue Origin's overall vision, which involves helping humanity extend its footprint out into the final frontier . For example, the company's New Shepard rocket-capsule combo , which is designed to take people and payloads to suborbital space, is fully reusable. One New Shepard vehicle has flown seven uncrewed test flights, acing its landing each time. (New Shepard is not yet operational, but its first crewed spaceflights could happen soon .) Blue Origin continues to make good progress on New Glenn and its launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, company representatives wrote in today's update. The company has already scored New Glenn launch contracts with Eutelsat, Mu Space, OneWeb, Sky Perfect JSAT and Telesat, as Space News noted . And NASA recently made New Glenn eligible to compete for contracts under the agency's Launch Services II program, which applies to launches through December 2027. "New Glenn is proceeding to fulfill its current commercial contracts, pursue a large and growing commercial market, and enter into new civil space launch contracts," Blue Origin representatives wrote in today's update. "We hope to launch NSSL payloads in the future, and remain committed to serving the U.S. national defense mission." We'll have to wait another year to see Blue Origin's giant orbital rocket get off the ground.

Blue Origin , which is run by Amazon.com founder Jeff Bezos , announced today (Feb. 25) that it's pushing the target date for the debut launch of its heavy-lift New Glenn rocket from late 2021 to the fourth quarter of 2022.

"This updated maiden flight target follows the recent Space Force decision to not select New Glenn for the National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 2 Launch Services Procurement (LSP)," Blue Origin representatives wrote in an update today . Related: NASA taps Blue Origin's New Glenn to launch future missions
Blue Origin and Northrop Grumman lost out to SpaceX and United Launch Alliance in that national-security launch decision, which the Space Force announced in August 2020 .

New Glenn is a two-stage rocket that stands 322 feet tall (98 meters) and is named after NASA astronaut John Glenn, who in February 1962 became the first American to circle Earth. (Cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin was the first person overall, pulling off the feat in April 1961.)

The rocket will be capable of launching 50 tons (45 metric tons) to low Earth orbit when it's up and running, according to its specifications page . Bezos has said he hopes New Glenn will fly people as well as payloads.

Each New Glenn first stage will be capable of launching 25 missions, Blue Origins representatives say. Shortly after liftoff, the booster will come back to Earth and land on a ship at sea, as we've already seen the first stages of SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets do.

Such reuse is key to Blue Origin's overall vision, which involves helping humanity extend its footprint out into the final frontier . For example, the company's New Shepard rocket-capsule combo , which is designed to take people and payloads to suborbital space, is fully reusable. One New Shepard vehicle has flown seven uncrewed test flights, acing its landing each time. (New Shepard is not yet operational, but its first crewed spaceflights could happen soon .)

Blue Origin continues to make good progress on New Glenn and its launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, company representatives wrote in today's update. The company has already scored New Glenn launch contracts with Eutelsat, Mu Space, OneWeb, Sky Perfect JSAT and Telesat, as Space News noted . And NASA recently made New Glenn eligible to compete for contracts under the agency's Launch Services II program, which applies to launches through December 2027.

"New Glenn is proceeding to fulfill its current commercial contracts, pursue a large and growing commercial market, and enter into new civil space launch contracts," Blue Origin representatives wrote in today's update. "We hope to launch NSSL payloads in the future, and remain committed to serving the U.S. national defense mission."

sources.title: Blue Origin launches twin NASA Mars probes in second flight of New Glenn rocket
passages: The next such window opens in 2026.To make Wednesday's New Glenn launch work in 2025, mission planners with Advanced Space LLC came up with an innovative flight plan, one that will take Blue and Gold longer to reach Mars but will enable more flexible trajectories for future missions.The probes were deployed on a trajectory that will carry them a million miles out, well past the moon's orbit, where they will loiter for the next 11 months before heading back toward Earth.Passing within 600 miles of Earth in November 2027, the ESCAPADE probes will make velocity-boosting gravity assist flybys, augmented by onboard propulsion, to finally head for Mars.In all, the twin spacecraft will spend a full year in that initial kidney bean-shaped orbit out past the moon and back, and another 10 months in transit to Mars.

But for a variety of reasons, the Mars satellites mission ultimately ended up on New Glenn's second flight.Mars launch windows typically open every two years when Earth and the red planet reach favorable positions in their orbits to permit direct flights using current rockets.

Much like returning SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, the larger New Glenn booster will be hauled back to Port Canaveral and, depending on its condition, be refurbished and readied for use on an upcoming New Glenn flight.The second stage, meanwhile, pressed ahead, carrying out two firings of its twin engines to reach the planned Earth-escape trajectory.

ET, majestically pushing the booster skyward atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust.The launch came three days late due to stormy weather on Earth and in space, where a powerful solar storm buffeted Earth's atmosphere with a torrent of high-energy radiation that could have caused electrical problems with the rocket or its payloads.The storm had abated by launch time Wednesday, and Blue Origin employees, looking on from viewing sites several miles from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station launch pad, cheered and applauded as the booster climbed skyward, followed moments later by the booming roar of its engines sweeping across the Space Coast.
This time around, the big rocket flew itself to an on-target touchdown, prompting more cheers and applause from Blue Origin workers.

extraction.body: ET, majestically pushing the booster skyward atop 3.8 million pounds of thrust.The launch came three days late due to stormy weather on Earth and in space, where a powerful solar storm buffeted Earth's atmosphere with a torrent of high-energy radiation that could have caused electrical problems with the rocket or its payloads.The storm had abated by launch time Wednesday, and Blue Origin employees, looking on from viewing sites several miles from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station launch pad, cheered and applauded as the booster climbed skyward, followed moments later by the booming roar of its engines sweeping across the Space Coast. The New Glenn's maiden flight last January successfully boosted a Blue Origin payload into orbit, but the reusable first stage failed in its attempt to reach an offshore landing ship, named after Bezos' mother, Jacklyn. The 188-foot-tall first stage launched Wednesday, nicknamed "Never Tell Me The Odds," featured a variety of upgrades to improve performance. This time around, the big rocket flew itself to an on-target touchdown, prompting more cheers and applause from Blue Origin workers. Much like returning SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, the larger New Glenn booster will be hauled back to Port Canaveral and, depending on its condition, be refurbished and readied for use on an upcoming New Glenn flight.The second stage, meanwhile, pressed ahead, carrying out two firings of its twin engines to reach the planned Earth-escape trajectory. Thirty-three minutes after liftoff, the ESCAPADE satellites were released to fly on their own.The NASA-sponsored payload, managed by the University of California, Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory, is made up of two small, low-budget satellites known as Blue and Gold that make up the heart of the ESCAPADE mission. The acronym stands for Escape, Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers.The probes were built for UC Berkeley by Rocketlab under a NASA program intended to develop lower-cost, fast-track planetary missions.ESCAPADE cost $107.4 million, a bargain compared to the cost of more traditional, more sophisticated planetary spacecraft that can cost hundreds of millions to well over a billion dollars each.The ESCAPADE probes were originally expected to hitch a ride to Mars a few years ago with NASA's Psyche asteroid probe. But for a variety of reasons, the Mars satellites mission ultimately ended up on New Glenn's second flight.Mars launch windows typically open every two years when Earth and the red planet reach favorable positions in their orbits to permit direct flights using current rockets. The next such window opens in 2026.To make Wednesday's New Glenn launch work in 2025, mission planners with Advanced Space LLC came up with an innovative flight plan, one that will take Blue and Gold longer to reach Mars but will enable more flexible trajectories for future missions.The probes were deployed on a trajectory that will carry them a million miles out, well past the moon's orbit, where they will loiter for the next 11 months before heading back toward Earth.Passing within 600 miles of Earth in November 2027, the ESCAPADE probes will make velocity-boosting gravity assist flybys, augmented by onboard propulsion, to finally head for Mars.In all, the twin spacecraft will spend a full year in that initial kidney bean-shaped orbit out past the moon and back, and another 10 months in transit to Mars. "We know that atmospheric escape from Mars is a major driver for the evolution of the Martian climate. We know that Mars at least was episodically warm and wet for a couple billion years, but hasn't been so for about 2 billion years or so. And we think atmospheric escape is a major reason for that."Blue and Gold will provide what amounts to a stereo view of those processes."If you only have one spacecraft, you can either measure what the sun is throwing at Mars, the so-called space weather environment upstream of Mars, or you can measure the conditions close to Mars in its upper atmosphere, where the atmosphere is escaping," Lillis said."You can't be in two places at once. We've never had that before, and that's really exciting," Lillis said.

extraction.body: Last week’s explosion of a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket on the pad at Cape Canaveral prompted dire predictions that the company might not be able to launch again until late 2027 at the earliest. CEO Dave Limp, though, said that’s not the case. “Now that we’ve had access to the pad and integration facility, we can share a bit of good news,” he said in an update on X. “We will fly again before the end of this year.” He said the propellant farm, oxygen, liquid hydrogen and liquefied natural gas tanks were all in decent shape. “This is good luck because these are very long lead items. The water tower is also good. The big support tower is damaged, but it can be repaired in place rather than torn down and replaced,” he said. Here's our video of the explosion at Launch Complex 36. It happened about 9 pm ET (0100 UTC) as Blue Origin was beginning a static fire test of its New Glenn rocket. The pad was engulfed in a fireball from a static fire test last Thursday. A New Glenn rocket had been preparing for what would have been the fourth launch of its kind for Jeff Bezos’ rocket company when it burst into a mushroom cloud. The nighttime explosion could be seen as far away as Orlando and measured 2.5 on the Richter scale, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. The rocket and the transporter erector tower that was holding it in place for the test were destroyed while one of the two lightning towers on the pad crumbled to the ground. Limp said the company had already been working on eliminating the need for the transporter-erector in favor of an alternative concept. “We’ll now go directly to that; so we don’t need a new transporter-erector,” he said. He also said rocket parts that had been within a neighboring building fared well. That includes what for now is the lone remaining New Glenn first stage, “Never Tell Me The Odds,” which was flown and recovered on the rocket’s second and third missions. Limp also noted that while the company had been working at an adjacent launch pad at Canaveral’s Launch Complex 36 to support a planned larger version of the New Glenn rocket in the future, the company would not simply shift efforts to that, and would keep its efforts going for the current rocket design. The first and second stages for New Glenn continue to be manufactured at the company’s massive site on neighboring Merritt Island. Limp said that work has been going well. “We’re going to continue that at pace as planned and store the stages for use,” he said. SpaceX suffered a similar launch pad explosion a decade ago at Canaveral’s Space Launch Complex 40, and was not able to fly again from that pad for another 15 months. Limp, though, said he expects a much more optimistic timeline. Before the explosion, Blue Origin had been looking to fly the first of 24 contracted missions for the Amazon Leo satellite constellation. The 48 satellites were not installed on the rocket when it exploded, but those will have to wait. Blue Origin had also planned on launching its first moon mission with its uncrewed Blue Moon MK1 lander as part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services mission as early as this fall. Earlier this year, Limp stated he hoped New Glenn would launch at least eight times. New Kennedy Space Center Director Brian Hughes said Tuesday during a Space Florida board meeting that NASA was keen to get Blue Origin back online. “We certainly will do everything in our power at NASA and working with our friends at Space Force to be there as partners to make that happen,” he said. Blue Origin was also in line to fly the larger Blue Moon MK2, a crew-capable version of its lander, as part of the Artemis III mission, which seeks to test out the ability of NASA’s Orion spacecraft to dock with moon landers during a low-Earth orbit mission that was aiming to fly by mid 2027. “So the impact to NASA’s planning exists,” Hughes said. “We obviously … had launch needs that were scheduled to be met by Blue, so part of the reason we’ll be rooting for them to get back on their feet as quick as possible is some of that planning.” He noted with surprise just how resilient some of the launch pad infrastructure had been despite the explosion, crediting the design and planning that has gone into the newer launch pads on the Space Coast. He said getting back to business at LC-36 before the end of the year isn’t out of the question. “It is ambitious, but I would never count out the folks in those companies, because they have a pretty good record of turning ambition into action,” he said. passages: Last week’s explosion of a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket on the pad at Cape Canaveral prompted dire predictions that the company might not be able to launch again until late 2027 at the earliest.
CEO Dave Limp, though, said that’s not the case.
“Now that we’ve had access to the pad and integration facility, we can share a bit of good news,” he said in an update on X. “We will fly again before the end of this year.”
He said the propellant farm, oxygen, liquid hydrogen and liquefied natural gas tanks were all in decent shape.

“This is good luck because these are very long lead items. The water tower is also good. The big support tower is damaged, but it can be repaired in place rather than torn down and replaced,” he said.
Here's our video of the explosion at Launch Complex 36. It happened about 9 pm ET (0100 UTC) as Blue Origin was beginning a static fire test of its New Glenn rocket.

The pad was engulfed in a fireball from a static fire test last Thursday. A New Glenn rocket had been preparing for what would have been the fourth launch of its kind for Jeff Bezos’ rocket company when it burst into a mushroom cloud. The nighttime explosion could be seen as far away as Orlando and measured 2.5 on the Richter scale, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
The rocket and the transporter erector tower that was holding it in place for the test were destroyed while one of the two lightning towers on the pad crumbled to the ground.
Limp said the company had already been working on eliminating the need for the transporter-erector in favor of an alternative concept.
“We’ll now go directly to that; so we don’t need a new transporter-erector,” he said.

He also said rocket parts that had been within a neighboring building fared well. That includes what for now is the lone remaining New Glenn first stage, “Never Tell Me The Odds,” which was flown and recovered on the rocket’s second and third missions.

Limp also noted that while the company had been working at an adjacent launch pad at Canaveral’s Launch Complex 36 to support a planned larger version of the New Glenn rocket in the future, the company would not simply shift efforts to that, and would keep its efforts going for the current rocket design.
The first and second stages for New Glenn continue to be manufactured at the company’s massive site on neighboring Merritt Island. Limp said that work has been going well.
“We’re going to continue that at pace as planned and store the stages for use,” he said.
SpaceX suffered a similar launch pad explosion a decade ago at Canaveral’s Space Launch Complex 40, and was not able to fly again from that pad for another 15 months.
Limp, though, said he expects a much more optimistic timeline.

Before the explosion, Blue Origin had been looking to fly the first of 24 contracted missions for the Amazon Leo satellite constellation. The 48 satellites were not installed on the rocket when it exploded, but those will have to wait.
Blue Origin had also planned on launching its first moon mission with its uncrewed Blue Moon MK1 lander as part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services mission as early as this fall.
Earlier this year, Limp stated he hoped New Glenn would launch at least eight times.
New Kennedy Space Center Director Brian Hughes said Tuesday during a Space Florida board meeting that NASA was keen to get Blue Origin back online.
“We certainly will do everything in our power at NASA and working with our friends at Space Force to be there as partners to make that happen,” he said.

Blue Origin was also in line to fly the larger Blue Moon MK2, a crew-capable version of its lander, as part of the Artemis III mission, which seeks to test out the ability of NASA’s Orion spacecraft to dock with moon landers during a low-Earth orbit mission that was aiming to fly by mid 2027.

“So the impact to NASA’s planning exists,” Hughes said. “We obviously … had launch needs that were scheduled to be met by Blue, so part of the reason we’ll be rooting for them to get back on their feet as quick as possible is some of that planning.”

He noted with surprise just how resilient some of the launch pad infrastructure had been despite the explosion, crediting the design and planning that has gone into the newer launch pads on the Space Coast.
He said getting back to business at LC-36 before the end of the year isn’t out of the question.
“It is ambitious, but I would never count out the folks in those companies, because they have a pretty good record of turning ambition into action,” he said.

sources.pageTitle: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters - Ars Technica

AMD posts record first-quarter results, driven by skyrocketing data center CPU demand — company expects consumer and gaming revenue to decline in Q2 over rising memory and component costs | Tom's Hardware
AMD doubles data center revenue year over year, but gaming revenue plunged by 31% — CEO Lisa Su says prices have 'weighed on' consumer demand but is 'optimistic' about client market | Tom's Hardware
AMD rakes in cash with best quarterly revenue ever amid datacenter business rise, but gaming business craters | Tom's Hardware

sources.title: AMD posts record first-quarter results, driven by skyrocketing data center CPU demand — company expects consumer and gaming revenue to decline in Q2 over rising memory and component costs - Tom's Hardware
passages: On Tuesday, AMD reported its financial results for the first quarter of 2026.

Driven by record demand for AMD's EPYC server processors, Ryzen CPUs, and Instinct accelerators, the company's revenue totaled $10.253 billion, slightly down quarter-over-quarter (QoQ), but up significantly year-over-year (YoY).
Furthermore, AMD raised its long-term outlook for the server CPU market, expecting it to reach $120 billion by 2030 due to increased demand from AI and agentic AI workloads.
At the same time, the company admitted that sales of its AI accelerators were down sequentially.
Looking ahead, we expect server growth to accelerate meaningfully as we scale supply to meet demand."
AMD said server CPU sales increased more than 50% from the same quarter last year, with both cloud and enterprise demand growing over 50%.
AMD warned that both client and gaming revenue in the second half of the year would decline by more than 20% compared to the first half because of higher memory and component costs.
"In response to this demand, we are working closely with our supply chain partners to meaningfully increase our wafer and back-end capacity to support this growth," Su said.
Client revenue alone reached $2.9 billion, up 26%, driven by strong Ryzen processor demand and commercial PC share gains.
Gaming revenue rose 11% to $720 million due to stronger Radeon GPU demand.

"[Q2 results will be ]driven by a very strong growth in our data center segment, [modest] growth in our client and the gaming segment, and a double-digit growth in our embedded segment," said Jean Hu, AMD executive vice president, CFO and treasurer.
The business unit generated $338 million operating income, up from $328 million a year ago.
AMD projects Q2 2026 revenue to reach about $11.2 billion ± $300 million.
The company also expects non-GAAP gross margin to be around 56%.

"In graphics, revenue increased year-over-year, led by demand for our latest generation Radeon nine thousand series GPUs. sources.title: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters
passages: AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company’s gaming segment cratered.
AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs .
AMD CFO Jean Hu said, “We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%.
As reported by Tom’s Hardware , Intel’s Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion.
That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel’s revenue for the first time in history.
The gaming segment of AMD’s business is composed of two main sources.
There are semi-custom processors that AMD supplies to other manufacturers’ consoles, as well as its own Radeon graphics business.
Embedded segment revenue, or all the SoCs , FPGAs , and boards under AMD’s umbrella that go into other hardware, was $1.1 billion, up 29 percent.
AMD attributed this growth to gains made in the “aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial end markets.”

AMD also announced that Windows-based systems running on its Ryzen AI Halo platform will be “coming soon.” Known as Project Zenith , the effort will support a developer-focused Windows experience on the current PRO 400 Series platform .

On the call, Su stated that AMD “started shipping MI455X in volume in the quarter, and lead customers, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle, brought their first Helios racks online quickly.”
The new AMD Threadripper Halo Station , which AMD first showed at IFA in September , pairs a Threadripper 9995WX CPU with up to four Instinct MI350P GPUs and can run trillion-parameter LLMs locally.
The system is slated for a release sometime in 2027, with pricing still to be announced.

AMD CFO Jean Hu said, “We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel’s revenue for the first time in history. The data center segment of AMD’s business was up 97 percent year over year, with a record $8.5 billion. AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs . Sales of AMD Ryzen mobile chips led growth in the Client business, which includes desktop Ryzen processors and posted $2.95 billion in revenue, up 7 percent year over year. Gaming revenue fell sharply for the company, posting a 40 percent drop in revenue at $773 million, which AMD attributes to “lower semi-custom and graphics revenue.” Operating margins in AMD’s data center business expanded from 25 percent to 34 percent, with operating income surging 168 percent to $2.88 billion. Embedded segment revenue, or all the SoCs , FPGAs , and boards under AMD’s umbrella that go into other hardware, was $1.1 billion, up 29 percent. There are semi-custom processors that AMD supplies to other manufacturers’ consoles, as well as its own Radeon graphics business. Where things can get confusing is that Ryzen processors, like those commonly installed in gaming PCs, are counted under the company’s client business, not gaming. According to AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su , “In Gaming, revenue declined 40% year over year to $773 million, primarily due to lower semi-custom sales as expected at this stage of the console cycle.” The financial results do not break down the split between console chip sales and PC graphics cards. sources.title: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters
passages: AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company’s gaming segment cratered.
AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs .
AMD CFO Jean Hu said, “We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%.
As reported by Tom’s Hardware , Intel’s Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion.
That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel’s revenue for the first time in history.
The gaming segment of AMD’s business is composed of two main sources.
There are semi-custom processors that AMD supplies to other manufacturers’ consoles, as well as its own Radeon graphics business.
Embedded segment revenue, or all the SoCs , FPGAs , and boards under AMD’s umbrella that go into other hardware, was $1.1 billion, up 29 percent.
AMD attributed this growth to gains made in the “aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial end markets.”

AMD also announced that Windows-based systems running on its Ryzen AI Halo platform will be “coming soon.” Known as Project Zenith , the effort will support a developer-focused Windows experience on the current PRO 400 Series platform .

On the call, Su stated that AMD “started shipping MI455X in volume in the quarter, and lead customers, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle, brought their first Helios racks online quickly.”
The new AMD Threadripper Halo Station , which AMD first showed at IFA in September , pairs a Threadripper 9995WX CPU with up to four Instinct MI350P GPUs and can run trillion-parameter LLMs locally.
The system is slated for a release sometime in 2027, with pricing still to be announced.

story.title: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters

facts.text: On Tuesday, AMD reported its financial results for the first quarter of 2026.

Driven by record demand for AMD's EPYC server processors, Ryzen CPUs, and Instinct accelerators, the company's revenue totaled $10.253 billion, slightly down quarter-over-quarter (QoQ), but up significantly year-over-year (YoY).
Furthermore, AMD raised its long-term outlook for the server CPU market, expecting it to reach $120 billion by 2030 due to increased demand from AI and agentic AI workloads.
At the same time, the company admitted that sales of its AI accelerators were down sequentially.
Looking ahead, we expect server growth to accelerate meaningfully as we scale supply to meet demand."
AMD said server CPU sales increased more than 50% from the same quarter last year, with both cloud and enterprise demand growing over 50%.
AMD warned that both client and gaming revenue in the second half of the year would decline by more than 20% compared to the first half because of higher memory and component costs.
"In response to this demand, we are working closely with our supply chain partners to meaningfully increase our wafer and back-end capacity to support this growth," Su said.
Client revenue alone reached $2.9 billion, up 26%, driven by strong Ryzen processor demand and commercial PC share gains.
Gaming revenue rose 11% to $720 million due to stronger Radeon GPU demand.

"[Q2 results will be ]driven by a very strong growth in our data center segment, [modest] growth in our client and the gaming segment, and a double-digit growth in our embedded segment," said Jean Hu, AMD executive vice president, CFO and treasurer.
The business unit generated $338 million operating income, up from $328 million a year ago.
AMD projects Q2 2026 revenue to reach about $11.2 billion ± $300 million.
The company also expects non-GAAP gross margin to be around 56%.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.

That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel’s revenue for the first time in history.

extraction.body: After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers. In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear. "National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future." In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!" According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress. Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%. Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers. South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline." In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C." Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers." Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said. Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign. "When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight." Riley Wealth."The hyperscalers already have data centers, so those assets are more valuable now because there's not going to be an overbuild of data centers. That far outstrips smaller AI cloud rivals such as CoreWeave and Nebius.Shares of smaller players including Applied Digital and Iren plunged between 6% and 13% on fears that curbs on data-center construction could derail their debt-fueled expansion plans. extraction.body: After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers. In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear. "National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future." In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!" According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress. Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%. Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers. South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline." In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C." Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers." Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said. Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign. "When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight."
