extraction.body: TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — A gunman plowed a car into a courtyard on Citibank’s sprawling Tampa business campus on Wednesday and opened fire with a rifle, killing a woman before a security guard fatally shot him, authorities said. The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office did not give a motive for the shooting or say whether the gunman and his lone victim knew each other. The attack sent workers scrambling as the suspect crashed his car among outdoor tables where people were eating lunch, then started shooting, said Chief Deputy Frank Losat of the sheriff’s office. He said 3,200 people were on the campus at work during the attack. The gunman fatally shot the woman before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria, Losat said. The guard and the gunman exchanged fire, and the guard killed him, Losat said. “Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely,” Losat told a news conference. ”So kudos to that security guard.” The names of the gunman and the woman killed were not immediately released. Losat said four other people were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. He didn’t know whether any of them had been shot or struck by the gunman’s vehicle. The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant’s employees. David Dzien, a Citibank vice president, told The Associated Press he was returning to work after lunch when he saw the shooter’s sedan crash through a fence about 150 yards (137 meters) away from him, followed by an “incredible clatter” that he later realized was gunfire. People near the crashed car suddenly dispersed and others began to scream, Dzien said, as he sprinted back into the building and evacuated through a fire escape. “I can still hear the particular type of scream,” he said, “and I’m still trying to process it, frankly.” The attack occurred on a day when “VIPs” who don’t normally work at the complex were present for a “quarterly review,” Dzien said. Sheriff’s deputies began arriving at the campus within a minute of the first 911 call, Losat said. The response was huge, with more than 360 deputies — many in tactical gear — rushing to the scene. Those deputies spent 2 1/2 hours searching and clearing the building where the shootings occurred plus adjacent office buildings, Losat said. Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from responding officers described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search as people were found sheltering in locked rooms and closets, then carefully escorted from the buildings and parking garage. Citigroup said in a statement that it was “aware of an incident” at the complex and was cooperating with authorities. Employees at the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel, a few hundred feet from the Citibank complex, were having a monthly employee luncheon in the hotel’s ballroom when they saw a massive flood of police vehicles headed toward the campus. General Manager Matt Chauvin said Citibank employees ran over and told the front desk there was an active shooter. “We at first locked the doors and, you know, went into lockdown, but the employees kept coming over,” Chauvin said. Chauvin estimated the hotel sheltered about 300 Citibank workers. Hotel staff gave them water and lunch, and let some go into hotel rooms “to sort of decompress or make phone calls.” “Luckily we were far enough away that they were all safe,” he said. Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. AP journalists Cybele Mayes-Osterman in Chicago, R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this story. extraction.body: HILLSBOROUGH COUNTY, Fla. — Sheriff Chad Chronister said the Citibank security guard who shot an armed suspect Wednesday was a hero . During a news conference Thursday afternoon, the sheriff provided more details about the incident in which the suspect and a woman were killed. It happened just after noon at the Citibank complex near Interstate 75 and Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Boulevard in Brandon. “Our suspect took one life, and that’s one life too many,” Chronister said, stating that the suspect was carrying 90 rounds of ammunition. The suspect was identified as Jacob Pearson, 35, of Orlando. He was married with a 7-year-old child. Pearson, who didn’t have a previous criminal record, according to Chronister, died at a local hospital. The woman who was killed was identified as Leanne Selman, 41, of Palm Harbor. She worked at Citibank for nine years. Chronister said the security guard’s name is John Fraley. Four people suffered non-life-threatening injuries. Chronister said that some of those injuries likely happened while they were running away from the scene. The sheriff said that at about 9 a.m. Wednesday, Pearson contacted an attorneys' office that is contracted by Citibank for collection. The suspect was angry about a summons over a $2,500 payment. Chronister said the man said, "unless you want me to go over there with my AR-15," to cancel the case. The attorneys' office then contacted security at Citibank. The Orlando Police Department went to Pearson's home to do a welfare check, Chronister said, but he was not there. Chronister said the suspect's wife has been cooperating with investigators. A Citibank employee speaking at Thursday's news conference said resources are being offered to employees struggling in the aftermath of the shooting. He said the company is grateful for its security team and local law enforcement. The sheriff's office showed video from the scene during Thursday's news conference. From the sky, a gray sedan that broke through a fence can be seen making its way into one of the campus' courtyards. The car was just the first tool law enforcement said the shooter used before he fatally shot Leanne Selman. It's a tactic that Rob Chadwick, former FBI active shooter response trainer, said is a trend. "We've seen a significant uptick in what I'll call vehicle-borne attacks or initiated by a vehicle that are designed to defeat that outer layer," he said. When the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office got on campus, deputies found the shooter had been shot by the security guard. Bodycam footage shows deputies arriving, searching and directing workers. "I believe textbook response, at least the body cameras that I reviewed," Chadwick said. "Obviously, you know, (it) just happened. And their response was absolutely in keeping with the training that, you know, we have been putting out for years now." Chadwick said that the deputies are there to save, protect and stay vigilant. "One of the things that the officers are trained to look for is potentially an accomplice or the shooter, him or herself, trying to escape," he said. "You know, in the crowd, so to speak. We saw that at Marjory Stoneman Douglas." More than 360 officers were at the scene, working with more than 3,000 employees at the campus. Chadwick said he thought the workers made the response easier. "People understand that run, hide, fight type of mentality. They also understand, you know, that just because the police have now arrived, it's not over," he said.

extraction.body: An armed security guard was hailed as a hero by authorities Wednesday after engaging a gunman who drove onto the busy Citibank Center property in Tampa, Florida, fatally shot a woman, and then opened fire inside the building's cafeteria. The suspect crashed into an outdoor seating area where multiple people were eating lunch just after 12 p.m. upon driving through a fence at the Sabal Park Office Development, Frank Losat, a chief deputy with the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office, told reporters at the scene. The gunman then got out of his vehicle with a rifle and fatally shot a woman. An armed security guard employed by Citibank shot the suspect inside a nearby building's cafeteria during a gunfire exchange, authorities said. The gunman was taken to Tampa General Hospital where he later died. "The security guard that's employed by Citibank stopped the threat," Losat said. So kudos to that security guard and the people they employ." Four people were also treated at a local hospital for injuries that were not life-threatening. It is unclear where the victims were wounded during the incident. SHOOTING AFTER MAGIC CITY CLASSIC IN ALABAMA LEAVES 1 DEAD, 8 INJURED Officials said deputies with the sheriff's office responded to the scene within minutes of the reported shooting. At the time the chaotic scene broke out, there were 3,200 Citibank employees on the property, Losat said. "With that being said, with that many witnesses… we will be doing interviews well into the night," Losat said. Our crime scene will be processing the scene, which will take several hours, if not until tomorrow." Losat did not release the name of the suspected gunman or the victim, pending notification to the next of kin. Authorities have cleared the Citibank property. FLORIDA A&M UNIVERSITY SHOOTING LEAVES 12 INJURED, INCLUDING 6 CHILDREN, NEAR FOOTBALL STADIUM Nearby Hillsborough College encouraged students and staff to shelter in place at the time of the incident. The scene showed adults with children moving away from the business campus, which has a daycare center, affiliate FOX 13 Tampa Bay reported. "We are aware of an incident impacting our site in Tampa, Florida and are coordinating with law enforcement," Citibank said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Citibank employees were asked to meet at the triage area in the parking lot of the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel. Families of employees were instructed to meet at the reunification site at Staybridge Suites Tampa East. "The low-rise campus is surrounded by lushly landscaped berms with outdoor plazas, fountains, and waterfalls to provide a secluded, tranquil environment," the website states. "Each building is interconnected by enclosed walkways to ensure personnel comfort and building security as well as provide a homogenous atmosphere among the individual buildings and associated staff." This is a developing story.

extraction.body: TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — A gunman plowed a car into a courtyard on Citibank’s sprawling Tampa business campus on Wednesday and opened fire with a rifle, killing a woman before a security guard fatally shot him, authorities said. The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office did not give a motive for the shooting or say whether the gunman and his lone victim knew each other. The attack sent workers scrambling as the suspect crashed his car among outdoor tables where people were eating lunch, then started shooting, said Chief Deputy Frank Losat of the sheriff’s office. He said 3,200 people were on the campus at work during the attack. The gunman fatally shot the woman before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria, Losat said. The guard and the gunman exchanged fire, and the guard killed him, Losat said. “Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely,” Losat told a news conference. ”So kudos to that security guard.” The names of the gunman and the woman killed were not immediately released. Losat said four other people were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. He didn’t know whether any of them had been shot or struck by the gunman’s vehicle. The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant’s employees. David Dzien, a Citibank vice president, told The Associated Press he was returning to work after lunch when he saw the shooter’s sedan crash through a fence about 150 yards (137 meters) away from him, followed by an “incredible clatter” that he later realized was gunfire. People near the crashed car suddenly dispersed and others began to scream, Dzien said, as he sprinted back into the building and evacuated through a fire escape. “I can still hear the particular type of scream,” he said, “and I’m still trying to process it, frankly.” The attack occurred on a day when “VIPs” who don’t normally work at the complex were present for a “quarterly review,” Dzien said. Sheriff’s deputies began arriving at the campus within a minute of the first 911 call, Losat said. The response was huge, with more than 360 deputies — many in tactical gear — rushing to the scene. Those deputies spent 2 1/2 hours searching and clearing the building where the shootings occurred plus adjacent office buildings, Losat said. Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from responding officers described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search as people were found sheltering in locked rooms and closets, then carefully escorted from the buildings and parking garage. Citigroup said in a statement that it was “aware of an incident” at the complex and was cooperating with authorities. Employees at the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel, a few hundred feet from the Citibank complex, were having a monthly employee luncheon in the hotel’s ballroom when they saw a massive flood of police vehicles headed toward the campus. General Manager Matt Chauvin said Citibank employees ran over and told the front desk there was an active shooter. “We at first locked the doors and, you know, went into lockdown, but the employees kept coming over,” Chauvin said. Chauvin estimated the hotel sheltered about 300 Citibank workers. Hotel staff gave them water and lunch, and let some go into hotel rooms “to sort of decompress or make phone calls.” “Luckily we were far enough away that they were all safe,” he said. Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. AP journalists Cybele Mayes-Osterman in Chicago, R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this story. extraction.body: HILLSBOROUGH COUNTY, Fla. — Sheriff Chad Chronister said the Citibank security guard who shot an armed suspect Wednesday was a hero . During a news conference Thursday afternoon, the sheriff provided more details about the incident in which the suspect and a woman were killed. It happened just after noon at the Citibank complex near Interstate 75 and Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Boulevard in Brandon. “Our suspect took one life, and that’s one life too many,” Chronister said, stating that the suspect was carrying 90 rounds of ammunition. The suspect was identified as Jacob Pearson, 35, of Orlando. He was married with a 7-year-old child. Pearson, who didn’t have a previous criminal record, according to Chronister, died at a local hospital. The woman who was killed was identified as Leanne Selman, 41, of Palm Harbor. She worked at Citibank for nine years. Chronister said the security guard’s name is John Fraley. Four people suffered non-life-threatening injuries. Chronister said that some of those injuries likely happened while they were running away from the scene. The sheriff said that at about 9 a.m. Wednesday, Pearson contacted an attorneys' office that is contracted by Citibank for collection. The suspect was angry about a summons over a $2,500 payment. Chronister said the man said, "unless you want me to go over there with my AR-15," to cancel the case. The attorneys' office then contacted security at Citibank. The Orlando Police Department went to Pearson's home to do a welfare check, Chronister said, but he was not there. Chronister said the suspect's wife has been cooperating with investigators. sources.title: Meta warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder
passages: Speaking at the WSJ Tech conference on Wednesday, the Meta exec pointed out that the backlash against data centers — which was very much on the ballot during this election season — was also tied to people’s feelings about AI technology overall.

Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that the Democratic wins in the midterm elections are going to make it a lot harder for companies to build data centers, adding that the industry has “not done as good a job as we needed to explain the benefits of these investments.”
Today, the company has data centers in 23 states, she said, and five of them, including one in Texas, are planned as projects of 1 gigawatt or more.
Meta has pinned its hopes on its AI investments, particularly its consumer AI agent Muse scaling far beyond the 10 million users it has today, to become a business that one day serves billions.
Specifically, communities only want data centers when it benefits them in some way, she explained, laying out the approach that Meta today uses to close its data center deals in local communities.

Successful projects see Meta paying for its own electricity, directing any tax surpluses as a result of the data centers toward teachers and first responders, keeping the labor force local, and getting bipartisan support for the project, among other things.
But Meta is now worried that it could lose some of its investments after politicians ran on anti-data-center platforms during the midterms.
Going forward, she expects data center projects to come under more review and be weighed against whether the constituents actually want them.

sources.title: Meta Warns Election Backlash Could Derail AI Buildout
passages: Meta's warning about election backlash threatening data center expansion marks a pivotal moment for the AI industry.
Meta is sounding the alarm that mounting political opposition to data center construction could seriously hamper its AI ambitions.
The data center backlash also highlights a broader tension in AI development.

For Meta and its rivals, the path forward likely requires not just more capital, but better community engagement and potentially a fundamental rethinking of data center design to address power and water concerns.

extraction.body: Meta is sounding the alarm that mounting political opposition to data center construction could seriously hamper its AI ambitions. The warning comes as communities across the country push back against massive infrastructure projects that demand enormous amounts of power and water. With AI rivals racing to expand computing capacity, Meta's caution signals a potential infrastructure bottleneck that could reshape the entire industry's growth trajectory. Meta just threw cold water on the AI infrastructure boom. The social media giant is warning investors and policymakers that rising political opposition to data center construction could make it harder to execute the massive buildout needed to compete in artificial intelligence. It's a striking admission from a company that's been racing to catch OpenAI and Google in the AI arms race. Meta's warning lands just as the dust settles from the 2026 midterm elections, where voters across multiple states rejected data center projects in what amounted to a stunning rebuke of AI infrastructure expansion. For Meta, the political headwinds couldn't come at a worse time. The company just announced plans for a $25 billion bond sale specifically to fund AI infrastructure spending, one of the largest debt raises in tech history. That capital is earmarked for data centers packed with Nvidia GPUs and custom chips designed to train and run increasingly sophisticated AI models. The backlash reflects a growing disconnect between Silicon Valley's AI ambitions and the communities expected to host the infrastructure. Modern AI data centers can consume as much electricity as a small city, with some facilities requiring 100 megawatts or more of continuous power. In drought-prone regions, that's become a political lightning rod. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have all encountered local resistance to data center projects over the past year. But Meta's public warning suggests the company sees this as more than a temporary speed bump. It's a structural challenge that could fundamentally limit how fast any company can scale AI infrastructure in the United States. The political opposition also threatens to widen the gap between AI leaders and challengers. OpenAI, which got an earlier start on infrastructure deals, may find itself with a built-in advantage if new projects face years of regulatory delays and community battles. Meanwhile, Meta has been pouring resources into AI development, recently rolling out conversational voice features and animated avatars to its Muse app as it tries to compete with ChatGPT. The infrastructure crunch is already reshaping investment patterns. NextDC, an Australian data center operator, saw its stock soar 43% after Goodman and Digital Realty bought stakes, partly because international locations face less political resistance than U.S. sites. Some analysts now expect tech giants to shift more infrastructure spending overseas, potentially giving foreign competitors better access to cutting-edge AI capabilities. For Meta, the stakes extend beyond infrastructure. The company has been betting heavily that AI will drive its next wave of growth, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg positioning the company as a leader in open-source AI models and consumer AI products. Meta's AI-powered ad engine has already widened its revenue growth gap over Google Search to a five-year high, demonstrating real business impact from AI investments. But sustaining that advantage requires continuous infrastructure expansion. Training each new generation of AI models demands exponentially more computing power, and Meta can't afford to fall behind competitors in the race to build bigger, more capable systems. The company's warning suggests it sees real risk that political opposition could force it to slow down just as the AI competition heats up. The data center backlash also highlights a broader tension in AI development. While tech executives tout AI's potential to transform industries and boost productivity, local communities are left dealing with the immediate costs - higher electricity rates, strained water supplies, and increased truck traffic. Until the industry figures out how to share AI's benefits more broadly, expect political opposition to keep growing. Meta's warning about election backlash threatening data center expansion marks a pivotal moment for the AI industry. What started as a few local skirmishes over individual projects has evolved into a systemic political challenge that could reshape where and how fast AI infrastructure gets built. For Meta and its rivals, the path forward likely requires not just more capital, but better community engagement and potentially a fundamental rethinking of data center design to address power and water concerns. The companies that crack that puzzle will have a serious advantage in the AI race ahead.

extraction.body: Meta is sounding the alarm that mounting political opposition to data center construction could seriously hamper its AI ambitions. The warning comes as communities across the country push back against massive infrastructure projects that demand enormous amounts of power and water. With AI rivals racing to expand computing capacity, Meta's caution signals a potential infrastructure bottleneck that could reshape the entire industry's growth trajectory. Meta just threw cold water on the AI infrastructure boom. The social media giant is warning investors and policymakers that rising political opposition to data center construction could make it harder to execute the massive buildout needed to compete in artificial intelligence. It's a striking admission from a company that's been racing to catch OpenAI and Google in the AI arms race. Meta's warning lands just as the dust settles from the 2026 midterm elections, where voters across multiple states rejected data center projects in what amounted to a stunning rebuke of AI infrastructure expansion. For Meta, the political headwinds couldn't come at a worse time. The company just announced plans for a $25 billion bond sale specifically to fund AI infrastructure spending, one of the largest debt raises in tech history. That capital is earmarked for data centers packed with Nvidia GPUs and custom chips designed to train and run increasingly sophisticated AI models. The backlash reflects a growing disconnect between Silicon Valley's AI ambitions and the communities expected to host the infrastructure. Modern AI data centers can consume as much electricity as a small city, with some facilities requiring 100 megawatts or more of continuous power. In drought-prone regions, that's become a political lightning rod. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have all encountered local resistance to data center projects over the past year. But Meta's public warning suggests the company sees this as more than a temporary speed bump. It's a structural challenge that could fundamentally limit how fast any company can scale AI infrastructure in the United States. The political opposition also threatens to widen the gap between AI leaders and challengers. OpenAI, which got an earlier start on infrastructure deals, may find itself with a built-in advantage if new projects face years of regulatory delays and community battles. Meanwhile, Meta has been pouring resources into AI development, recently rolling out conversational voice features and animated avatars to its Muse app as it tries to compete with ChatGPT. The infrastructure crunch is already reshaping investment patterns. NextDC, an Australian data center operator, saw its stock soar 43% after Goodman and Digital Realty bought stakes, partly because international locations face less political resistance than U.S. sites. Some analysts now expect tech giants to shift more infrastructure spending overseas, potentially giving foreign competitors better access to cutting-edge AI capabilities. For Meta, the stakes extend beyond infrastructure. The company has been betting heavily that AI will drive its next wave of growth, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg positioning the company as a leader in open-source AI models and consumer AI products. Meta's AI-powered ad engine has already widened its revenue growth gap over Google Search to a five-year high, demonstrating real business impact from AI investments. But sustaining that advantage requires continuous infrastructure expansion. Training each new generation of AI models demands exponentially more computing power, and Meta can't afford to fall behind competitors in the race to build bigger, more capable systems. The company's warning suggests it sees real risk that political opposition could force it to slow down just as the AI competition heats up. The data center backlash also highlights a broader tension in AI development. While tech executives tout AI's potential to transform industries and boost productivity, local communities are left dealing with the immediate costs - higher electricity rates, strained water supplies, and increased truck traffic. Until the industry figures out how to share AI's benefits more broadly, expect political opposition to keep growing. Meta's warning about election backlash threatening data center expansion marks a pivotal moment for the AI industry. What started as a few local skirmishes over individual projects has evolved into a systemic political challenge that could reshape where and how fast AI infrastructure gets built. For Meta and its rivals, the path forward likely requires not just more capital, but better community engagement and potentially a fundamental rethinking of data center design to address power and water concerns. The companies that crack that puzzle will have a serious advantage in the AI race ahead.

sources.title: Nothing says it is making an 'AI-first' device to help artificial intelligence have its iPhone moment - The Independent
passages: Consumer tech brand Nothing, best known for its transparent phones, says that it is about to release an “ AI -first” device.

But Nothing’s chief executive, Carl Pei, suggested that many of those companies and commentators are confused about how exactly such devices will break into the mainstream, and have their “ iPhone moment”.

AI is “the most important technology of our lifetime, and the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life,” Mr Pei wrote in a long post on X .
He noted that the original iPhone moment only arrived after 30 years of work on mobile devices, which began with “pagers on doctors' belts and finished with a supercomputer in every pocket”.
He suggested that Nothing is in a “rare position” to make such a device, because of the fact that it builds its devices from end to end and is already trusted by tens of millions of users.
He did not say exactly what form Nothing’s device would take.
But it has “no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app”, and will ship from next month, he said.
It will be the latest company to try and harness the excitement about artificial intelligence by building a new device around it.
The long post appeared to be a shot at some other companies that have tried to pitch their devices as iPhone killers, and a way of running their entire lives.

That has already ended in failure for many of the products that have actually launched, such as Humane’s AI Pin, which was heralded as the first post-iPhone device at its launch but led to the collapse of the company who made it last year .

story.title: Nothing says it is making an 'AI-first' device to help artificial intelligence have its iPhone moment - The Independent

facts.text: Consumer tech brand Nothing, best known for its transparent phones, says that it is about to release an “ AI -first” device.

But Nothing’s chief executive, Carl Pei, suggested that many of those companies and commentators are confused about how exactly such devices will break into the mainstream, and have their “ iPhone moment”.

AI is “the most important technology of our lifetime, and the whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life,” Mr Pei wrote in a long post on X .
He noted that the original iPhone moment only arrived after 30 years of work on mobile devices, which began with “pagers on doctors' belts and finished with a supercomputer in every pocket”.
He suggested that Nothing is in a “rare position” to make such a device, because of the fact that it builds its devices from end to end and is already trusted by tens of millions of users.
He did not say exactly what form Nothing’s device would take.
But it has “no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app”, and will ship from next month, he said.
It will be the latest company to try and harness the excitement about artificial intelligence by building a new device around it.
The long post appeared to be a shot at some other companies that have tried to pitch their devices as iPhone killers, and a way of running their entire lives.

That has already ended in failure for many of the products that have actually launched, such as Humane’s AI Pin, which was heralded as the first post-iPhone device at its launch but led to the collapse of the company who made it last year .
Pei has teased an AI-first device for some time and the company has also said that it plans to release a pair of AI-linked smart glasses, as well as earbuds with AI integrations.
"The whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone's life," Pei wrote.

extraction.body: Researchers, alumni, faculty, and students in the fields of healthcare innovation, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence gathered on Oct. 29 for the 2026 Sikand Symposium at Cal State LA. With the theme of “ AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine ,” the symposium brought together speakers from Cal State LA, UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and the Sikand Foundation to share their expertise on how computational modeling and artificial intelligence can advance healthcare innovation. The keynote speaker for the symposium, Minjeong Jeon, a professor of advanced quantitative methods at the UCLA School of Education and Information Studies, kicked off the event with her presentation. Jeon discussed her research on measurement science and how network approaches can connect patients and symptoms more accurately. In layman’s terms, people with the same condition—depression, in the case of Jeon’s study—do not necessarily exhibit the same symptoms. Jeon’s proposed model and graphs aim to help researchers better understand the differing health cases of people who are dealing with medical conditions. Jeon also discussed the use of artificial intelligence models in these applications and precision medicine, but emphasized that “AI is only as clinically meaningful as the measurement system behind it.” She hopes student researchers “think about measurement” more precisely when they conduct studies in these fields and work with their data. Student researchers also showcased their collaborative projects during a poster session. One was a study that Cal State LA student researcher Brian Ta worked on, entitled “Can We Trust the Evidence Behind a Biomedical AI Decision?” In his presentation, Ta discussed the importance of understanding how AI can be used in biomedicine. He proposed methods to ensure AI systems have a multifactor authorization system in place to check who made the decisions, where the research came from, and whether that research is complete. Ta’s study recognizes the benefits of AI in this field, but also understands that responsible practices must be in place, especially when dealing with results that can affect medicine and people’s lives. Another project was a collaborative study by student researcher Hector Gardea. It was titled “Physical State Classifier for Closed-loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson’s Disease.” Conducted in collaboration with Duke University, the project focused on using wearable technology to track different levels of tremors in participants with Parkinson’s disease. Gardea discussed how an Apple Watch equipped with an accelerometer detects shaking motions and classifies them more accurately. extraction.body: Researchers, alumni, faculty, and students in the fields of healthcare innovation, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence gathered on Oct. 29 for the 2026 Sikand Symposium at Cal State LA. With the theme of “ AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine ,” the symposium brought together speakers from Cal State LA, UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and the Sikand Foundation to share their expertise on how computational modeling and artificial intelligence can advance healthcare innovation. The keynote speaker for the symposium, Minjeong Jeon, a professor of advanced quantitative methods at the UCLA School of Education and Information Studies, kicked off the event with her presentation. Jeon discussed her research on measurement science and how network approaches can connect patients and symptoms more accurately. In layman’s terms, people with the same condition—depression, in the case of Jeon’s study—do not necessarily exhibit the same symptoms. Jeon’s proposed model and graphs aim to help researchers better understand the differing health cases of people who are dealing with medical conditions. Jeon also discussed the use of artificial intelligence models in these applications and precision medicine, but emphasized that “AI is only as clinically meaningful as the measurement system behind it.” She hopes student researchers “think about measurement” more precisely when they conduct studies in these fields and work with their data. Student researchers also showcased their collaborative projects during a poster session. One was a study that Cal State LA student researcher Brian Ta worked on, entitled “Can We Trust the Evidence Behind a Biomedical AI Decision?” In his presentation, Ta discussed the importance of understanding how AI can be used in biomedicine. He proposed methods to ensure AI systems have a multifactor authorization system in place to check who made the decisions, where the research came from, and whether that research is complete. Ta’s study recognizes the benefits of AI in this field, but also understands that responsible practices must be in place, especially when dealing with results that can affect medicine and people’s lives. Another project was a collaborative study by student researcher Hector Gardea. It was titled “Physical State Classifier for Closed-loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson’s Disease.” Conducted in collaboration with Duke University, the project focused on using wearable technology to track different levels of tremors in participants with Parkinson’s disease. Gardea discussed how an Apple Watch equipped with an accelerometer detects shaking motions and classifies them more accurately. In addition, the symposium featured startup presentations from the LA BioStart training program at Cal State LA, along with research highlights and panels presented by faculty in the university’s College of Engineering, Computer Science, and Technology (ECST). Researchers presented studies on how machine learning can be used to track pollution or even in applications like detecting breast cancer. Participants also had the opportunity to take part in hands-on workshops and coding activities. The event was hosted by the Sikand Center for Sustainable and Intelligent Infrastructure (Sikand SITI Center), housed within Cal State LA’s College of ECST. extraction.body: Researchers, alumni, faculty, and students in the fields of healthcare innovation, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence gathered on Oct. 29 for the 2026 Sikand Symposium at Cal State LA. With the theme of “ AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine ,” the symposium brought together speakers from Cal State LA, UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and the Sikand Foundation to share their expertise on how computational modeling and artificial intelligence can advance healthcare innovation. The keynote speaker for the symposium, Minjeong Jeon, a professor of advanced quantitative methods at the UCLA School of Education and Information Studies, kicked off the event with her presentation. Jeon discussed her research on measurement science and how network approaches can connect patients and symptoms more accurately. In layman’s terms, people with the same condition—depression, in the case of Jeon’s study—do not necessarily exhibit the same symptoms. Jeon’s proposed model and graphs aim to help researchers better understand the differing health cases of people who are dealing with medical conditions. Jeon also discussed the use of artificial intelligence models in these applications and precision medicine, but emphasized that “AI is only as clinically meaningful as the measurement system behind it.” She hopes student researchers “think about measurement” more precisely when they conduct studies in these fields and work with their data. Student researchers also showcased their collaborative projects during a poster session. One was a study that Cal State LA student researcher Brian Ta worked on, entitled “Can We Trust the Evidence Behind a Biomedical AI Decision?” In his presentation, Ta discussed the importance of understanding how AI can be used in biomedicine. He proposed methods to ensure AI systems have a multifactor authorization system in place to check who made the decisions, where the research came from, and whether that research is complete. Ta’s study recognizes the benefits of AI in this field, but also understands that responsible practices must be in place, especially when dealing with results that can affect medicine and people’s lives. Another project was a collaborative study by student researcher Hector Gardea. It was titled “Physical State Classifier for Closed-loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson’s Disease.” Conducted in collaboration with Duke University, the project focused on using wearable technology to track different levels of tremors in participants with Parkinson’s disease. Gardea discussed how an Apple Watch equipped with an accelerometer detects shaking motions and classifies them more accurately. In addition, the symposium featured startup presentations from the LA BioStart training program at Cal State LA, along with research highlights and panels presented by faculty in the university’s College of Engineering, Computer Science, and Technology (ECST). Researchers presented studies on how machine learning can be used to track pollution or even in applications like detecting breast cancer. Participants also had the opportunity to take part in hands-on workshops and coding activities. extraction.body: Researchers, alumni, faculty, and students in the fields of healthcare innovation, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence gathered on Oct. 29 for the 2026 Sikand Symposium at Cal State LA. With the theme of “ AI and Sustainable Healthcare Systems: Intelligent Infrastructure and Precision Medicine ,” the symposium brought together speakers from Cal State LA, UCLA, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, and the Sikand Foundation to share their expertise on how computational modeling and artificial intelligence can advance healthcare innovation. The keynote speaker for the symposium, Minjeong Jeon, a professor of advanced quantitative methods at the UCLA School of Education and Information Studies, kicked off the event with her presentation. Jeon discussed her research on measurement science and how network approaches can connect patients and symptoms more accurately. In layman’s terms, people with the same condition—depression, in the case of Jeon’s study—do not necessarily exhibit the same symptoms. Jeon’s proposed model and graphs aim to help researchers better understand the differing health cases of people who are dealing with medical conditions. Jeon also discussed the use of artificial intelligence models in these applications and precision medicine, but emphasized that “AI is only as clinically meaningful as the measurement system behind it.” She hopes student researchers “think about measurement” more precisely when they conduct studies in these fields and work with their data. Student researchers also showcased their collaborative projects during a poster session. One was a study that Cal State LA student researcher Brian Ta worked on, entitled “Can We Trust the Evidence Behind a Biomedical AI Decision?” In his presentation, Ta discussed the importance of understanding how AI can be used in biomedicine. He proposed methods to ensure AI systems have a multifactor authorization system in place to check who made the decisions, where the research came from, and whether that research is complete. Ta’s study recognizes the benefits of AI in this field, but also understands that responsible practices must be in place, especially when dealing with results that can affect medicine and people’s lives. Another project was a collaborative study by student researcher Hector Gardea. It was titled “Physical State Classifier for Closed-loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson’s Disease.” Conducted in collaboration with Duke University, the project focused on using wearable technology to track different levels of tremors in participants with Parkinson’s disease. Gardea discussed how an Apple Watch equipped with an accelerometer detects shaking motions and classifies them more accurately. In addition, the symposium featured startup presentations from the LA BioStart training program at Cal State LA, along with research highlights and panels presented by faculty in the university’s College of Engineering, Computer Science, and Technology (ECST). Researchers presented studies on how machine learning can be used to track pollution or even in applications like detecting breast cancer. Participants also had the opportunity to take part in hands-on workshops and coding activities. Jeon also discussed the use of artificial intelligence models in these applications and precision medicine, but emphasized that “AI is only as clinically meaningful as the measurement system behind it.” She hopes student researchers “think about measurement” more precisely when they conduct studies in these fields and work with their data.
Student researchers also showcased their collaborative projects during a poster session.
One was a study that Cal State LA student researcher Brian Ta worked on, entitled “Can We Trust the Evidence Behind a Biomedical AI Decision?”

In his presentation, Ta discussed the importance of understanding how AI can be used in biomedicine. He proposed methods to ensure AI systems have a multifactor authorization system in place to check who made the decisions, where the research came from, and whether that research is complete.

Ta’s study recognizes the benefits of AI in this field, but also understands that responsible practices must be in place, especially when dealing with results that can affect medicine and people’s lives.
Another project was a collaborative study by student researcher Hector Gardea. It was titled “Physical State Classifier for Closed-loop Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson’s Disease.”

Conducted in collaboration with Duke University, the project focused on using wearable technology to track different levels of tremors in participants with Parkinson’s disease. Gardea discussed how an Apple Watch equipped with an accelerometer detects shaking motions and classifies them more accurately.

In addition, the symposium featured startup presentations from the LA BioStart training program at Cal State LA, along with research highlights and panels presented by faculty in the university’s College of Engineering, Computer Science, and Technology (ECST). Researchers presented studies on how machine learning can be used to track pollution or even in applications like detecting breast cancer.
Participants also had the opportunity to take part in hands-on workshops and coding activities.

The event was hosted by the Sikand Center for Sustainable and Intelligent Infrastructure (Sikand SITI Center), housed within Cal State LA’s College of ECST. The center supports multidisciplinary research, education, and professional development focused on urban sustainability and its components.

The loss of smell (anosmia or hyposmia) is a major problem that affects around 20% of the global population. These include a wristband-type device that would allow users to carry it and lift it to the nose when they want to catch a whiff of a scent, and a necklace version where five odor channels align like pearls on a string, opening only after a signal is received.

extraction.body: Our sense of smell shapes how we navigate our environment, but it's a sensation that's notoriously difficult to recreate in the digital world. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed a device that uses an artificial intelligence e-nose to detect and analyze odors. Combined with a wearable release system called Scentronic, which uses machine learning algorithms to classify data in real time, the system passed the smell test in the lab by encouraging better interactions between humans and machines. This work combines innovations in hardware and software to bring new solutions to societal challenges. Our long-term goal here is to incorporate these systems into compact and personalized devices." Jinghua Li, senior author of the study and assistant professor of materials science and engineering, The Ohio State University Used in everything from medical research to online game entertainment, human-to-machine interfaces serve as digital conduits that connect people across incredible distances. Yet the majority of these systems focus on biophysical signals, such as haptic (touch-related), audio and visual cues, rather than smell, a sense critical for perception, flavor and emotional experiences. However, this study establishes a framework for an accurate, hands-free controlled olfactory stimulation device. After being trained on five distinct food scents - coffee, beer, red wine, orange and chocolate cake - field testing revealed that participants could identify individual odors about 73% of the time, and paired scents about 71% of the time. The team also found that even when Scentronic was used in tandem with interfaces that could generate taste, their results demonstrated the feasibility of programmable, cost-effective odor delivery systems to create engaging multisensory experiences, said Li. "We did see that some people are more sensitive to certain odorants than others," she said. "Despite being easy to distinguish, there was still lots of variation in intensity among individuals." The study was recently published in Science Advances. Despite being a prototype, Scentronic's design is so flexible that researchers created multiple versions to serve potential consumers. These include a wristband-type device that would allow users to carry it and lift it to the nose when they want to catch a whiff of a scent, and a necklace version where five odor channels align like pearls on a string, opening only after a signal is received. Although initially fitted with the user's comfort and functionality in mind, the ease with which these sensors were adapted to further demonstrations highlights the system's seamless ability to enhance extended reality experiences beyond mere sight and sound, said Li. Such versatility suggests Scentronic has many potential real-world applications, from supporting future assistive technologies and enhancing virtual training environments to becoming sensory aids in medical contexts, including as a way to reduce the need for frequent clinic visits, improve patient comfort and enable timely, personalized care, said Li. " The loss of olfaction is related to many neurological diseases and infections," she said. "As a result, it's important that we create technologies to first decouple the secrets within our olfactory systems and then try to reconstruct them based on that information. " Still, while it'll be a long time before the internet is fully scratch-and-sniff capable, next steps involve advancing the work by testing other ways to incorporate the team's devices into people's daily accessories, including wearable electronics like watches or other smart jewelry. "There are many potential opportunities for these technologies to shine," she said. "The initial demonstrations are promising, so digitized smells may arrive sooner than you think." Other Ohio State co-authors include Chunyu Yang, Qi Wang, Antonia Akoto-Yeboah, Shaoru Cheng, Billings Amoah, Yizhen Jia, Shulin Chen, Akhil Canumalla, Kai Zhao and Christopher Simons, as well as Chen Wang from Zhejiang Laboratory in China. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation, the Center for Brain Injury Recovery & Discovery Pilot Award at Ohio State, and the Ohio State Alumni Grant for Graduate Research and Scholarship. Dr. Laura Ajram leads the British Neuroscience Association, focusing on enhancing neuroscience research through strategic partnerships and patient engagement. Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: There is new hope for people who have lost their smell. Scientists have successfully tested a breakthrough device that lets people detect the presence of certain odors. This innovative system helps them "smell" again by translating odors into feelings (like touch) inside the nose. The loss of smell (anosmia or hyposmia) is a major problem that affects around 20% of the global population. It can be caused by a variety of factors, such as infections, medications, or injuries and may be permanent or temporary. Unlike hearing loss or vision impairment, where cochlear implants or prosthetics are available, there are no implants or devices that can restore the sense of smell. This new research may be a vital step toward developing a practical solution for more than a billion people. The team behind the device describes their work in a paper published in the journal Science Advances . They developed a system that captures odors using an artificial nose (e-nose) and translates that chemical information into a specific digital code. This code is then passed through an intranasal electrical stimulator (a small magnetic clip) placed on the septum, the wall separating the nostrils, to trigger the trigeminal nerve. Once triggered by an electrical pulse, individuals perceive the code as a distinct sensation. They're not actually smelling, rather, their brain is learning to associate this unique feeling with a specific odor so that they can tell different odors apart. The concept behind the technology is called sensory substitution, where one functional sense transmits information from a sense that is defective. The nasal cavity has two sensory systems, which are the olfactory system for smell and the trigeminal system for temperature, touch and irritation. In this research, the device leverages the trigeminal nerve to deliver information that the olfactory nerve can no longer transmit. "This substitution approach does not allow patients to smell real odors, it is a genuine first substitution solution that we could imagine offering to patients in the future," wrote the researchers in their paper. The study authors tested their innovation on 65 people (13 with normal smell and 52 with smell loss) across four experiments. All were able to detect odorant molecules, and most could distinguish between two distinct odors. The device also worked just as well for patients who couldn't smell as it did for healthy people, meaning the trigeminal system is a reliable pathway for transmitting coded signals for everyone. The work is still in the early stages. Among the next steps for the researchers will be to increase the number of odorants and stimulation patterns tested and to turn the lab prototype into a wearable, miniaturized device for everyday use. extraction.body: Our sense of smell shapes how we navigate our environment, but it's a sensation that's notoriously difficult to recreate in the digital world. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed a device that uses an artificial intelligence e-nose to detect and analyze odors. Combined with a wearable release system called Scentronic, which uses machine learning algorithms to classify data in real time, the system passed the smell test in the lab by encouraging better interactions between humans and machines. This work combines innovations in hardware and software to bring new solutions to societal challenges. Our long-term goal here is to incorporate these systems into compact and personalized devices." Jinghua Li, senior author of the study and assistant professor of materials science and engineering, The Ohio State University Used in everything from medical research to online game entertainment, human-to-machine interfaces serve as digital conduits that connect people across incredible distances. Yet the majority of these systems focus on biophysical signals, such as haptic (touch-related), audio and visual cues, rather than smell, a sense critical for perception, flavor and emotional experiences. However, this study establishes a framework for an accurate, hands-free controlled olfactory stimulation device. After being trained on five distinct food scents - coffee, beer, red wine, orange and chocolate cake - field testing revealed that participants could identify individual odors about 73% of the time, and paired scents about 71% of the time. The team also found that even when Scentronic was used in tandem with interfaces that could generate taste, their results demonstrated the feasibility of programmable, cost-effective odor delivery systems to create engaging multisensory experiences, said Li. "We did see that some people are more sensitive to certain odorants than others," she said. "Despite being easy to distinguish, there was still lots of variation in intensity among individuals." The study was recently published in Science Advances. Despite being a prototype, Scentronic's design is so flexible that researchers created multiple versions to serve potential consumers. These include a wristband-type device that would allow users to carry it and lift it to the nose when they want to catch a whiff of a scent, and a necklace version where five odor channels align like pearls on a string, opening only after a signal is received. Although initially fitted with the user's comfort and functionality in mind, the ease with which these sensors were adapted to further demonstrations highlights the system's seamless ability to enhance extended reality experiences beyond mere sight and sound, said Li. Such versatility suggests Scentronic has many potential real-world applications, from supporting future assistive technologies and enhancing virtual training environments to becoming sensory aids in medical contexts, including as a way to reduce the need for frequent clinic visits, improve patient comfort and enable timely, personalized care, said Li. " The loss of olfaction is related to many neurological diseases and infections," she said. "As a result, it's important that we create technologies to first decouple the secrets within our olfactory systems and then try to reconstruct them based on that information. " Still, while it'll be a long time before the internet is fully scratch-and-sniff capable, next steps involve advancing the work by testing other ways to incorporate the team's devices into people's daily accessories, including wearable electronics like watches or other smart jewelry. "There are many potential opportunities for these technologies to shine," she said. "The initial demonstrations are promising, so digitized smells may arrive sooner than you think." Other Ohio State co-authors include Chunyu Yang, Qi Wang, Antonia Akoto-Yeboah, Shaoru Cheng, Billings Amoah, Yizhen Jia, Shulin Chen, Akhil Canumalla, Kai Zhao and Christopher Simons, as well as Chen Wang from Zhejiang Laboratory in China. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation, the Center for Brain Injury Recovery & Discovery Pilot Award at Ohio State, and the Ohio State Alumni Grant for Graduate Research and Scholarship. passages: Nothing's first AI-native product is arriving next month, CEO Carl Pei confirmed this week.
The company teased the device with an image showing rounded corners and curved edges, but kept the actual product under wraps.
The company has been building toward this release since then, and the confirmation keeps that timeline intact.
For now, the key takeaways are simple: it launches next month, it has no screen, and it's not an app.
Everything else remains a mystery until Nothing decides to show its hand.
Pei explained that Nothing is well-positioned to build this product because the company designs both hardware and software in-house.
That vertical integration lets the team control the full user experience, something Pei argues is essential for AI-native devices.
Nothing has a track record of drip-feeding information through teasers, so the coming weeks will likely bring more hints about what the device actually does.
Nothing is also rumored to be working on AI-powered wearables, including smart glasses with and without cameras.
The company recently raised $200 million in Series C funding, which Pei said would go toward expanding its AI ambitions.
Nothing has also been pushing software updates across its phone lineup, including the stable Android 17 rollout for the Phone (4a), (4a) Pro, (3a), and (3a) Pro.
The teaser image offers only a glimpse of the device's silhouette.
Pei said the product will carry the "personality and care" associated with Nothing's existing lineup, which includes phones and earbuds.
ACME Inc. is hiring a senior software line specialist to close the gap between AI-native development and production code — a role that exists because some bugs are immune to prompting.
The article also touches on how AI is expected to evolve from a productivity tool into something that works more proactively for users.
Pei suggested that new technologies typically gain traction in the workplace before moving into homes, hinting at where Nothing sees this product fitting.

sources.title: Incoming Democratic majorities put AI giants on notice

extraction.body: The period of Republican-controlled Washington's hands-off approach to the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence is about to end. Midterm voters across the country elected Democratic candidates who campaigned on legislative guardrails for AI and passed dozens of state and local ballot measures limiting construction of new data centers. SSRS exit polling found 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their votes for Congress. During a post-election press conference Wednesday with Democratic House leadership, Rep. And that was a bad decision politically and a bad decision on policy. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails on AI," Lieu, the vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus, said. Lieu co-chairs a House Democratic commission on AI formed by Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries last year. He said he and his colleagues will release a document outlining policy priorities for the new Congress. Many of the Democratic candidates who defeated incumbent Republicans ran in part on ideas for broad AI regulation. Less than 48 hours after Election Day, OpenAI announced new commitments for its data centers, including covering energy costs and investing in jobs. Democrats will likely advance policies requiring OpenAI and other AI giants to go much further than what their voluntary safety and accountability standards entail. New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies," the company said in a statement. Though Democrats won sizeable House and Senate majorities, they're not quite large enough to override a presidential veto. President Donald Trump has been a vocal opponent of regulating AI – which he calls SI, short for "super intelligence" – and a champion of data centers, but voters' resounding rejection of Republican policies may push him to find room for compromise.

extraction.body: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot. In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month. Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything. “Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said. Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would. “What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy—which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.” The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs. In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself. “Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip—from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote. Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year. While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027. The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens. “Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added. extraction.body: Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot. In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month. Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything. “Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said. Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would. “What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy—which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.” The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs. In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself. “Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip—from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote. Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year. While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027. The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens. “Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added. extraction.body: Software optimizes a physical model of the telescope to reduce noise. With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet. While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star’s light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope’s configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets. Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function. There are two ways to figure out what the point spread function is. One is to use the telescope to image a known target and use those observations to derive a mathematical description of the point spread function. This is effective at reducing noise but has its limits, as the behavior of the telescope hardware can change over time, and the point spread function may vary with the wavelengths being imaged. The alternative is to try to model the hardware’s behavior and use that model to derive a point spread function. But modern telescopes are incredibly complicated instruments, with many, many factors feeding into their performance in ways that can be difficult to ascertain, even with the full engineering schematics. As a result, these models simply contain too many parameters that need to be tuned to make this route computationally tractable. But anyone paying attention to the world of AI developments will recognize that we’ve become quite successful at tuning billions of parameters in neural networks, in part through a mathematical technique called gradient descent. And, because this is central to training large neural networks, people have put a lot of work into optimizing the performance of gradient descent on GPUs. So a team of researchers has developed a process they’re calling FLIP (a non-acronym for Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets) that uses a physical model of the hardware (in this case, the NIRCam on the James Webb Space Telescope) with 10 6 possible parameters, and then uses software to optimize all its parameters. The optimization starts with a simulated point spread function, then uses gradient descent to optimize its performance on data from an actual star. Run on a current GPU, this process only takes a bit more than half an hour. The researchers then fine-tune the results on the actual scientific image they are analyzing. This last part of the process is critical, since some variables will differ between observations. To test how this works, the researchers used observations of two stars with known exoplanets (HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani), along with a third (TYC 5899) that doesn’t have any known exoplanets but is known to vary a lot between observations. These are young stars, and two of them have massive planets that are still warm from their gravitational collapse, allowing them to have been imaged previously. Using Webb data, the team used FLIP to boost the signal-to-noise ratio by a factor of 1.5 to 2, depending on the observations. At a wavelength that can be used to detect carbon dioxide, they were able to spot one of the planets in the Webb data for the first time. sources.title: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
passages: Schools are gaining the ability to block Google’s AI tools, even those in search, while keeping other Google apps.
So schools get more control, even if they don’t get the AI-free search everyone seems to want.
When schools choose which AI features to use under this new system, search will be one of the options.

Schools can leave search off if they want, but opting in will require them to choose the standard AI features or the new Guided Learning version, which won’t give away answers as readily (or so Google claims).
Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts.
The company clarified in a tweet that it will allow schools to disable Gemini apps while leaving search active for students.
Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools .
Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn’t want to use AI.
When Google revealed its new policy, the company’s VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times , which interpreted the situation as Google will “turn off search” if schools reject AI.
This has a nefarious vibe, but it’s probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google’s educational AI system will operate.
Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies.
Many will argue that Google should let schools access web search without chatbots.
However, that’s just not something Google wants to support at any level because it sees AI as the future of search.
While other search engines have settings to turn off AI tools, Google steadfastly refuses to create such a toggle (and those no-AI tricks you rely on may not work forever).
Ultimately, this is the core problem not just for education customers, but for everyone who wants to limit their exposure to AI while using Google.
However, the vagueness of Google’s blog post and public statements didn’t fully explain what it plans to do.
There are still reasons to dislike Google’s approach, but here’s how the company explains the process for schools:
This clarification does not change the calculus for educators who want to allow students to search the Internet without AI tools.
Google won’t offer that, and switching to another provider is easier said than done.
Google still has by far the most expansive index of the Internet, leaving alternatives with numerous gaps.
This could give other provides a chance to improve and offer a more viable alternative to Google.
Google is technically offering schools more choice but not the choices anyone wants.

Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn’t want to use AI. Google didn’t see the backlash coming, but now that it’s here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what’s changing. The gist of the new policy, according to Google’s blog post, is that schools using Google apps will have to opt into its AI products going forward. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts. This has a nefarious vibe, but it’s probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google’s educational AI system will operate. Google’s approach may not be entirely altruistic, but it technically offers schools more choice and control than they have now. Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies. The company clarified in a tweet that it will allow schools to disable Gemini apps while leaving search active for students. If they don’t want any AI, they can leave it all off. Essentially, Google is giving schools that want to completely block AI the ability to go all the way, even removing search from student accounts. A Google spokesperson tells Ars that the company has not made any changes to the new policy it announced this week.
